long.title: What If You Never Needed To Sleep Again?
long.rel: Single dad Rio and his seven-year-old daughter Lily (supporting: Dr. Ortiz, a tech startup founder).
long.rule: Every twenty-four hours Rio must take a ten-minute still, eyes-closed reset, or growing blackouts begin.
long.plant: Lily sticks a glow-in-the-dark ceiling star on Rio's hospital badge, right over the heart.
long.choice: Sign for the fortune and push through alone... or hand over the needle and close your eyes.
long.script: Three in the morning. The ambulance doors... bang open. One stretcher. Then four... then nine. A tour bus slid off the interstate in freezing rain, and every patient is coming to your ER. Rio! Dr. Ortiz is pointing at bed six. A teenage boy, pale and shaking. He needs an IV line, and his veins are tiny. You're the best in the building... at tiny veins. Your hands are steady. They're always steady. You haven't slept in a year. Not one... single... minute. But tonight, something is wrong. The edges of the room are flickering, like a bulb... about to die. Your phone buzzes in your pocket. It's the startup. 'Sign by four, or the offer is gone.' On your badge, right over your heart, there's a little plastic star. Your daughter stuck it there. You have maybe a minute before your brain switches off... on its own. Can you finish the line? Should you even try? But let's go back. Your name is Rio. You're a night shift nurse at a big city hospital. You're also a single dad. Your daughter, Lily, is seven. And until last spring, you were tired... all the time. The CDC says most adults need at least seven hours of sleep a night. That's about a third of your life... with your eyes closed. Live to seventy-five, and that's around twenty-five years asleep. Then one morning, you wake up... and you never need to sleep again. No yawning. No crash. No coffee. Most people fall apart... after one rough night. After twenty-four hours awake, your driving is about as impaired as... a blood alcohol level of point one zero. You? Three hundred sixty-five nights awake... and sharp as a scalpel. There's just one rule. Every twenty-four hours, you need ten minutes. Eyes closed. Perfectly still. It isn't sleep... it's a reset. Skip it, and the gaps begin. Tiny blackouts, a few seconds long. Skip it again... and the gaps grow. Ten minutes a day. That's the whole price. Easy, right? So what if you never needed to sleep again? Week one. You gain eight hours a day. That's fifty-six hours a week. More than a full-time job... for free. You finally fold the laundry mountain. You fix the leaky faucet... at two in the morning. You read a whole novel before sunrise. The raccoons in the alley start to recognize you. Upside: your shift ends at seven, and you're at the school gate by eight. Every... single... morning. Lily runs out with her backpack bouncing. You made it again, Daddy? Of course you did. You always make it now. Downside: your neighbors notice. Your kitchen light never turns off. Ever. One of them leaves a note on your door. 'Are you okay in there?' You're more than okay... you're unstoppable. At work, the change is bigger. Night nurses fight their own body clocks. Your brain has a tiny master clock called the suprachiasmatic nucleus. At three in the morning, it wants you asleep. Most of your coworkers hit a wall around then. You? You're the wall everyone leans on. Dr. Ortiz, the attending physician, watches you start your fourth IV in ten minutes. She narrows her eyes. Rio... when do you actually sleep? You smile. I'm a morning person. It's not exactly a lie. Then the money. You pick up extra shifts. Then... double shifts. Your overtime check is so big, payroll calls to make sure it's real. The problem? Something quiet disappears. Dreams. Most vivid dreaming happens during REM sleep. A normal night has four or five sleep cycles, each about ninety minutes long. That's a few dreams a night, every night of your life. You? Zero. One whole year. No dreams at all. You don't even notice... until Lily asks. What did you dream about, Daddy? You open your mouth. Nothing comes out. Then a coworker posts a video. 'This nurse worked eighty hours this week and still looks fresh.' Three million views. And that's when the startup calls. A founder in a gray hoodie flies you out to a glass office. His company runs software that watches hospital computer systems all night long. He wants one person who never sleeps to lead the whole night operation. Every night... forever. The salary has so many zeros... you count them twice. Think about it, Rio. You'd never worry about rent again. Just one condition. You start next week, and the nights are ours. Now zoom out. What if everyone woke up with your power? More than three hundred thirty million Americans, eight extra hours each. That's billions of extra waking hours... every night. Factories would never stop. Highways would never empty. And the coffee industry? Gone... overnight. Amazing. And a little terrifying. And there's a cost. Sleep isn't just rest... it's housekeeping. In 2013, neuroscientist Maiken Nedergaard and her team found something remarkable... in mice. During sleep, the spaces between brain cells widened, and fluid flushed through, washing away waste. One of those waste products? A sticky protein called beta-amyloid. It's linked to Alzheimer's disease. Scientists call this cleaning network the glymphatic system. Normal people run it every night. You? You run it in ten minutes flat. That's what your reset really is. A power wash. Skip it, and the trash piles up. So what happens when you start the startup's trial week... and skip it? Night one, you feel fine. Night two, you lose three seconds in the parking garage. Just... gone. You're standing at your car with your keys out. How did you get here? Night three, you blink at a red light... and the light is green. Horns blare behind you. Drowsy driving causes tens of thousands of crashes a year in America. You know that. You've treated those patients. You tell yourself it's fine. It's only a few seconds. What's a few seconds? Here's the thing nobody at the startup knows. Bedtime at your house is... sacred. Every night before your shift, you sit on the edge of Lily's bed. She hates bedtime. Bedtime means you leave. So she drags it out. One more story. One more glass of water. One more question. Who watches you while you're awake, Daddy? You tuck the blanket under her chin. Go to sleep, bug. Somebody has to stay awake. That's your line. You've said it... a hundred times. She sighs like a tiny grandma. Why does it always have to be you? You don't have an answer. One night, she peels a glow-in-the-dark star off her ceiling. She presses it onto your hospital badge, right over your heart. There. Now you can find your way to sleep. You laugh. Bug, I don't sleep. I know... she says. That's why you need it. You leave it there. The nurses tease you. You don't care. On the night of the bus crash, it's still there. Glowing faintly. And you've skipped your reset for three days. Back to three in the morning. Bed six. The boy's blood pressure is dropping. He needs fluids, and he needs them now. The vein you need is about as wide as a strand of spaghetti. You line up the needle. A quarter inch to go. Then the world flickers. Black. One second... two. You're back. The needle hasn't moved... this time. Your heart is pounding. That was a gap. A real one. In the middle of a stick. Your phone buzzes again. 'Three minutes left. Don't let us down.' Behind you, more stretchers roll in. Dr. Ortiz is juggling four patients at once. Rio, you got six? Do you? You could push through. You've pushed through a hundred nights. But the gaps are growing. Three seconds now. Next time, maybe five. In five seconds, a needle can go straight through a vein. In five seconds, a tired nurse can grab the wrong bag. The startup wants a man who never stops. Lily wants a man who comes home. And the boy in bed six just needs someone steady. Right now... that might not be you. You look down. The little star on your badge glows green in the dim light. Somebody has to stay awake. But does it have to be you? It all comes down to one choice. Sign for the fortune and push through alone... or hand over the needle and close your eyes. You hand over the needle. Dr. Ortiz, I need ten minutes. I'm not safe right now. She stares at you. Then she takes the needle without a word, and slides it in on the first try. Go. You step into a dark supply closet and sit on a box of gauze. You switch off the light. It's pitch black, except for one thing. The star. Lily's star. Glowing on your chest. You close your eyes. And for the first time in a year... you dream. It's short. It's silly. Lily is riding a giant raccoon down the hallway, laughing. Ten minutes later, you open your eyes. The flicker is gone. Your head is clear, like a window after rain. You walk back out. The boy in bed six is sitting up, sipping apple juice. Dr. Ortiz nods at you. Welcome back. At four, your phone buzzes one last time. 'Final offer.' You type back. 'No thanks. I have a bedtime.' The next week, Dr. Ortiz turns an empty office into a quiet room. Dim light. One recliner. A sign on the door. 'Ten minutes. No shame.' Nurses start taking turns. Even the surgeons sneak in. And at home, your reset has a new time. You take your ten minutes lying next to Lily, right at her bedtime. Her stars glow on the ceiling. Daddy? Are you dreaming? Yeah, bug. Somebody has to stay awake... just not always me. So is any of this real? Partly... No human has ever lived without sleep. In the winter of 1963 and 1964, a high school student named Randy Gardner stayed awake for about eleven days. By the end, he struggled with memory, focus and mood. Guinness World Records stopped accepting attempts like that, because they're too dangerous. There's also a very rare genetic disease called fatal familial insomnia. People slowly lose the ability to sleep. It's devastating, and it shows sleep isn't optional. But some people... do need less. In 2009, a team led by geneticist Ying-Hui Fu found a gene variant in a mother and daughter. They felt rested on about six hours a night. Not zero... six. And nature has tricks of its own. Dolphins can sleep with half their brain at a time, so the other half keeps them swimming and breathing. Could humans ever learn to rest half a brain at a time? Nobody knows... yet. And here's a mystery even sleep scientists still argue about. Why do we dream at all? Every night, your brain builds strange little movies... then deletes most of them by breakfast. Some researchers think dreams help sort memories. Others think they're practice for danger. So what are they really for? Keep that question in your pocket... So would you trade your sleep for eight extra hours a day? Would you take the fortune, or the bedtime? So, real or not? Drop your verdict in the comments, and pick the power we should test next. long.title: What If Your Eyes Could Zoom 100 Times?
long.rel: Grandpa Walt, a longtime ballpark usher who taught Rio baseball (supporting: scout Hank).
long.rule: The more Rio zooms, the smaller his field of view becomes, and long zooms leave a dark circle that fades slowly, with two minutes of zoom costing twenty minutes of rest.
long.plant: Grandpa Walt gives every little leaguer a bright orange wristband and teaches them to stand still and wave it if lost.
long.choice: Sign the deal of a lifetime... or let go of the zoom and trust Grandpa.
long.script: A pop fly rises into the lights. Eight thousand fans look up. You look up too... and you read the ball. Not the logo... the stitches. One of them is frayed. It'll come down about two feet behind the shortstop. Will it? It does. Beside you, a man squints at the scoreboard. Hey, what's the score? You don't look at the scoreboard. You look at the pitcher's glove, three hundred feet away, and count the specks of dirt. Four to two, home team. Also... his glove needs a new lace. In the parking lot, a little girl drops an earring in the gravel. You find it... from forty feet away. She stares at you. Are you a wizard? And at home, you don't need your glasses to read the fine print on a cereal box. Or your neighbor's grocery list... through two windows. Sorry, neighbor. You didn't mean to. But now you know... he buys a lot of pudding. Your name is Rio. You run the scoreboard at a minor league ballpark called Riverside Field. And three weeks ago... your eyes changed. Most people have what doctors call twenty-twenty vision. That just means you see at twenty feet what a typical healthy eye sees at twenty feet. Eagles are believed to see several times sharper than we do. You? You can zoom one hundred times. A batter's face at the far end of the field? Close enough... to count freckles. The moon, about two hundred thirty-nine thousand miles away? You see it like you're floating a couple thousand miles above it. But there's one rule. The more you zoom... the less you see. At one hundred times, your whole world shrinks to a tiny circle. Everything outside that circle goes dark. No edges. No warning. Just... nothing. So the stronger your eyes get... the blinder you become. What if your eyes could zoom one hundred times? Upside: you never miss a play. The pitcher's mound is sixty feet, six inches from home plate. A ninety mile per hour fastball crosses that gap in less than half a second. A batter has a blink to decide. You? You can see which way the seams are spinning... before it leaves the hand. A baseball has one hundred eight double stitches. You've counted... twice. Upside: the hot dog guy loves you. You can see which section is waving for him from across the stadium. He sells out by the fourth inning. He calls you... his radar. Downside: your eyes get tired... fast. Focusing on anything close uses a tiny ring of muscle inside your eye, called the ciliary muscle. Eye doctors suggest the twenty twenty twenty rule. Every twenty minutes, look at something twenty feet away for twenty seconds. You? You need twenty minutes of rest after every two minutes of zoom. Otherwise, the headaches hit like a fastball to the forehead. Downside: you see too much. Like what? A coach's text message. A player's sad face in the dugout. A couple breaking up in the upper deck. You didn't ask to see any of it. Is it spying... if you can't help it? Then things get bigger. A wildfire crew asks you to watch a ridge from a fire tower. You spot one wisp of smoke, nine miles out... before anyone else. Upside: the fire stays small. Then the local news finds out. What do they call you? The Human Telescope. The comments go wild. Then a man in a crisp windbreaker shows up at the ballpark. His name is Hank. He's a scout for a big league club. He watched you call a curveball from the scoreboard booth... just by reading the pitcher's grip. Hank leans on the railing. Kid... do you know what that's worth? Every team in baseball would pay for those eyes. You could find the next superstar in a high school game in Iowa. From the parking lot... with a hot dog. He slides a contract across the counter. The money is more than you make in ten years. One catch? It starts tonight. You'd sit in the visiting team's booth and zoom in on every pitcher. Then send notes to the big league office. Every inning. No breaks. So what's the problem? The problem is the circle. Here's how your eye really works. Only a tiny spot in the center of your retina, the fovea, sees sharp detail. Hold your thumb out at arm's length. Your sharpest vision covers about the size of your thumbnail. Everything else is your peripheral vision. Blurrier, but wide. That's what spots a car drifting into your lane, or a ball flying at your head. Your brain mixes both views into one smooth picture. When you zoom, you trade the wide view away. All of it. And the longer you zoom, the slower the dark circle fades after. Last week you zoomed for ten minutes straight. Afterward, you could only see the middle of the world for almost an hour. You walked straight into a vending machine. It did not... apologize. Hank wants you zoomed in for three hours a night. What happens to the circle then? Nobody knows... not even you. Your grandpa, Walt, taught you baseball in this ballpark. He was an usher here for thirty-one years. He still comes to every home game, in section one twelve. He always brings sunflower seeds... and never finishes them. When you were six, he put a glove on your hand and gave you one piece of advice. Don't watch the ball, Rio. Watch the whole field. Why? The ball tells you where it is. The field tells you where it's going. You've heard it a thousand times. Eyes up. See the whole field. Grandpa Walt still volunteers with the little league team. And he has a trick. Every kid gets a bright orange wristband. He tells them the same thing every season. If you ever get lost, don't run. Stand still, raise your arm, and wave your orange. Silly? Actually, it's smart. Searchers say a lost kid who stays in one place is much easier to find. Tonight, the little leaguers are here for Kids Night. All twelve of them. Twelve orange wristbands... waving at you from section one twelve. Grandpa Walt winks up at the booth. Proud of you, kiddo. Whatever you decide. But here's the thing. Grandpa's eyes aren't what they were. Lately he calls you after games. What did I miss out there, kiddo? Was it a good one? And you tell him. Every play. Every stitch. It's the best part of your night. The fifth inning starts. You're in Hank's booth. Contract on the desk. Pen in your hand. Then the sky flashes. Far off, over the river. You count. One, two, three, four, five... boom. Sound travels about a mile every five seconds. How close is it? About one mile. Lightning can strike up to about ten miles from a storm. That's why weather experts say, when thunder roars, go indoors. The announcer's voice cracks over the speakers. Folks, please move calmly to the concourse. Eight thousand people stand up at once. Rain slams down... like gravel. And your phone buzzes. It's Grandpa Walt. Rio, we're missing one. The smallest one, the boy with the big glasses. He went to the restroom and didn't come back. I can't see him. I can't see anything in this rain. You zoom. Hard. One hundred times. The world becomes a pinhole. You sweep the stands seat by seat. A soggy program. A lost flip flop. A crying stranger. Big glasses? Not him. There are eight thousand seats. Your circle covers maybe twenty at a time. Four hundred looks. Even at one second each? Almost seven minutes. And you get two... before the headache. Lightning flashes. Three seconds... closer. Your head pounds. The dark edges creep inward. You're losing it. Hank grabs your shoulder. Kid, sit down. Security handles lost kids. Sign the contract, or I'm on a plane at midnight and the deal is dead. Your eyes are almost enough. Almost... But your circle is too small, and the stadium is too big. It all comes down to one choice. Sign the deal of a lifetime... or let go of the zoom and trust Grandpa. You put down the pen. You close your eyes. You breathe. Watch the whole field. You let the zoom go. All of it. The dark circle melts away, slowly, like fog off the infield. And for the first time in weeks, you just... look. Normal eyes. Wide eyes. The whole stadium at once. Umbrellas. Ponchos. Flashing lights. And there, in the far corner, under the left field foul pole, is a tiny flicker of orange. Waving... and standing perfectly still. Just like Grandpa told him. You grab the microphone. Section one oh four, left field foul pole! There's a little guy in an orange wristband. Please stay with him! Two ushers run. Ten seconds later... they've got him. Grandpa Walt is already hobbling down the concourse as fast as his knees allow. He wraps the boy in a hug so big the kid disappears. By the time you get there, both of them are soaked and laughing. Hank finds you on the concourse. He doesn't look angry. He looks... impressed. You know what, kid? Most scouts spend their whole life staring at one guy. You just found one kid in eight thousand... with your regular eyes. He tucks the contract into his jacket. If you ever want to watch baseball for me, call. Daytime games. Short shifts. Breaks every twenty minutes. And no more nights in a booth. Deal? The next home game, the little leaguers present you with a gift. A bright orange wristband, signed by all twelve kids. The fans in section one twelve give you a standing ovation. You're blushing so hard... you could light the scoreboard. And after the game, you don't call Grandpa Walt. You sit next to him in section one twelve. He offers you sunflower seeds. You tell him every play. Every stitch. And for the first time, you don't zoom in once. Eyes up, Grandpa. See the whole field. He grins and squeezes your hand. Now you're getting it, kiddo. But here's what keeps you up at night. When your circle melts away, there's always a tiny shimmer in the middle. Like something drawn on the inside of your eye. A pattern... It looks almost like a map. And last night, when you looked straight at the moon... the shimmer pointed somewhere. Where is it trying to take you? So what would you do with eyes that zoom one hundred times? Would you take the booth, or the whole field? Tell us in the comments. And if you've ever had someone teach you to see the bigger picture, tell us who it was. Hit like, and subscribe to Rio Animation for more fascinating videos!

long.title: What If You Could Hear Every Heartbeat Nearby?
long.rel: Marcus, Rio's best friend and roommate since freshman year of college (supporting: TV producer Tess).
long.rule: Background noise shrinks Rio's hearing range from fifty feet in quiet to about ten on a loud street, and in a roar every heartbeat blurs together.
long.plant: Marcus drums the Stayin' Alive CPR beat whenever he is nervous, a habit from the free CPR class they took in college.
long.choice: Keep talking to the camera and become a star... or drop the microphone and ask strangers for silence.
long.script: The coffee shop on your corner is packed. The barista smiles and says she's fine. Her heart... says otherwise. It's racing at one hundred twenty beats a minute. You leave her a big tip and a note. 'Breathe. You've got this.' She looks at you like you... read her diary. On the subway platform, a man in a suit is pacing. His heartbeat is slow and steady. Calm as a lake. So why is he pacing? Oh... He's practicing a wedding proposal. Under his breath... to a pigeon. And back at your apartment, you don't need a baby monitor for your neighbor's newborn. You can hear her tiny heart through the wall. One hundred forty beats a minute... like a little drumroll. You also know your landlord is standing outside your door... before he knocks. Every time. He still hasn't figured out why you say come in... before his hand hits the wood. Your name is Rio. You're an audio technician in New York City. You fix microphones for a living. And last month, you started hearing the one sound nobody can hear... heartbeats. Every heartbeat nearby. A normal adult heart beats about sixty to one hundred times a minute at rest. That's roughly one hundred thousand beats a day. The sound comes from valves snapping shut. Lub... dub. Doctors need a stethoscope pressed against the chest to hear it clearly. You? You can hear it from fifty feet away. Through walls. Through winter coats... through a crowded train. But there's one rule. Noise... shrinks your range. In a quiet room, you hear fifty feet. On a loud street, maybe ten. And when the world gets really loud... every heartbeat melts into one big roar. So the moment you need it most... it disappears. So what if you could hear every heartbeat nearby? Upside: nobody can lie to you. Well... sort of. When people get nervous, their heart rate often jumps. Your coworker swears he didn't eat your leftover pizza. His heart goes from seventy to one hundred five. Case... closed. Downside: it's not a lie detector. A racing heart can mean fear, excitement, too much coffee, or just climbing the stairs. Even police polygraphs, which track heart rate and breathing, are famous for being unreliable. So when your boss's heartbeat jumps during your review... is she lying? Or did she just drink a triple espresso? You'll never... know. Upside: first dates get easier. Your date says she loves jazz. Her heart doesn't even flutter. You take her bowling instead. She has the best night of her year. Then it gets serious. On the train, you hear an old woman's heartbeat stumble. Skip. Skip... pause. You've read about this. It might be an irregular rhythm called atrial fibrillation. You gently ask if she's feeling okay. Is she? She isn't. You get her off at the next stop and call for help. The doctors say you caught it early. Amazing. And kind of... terrifying. Because now... you can't stop listening. The New York subway carries millions of riders a day. That's millions of heartbeats, every single morning. And here's the thing. You can't turn it off... ever. And there's a cost. Your ears are not just more sensitive to heartbeats. They're more sensitive to everything. Inside your inner ear, there are thousands of tiny hair cells. They bend when sound waves hit them. Loud sound bends them too hard, and in humans, those hair cells don't grow back. Hearing experts warn that long exposure to sound above eighty-five decibels can damage hearing. A screeching subway train can top one hundred. For normal ears, that's a risk. For your ears? It's... a hammer. After every rush hour, there's a faint ringing in your head. It's a little louder every week. That ringing has a name... tinnitus. And yours never fully fades now. How long until the heartbeats are gone... and only the ringing is left? Then Tess calls. Tess is a TV producer. She saw a video of you helping the old woman on the train. Two million views. Her voice is all business. Rio, I'm building a primetime medical show around you. You walk into a crowd. You hear a heart in trouble. You save a life. Every week... on camera. She names the salary. You sit down... on the floor. Your best friend Marcus is sitting on your couch, eating cereal out of a mixing bowl. You've known Marcus since your freshman year of college. You were roommates in a dorm the size of a closet. You took a free CPR class together because it came with pizza. Marcus failed the first try. He kept laughing. The instructor made you both practice to the song Stayin' Alive. Why? It's about one hundred four beats a minute. That's right in the sweet spot. Marcus never forgot it. Now, every time he's nervous, he drums that beat. On tables. On steering wheels... on your shoulder. Bum, bum, bum, bum. And here's your secret. Marcus is the only heartbeat that calms you down. Steady. Slow... like an old clock. When the city gets too loud, you sit next to him and listen. And you always tell him the same thing. I hear you, man. That's your line. It's half a joke, half a promise. Now Marcus puts down the cereal. Primetime TV? That's huge. But are you okay? Your heart's been racing for weeks. You laugh. You can hear my heart now? He shrugs. I don't need superpowers. I'm your friend. Tess books the first shoot for Friday. A promo on the subway. Rush hour. Live on social media. Friday. Five fifteen in the afternoon. The train is jammed. More than a hundred people in your car. Tess's camera operator is filming over your shoulder. Marcus came along for moral support. He's squeezed in by the doors, drumming on the pole. Then the train stops... in the tunnel. The lights flicker... and go dim. Brakes scream. Steel on steel. Your range collapses. Every heartbeat turns into one big wall of noise. And then, buried somewhere in that wall... you hear something wrong. A heartbeat that isn't a beat at all. It's a flutter. A quiver. Fast and messy... like a bird trapped in a box. You know that sound. Ventricular fibrillation. The heart is quivering instead of pumping. That's cardiac arrest. Every year in America, more than three hundred fifty thousand people have cardiac arrest outside a hospital. Without help, a person can die within minutes. With every minute that passes without CPR, the chance of survival drops. Where is it coming from? Ten feet? Thirty? Left? Right? You can't tell. The screech is too loud. Your power is almost enough. Almost... You can hear that someone is dying. You just can't hear who. Tess shoves the microphone in your face. This is it, Rio! Tell the camera what you're hearing! This is the moment that makes the show! Narrate it! The camera light glares in your eyes. Thousands of people are watching live. If you do this right, you're a star by midnight. But stars talk. And you need silence. It all comes down to one choice. Keep talking to the camera and become a star... or drop the microphone and ask strangers for silence. You push the microphone away. You climb up on a seat. Everybody! Please! Someone in this car is in cardiac arrest. I need everyone to stop talking... right now. Please. Silence. A hundred people... hold their breath. Somebody's baby even stops fussing. The brakes finally go quiet. And your range grows. Ten feet. Twenty. Thirty... there. Far end of the car. A gray-haired man in a Mets cap, slumped against the window. You push through. He's not breathing normally. His heart isn't pumping. Someone call nine one one when we get signal! Is there an AED on this train? You lock your hands in the center of his chest. Push hard. Push fast. At least two inches deep for an adult. One hundred to one hundred twenty pushes a minute. But you're shaking. Your rhythm is all over the place. Too fast... then too slow. And then you hear it. Bum, bum, bum, bum. Marcus. He's kneeling next to you, drumming the beat on the floor of the train. Stayin' Alive... just like the dorm. Just like the pizza class. You lock onto his rhythm. One hundred four a minute. Push. Push. Push. Two minutes. Three. Your arms burn. Marcus swaps in. You count for him. Then the train lurches forward. The doors open at the next station. Firefighters rush in with a defibrillator. One shock. And in the quiet that follows... you hear it before anyone else. Lub. Dub. Lub. Dub. Weak. Then stronger... He's back. You fall back against the doors and start laughing and crying at the same time. Marcus grabs your hand. I hear you, man. Out on the platform, the whole car starts clapping. Strangers. Commuters. New Yorkers who never clap for anything. The man in the Mets cap is going to make it. He's a retired bus driver. He sends you a Christmas card every year now. Tess catches up with you. She's not mad... she's quiet. You know what, Rio? The clip of you asking for silence has more views than anything I've ever made. She offers you a new show. Not you hearing hearts. You teaching people CPR. Once a week. In subway stations. You say yes... with one condition. Marcus drums. And the ringing in your ears? You see a hearing doctor. She fits you with special earplugs that lower loud sounds but let soft ones through. On the train, they turn the screech down to a whisper. The ringing gets quieter, little by little. Now, when the city gets loud, you pop them in. You sit next to Marcus... and listen to that old clock. Steady. Slow. Bum, bum, bum, bum. So is any of this real? Hearing heartbeats from across a subway car? No. A heartbeat is quiet. Most of its sound is too low and too soft... to travel through air like that. But the idea of listening closer is very real. In 1816, a French doctor named René Laennec rolled up a sheet of paper. He held it to a patient's chest. He heard the heart more clearly than ever. That paper tube became the stethoscope. And today, machines can sense a heartbeat without touching you. In 2016, a team at MIT led by Dina Katabi used wireless signals to measure heartbeats... from across a room. They even used them to guess emotions. And there's a real condition called pulsatile tinnitus. Some people hear their own heartbeat whooshing in their ears. So could technology one day give everyone your power? And would we really want it? Here's something stranger. Some people can feel their own heartbeat without touching their pulse. Others... can't feel it at all. Scientists call this sense interoception. It might shape how strongly we feel emotions. So is your heart quietly telling you how to feel? Your turn. long.title: What If Your Nose Was 1,000 Times Stronger?
long.rel: Rio's mom, who has run a small-town Main Street bakery for thirty years (supporting: perfume house rep Maya).
long.rule: Rio's nose has a fuel tank of about two hundred deep sniffs that only refills with sleep.
long.plant: The old brass bell over the bakery door, which since childhood has meant drop everything and come running.
long.choice: Spend your last sniffs and win Paris... or forget the deal and get Mom out of that basement.
long.script: Vial number one ninety-eight. You lift it to your nose. Jasmine, bergamot, a whisper of cedar... and one drop of something that shouldn't be there. Burnt sugar. On the laptop screen, a man in a silver suit leans toward the camera. He's in Paris... watching. He runs one of the most famous perfume houses in the world. Two more vials, and the deal is yours. A new life. A penthouse... your name on a bottle. But your nose is almost empty. Three sniffs left. Maybe... two. And then you smell it. Faint. Sulfur... rotten eggs. Coming from somewhere below your feet. Your mom's bakery is old. The gas lines are older. And your mom went down to the basement... five minutes ago. Do you sniff the vial... or do you sniff the air? But let's go back. Your name is Rio. You're thirty-two. You grew up above a little bakery on Main Street. One stoplight... two churches. Your mom has run that bakery for thirty years. You came home last spring to help out after her knee surgery. And that's when... your nose changed. The human nose has about four hundred types of smell receptors. Is that a lot? It's actually pretty impressive. Some scientists think we can tell apart thousands of smells. One 2014 study claimed it might be a trillion. Other scientists argued with that math... a lot. A bloodhound? Its nose has up to three hundred million smell receptors. Yours had about six million. You? Now your nose is a thousand times stronger than any human's. But there's one rule. Your nose has a fuel tank. Every deep sniff burns a little. About two hundred big sniffs, and the tank is empty. Then you smell... nothing. Not smoke. Not coffee. Not even burnt toast. The tank only refills when you sleep. So, what if your nose was a thousand times stronger? Day one, you wake up at four in the morning. Not from your alarm... from the smell of yeast. It's coming from the bakery... two floors down... through a closed door. Upside: you never burn a loaf again. That beautiful golden crust? It comes from the Maillard reaction, when sugars and proteins brown in the heat. You can smell the exact second it starts. You pull every tray out at the perfect moment. Mom tastes a croissant and squints. Okay, who are you, and what did you do with my kid? Downside: the walk-in fridge. You open it, and you smell every onion, every egg, every forgotten yogurt in the back. Including one from March. You almost... faint. Upside: you find things. Your neighbor loses her wedding ring in a pile of leaves. You find it... in thirty seconds. It smells like her hand lotion. She hugs you so hard you almost lose a sniff. Downside: people. The man in line has a cold. The lady behind him had garlic for breakfast. A teenager is wearing what smells like an entire can of body spray. Do they know? You can smell it... from the parking lot. Then things get bigger. A couple in town are expecting a baby, and their dog keeps sniffing the nursery. You sniff too. There's a faint musty smell behind the wall. You tell them to check. It's mold. A leaky pipe. They fix it before the baby comes home. Then the town fair. Your mom enters her cinnamon rolls. The judge's sheet says 'grade A.' You whisper in her ear. The judge is lying... He hates cinnamon. You can smell his nervous sweat. Mom laughs so hard she snorts. And then someone films you naming twenty spices in a soup, blindfolded. The video goes everywhere. Ten million views... in a week. That's when Maya shows up. Maya works for a luxury perfume house in Paris. She wears a scent that costs more than your car. She sits at the corner table, orders black coffee, and gets right to it. Rio, do you know what we call our best perfumers in France? We call them... noses. The best ones train for years. Some of them can name hundreds of ingredients... by smell alone. You did it... in a week. She slides a folder across the table. A contract. A flight to Paris. A salary bigger than your town's whole budget. There's just one test left. Two hundred vials, live on video, with the boss watching. Two hundred vials. Two hundred sniffs. Your whole tank... in one night. Sound easy? What could go wrong? And there's a cost. Here's something scientists know. When you smell something for a long time, your brain starts tuning it out. It's called olfactory adaptation. It's why you can't smell your own house, but you notice everyone else's. Your nose isn't broken. Your brain is just saying, got it, no new information. For you, that fade is a thousand times stronger. And it's a thousand times more dangerous. Because the strongest smell in your life is the bakery. Butter. Flour. Sugar. Yeast. You're surrounded by it all day. And by evening, your brain has tuned out almost everything. You've started missing things. Last week you didn't notice a pan of nuts scorching until the smoke alarm went off. Mom shook her head. Some super nose, huh? Here's a strange fact. Natural gas has no smell at all. Gas companies add a chemical called mercaptan so we can smell a leak. It smells like rotten eggs. Most people can detect it at extremely tiny amounts. Unless their nose is... empty. Every morning before sunrise, you and Mom have a ritual. She opens the bakery door. She takes one slow breath. And she says the same thing she's said since you were five. Smells like home. Then she rings the little brass bell over the door. Ding... That bell is older than you are. When you were small, it meant one thing. Fresh bread is out... come running. You always did. You'd come flying down the stairs in your socks, every single time. Mom has a rule. When the bell rings, you drop everything. Customers know it too. The whole town knows it. One ring and the line forms out the door. Lately, though, she's quieter. She saw the contract on the counter. She doesn't ask about it. She just flips the sign and says, Paris, huh? They better feed you. But one night you find her sitting alone in the kitchen. She's holding your old baby blanket. She smells it. Then she smiles... a little sadly. You know what's funny? The smell of a person you love... it's one of the last things you forget. It's true. Smell is wired close to the parts of your brain that handle memory and emotion. That's why a scent can drop you straight into the past. You sit down next to her. Mom, wherever I go, this will always smell like home. She pats your hand. Then go find out what the world smells like. Test night. Maya sets up the vials on the bakery counter. The boss in Paris is on the laptop. Mom is downstairs, relighting the old backup oven in the basement. The main oven quit an hour ago. Ninety-five sniffs. A hundred forty... a hundred eighty. Your tank is nearly dry. The world is going gray around the edges. Smells are getting thin, like a radio losing signal. Vial one ninety-eight. Burnt sugar. Then... sulfur. Faint. Rotten eggs. Gas. Your stomach drops. How much? Where from? A gas leak in a closed basement can build up quietly. And Mom is down there... with a match. You try to track it. You take a sniff. It's everywhere and nowhere. Your nose is too tired to point the way. Is it the old pipe by the stairs? The oven? You can't tell. Your power is almost enough. Almost... Maya taps the screen. Rio, two more vials. Just two. The boss doesn't wait. If you stop now, the deal is over. You have maybe two sniffs left. Use them on the vials, and you go to Paris. Use them on the leak, and you might still not find it. It all comes down to one choice. Spend your last sniffs and win Paris... or forget the deal and get Mom out of that basement. You put down the vial. Maya, I'm sorry. Everybody out. Now. Don't touch the lights. Light switches can make a tiny spark. So can a phone. Do you run downstairs and flip a switch? No. You reach up... and you ring the brass bell. Ding. Ding. Ding. And from the basement, you hear footsteps. Fast ones. Mom comes up the stairs, wiping flour on her apron. Whoa, what's wrong? Who's ringing like that? Out, Mom. Gas. Don't light anything. She doesn't argue. She grabs your hand, and the two of you walk out onto Main Street together. Maya follows with her laptop. You call the gas company from the sidewalk. Ten minutes later, a truck pulls up with flashing yellow lights. The crew goes in with a gas detector. They find a cracked fitting on the old line. Right next to the backup oven. One of them shakes his head. Another few minutes with a match down there? Ma'am, you were very lucky. Mom looks at you. Then at the bell. Then she starts crying and laughing at the same time. You remembered the bell. You laugh too. Mom, you trained me. Twenty-seven years. Fresh bread. Come running. By sunrise, half the town is standing outside the bakery in their pajamas. Someone brings coffee... in a giant thermos. The fire chief shakes your hand. The pastor shows up with a cooler of donuts... from the other bakery. Everybody pretends not to notice. And Maya? She closes her laptop. Then she sits on the curb next to you. The boss wants to know why you stopped. You tell her the truth. Because perfume is nice... but my mom is better. Maya is quiet for a long time. Then she makes a call in rapid French. A week later, a new letter arrives. Not a job in Paris. A small contract to create one scent. You get to make it right here, in the bakery. They call it Main Street. Butter, warm bread, cinnamon, and a tiny note of brass. You sleep ten hours that night. Your tank refills to the top. The next morning, Mom opens the bakery door. And for the first time in months, you smell it again. Really smell it. Not tuned out. Not faded. Just... warm. She takes one slow breath. Then she nudges you. Well? You smile. Smells like home. But that morning, there's something else in the air. A smell you've never smelled before. Not food. Not flowers. Not gas. It's sweet and electric, like lightning and oranges. It's coming from the woods outside town. And the dogs are all facing the same way. What is it? So what would you do with a nose a thousand times stronger? Would you chase Paris, or stay for the bread? Tell us in the comments. And if one smell always takes you straight back home, tell us what it is. Hit like, and subscribe to Rio Animation for more fascinating videos!

long.title: What If You Remembered Every Second Of Your Life?
long.rel: Rio's grandma, who raised him and now lives with him with Alzheimer's (supporting: prosecutor Ben).
long.rule: Rio can jump to any moment of his life, but each memory replays only in real time, with no fast forward.
long.plant: Grandma's daily story of her 1965 courthouse wedding: a borrowed tie, one yellow rose, and the wooden bench under the stained glass eagle window on the second floor.
long.choice: Stay on the stand and become famous... or ask for a recess and go find Grandma.
long.script: Where are your keys? You know. Top drawer, left side... under the takeout menu. You put them there eleven days ago, at six forty-two in the evening... while humming. Where's your parking spot? Level three, row G. Who ordered the oat milk latte at the office party last December? The new intern. Extra hot. She also said she'd pay you back... for a lunch in 2021. She still owes you... nine dollars and fifty cents. You haven't forgotten. You can't... forget. Your coworker swears he never promised to cover your Friday shift. You close your eyes. It's April. A Tuesday... Ten fourteen in the morning. He's eating a blueberry muffin. He says, sure, I owe you one. Crumb on his chin... left side. You tell him all of this. He covers the shift. He also stops talking to you... for a week. Your name is Rio. You're thirty-two. You work as a court reporter at the county courthouse. You type every word said in court, at more than two hundred words a minute. And you remember every second of your life. Every... single... one. Most people don't. In the 1880s, a German scientist named Hermann Ebbinghaus tested his own memory with nonsense syllables. He found that much of what we learn fades... within a day. Most adults can't remember anything before about age three. And your short-term memory holds only a handful of things at once. You? Thirty-two years. That's about... a billion seconds. You can visit any one of them. But there's one rule. You can jump to any moment, sure. But once you're inside a memory, it plays at normal speed. No fast forward. No skipping. Ten minutes of memory takes ten real minutes to watch. So what if you remembered every second of your life? Upside: school would have been easy. You never studied. You just remembered the textbook. Every page. Including the doodle in the margin of page eighty-one. Upside: you never forget a birthday. Or a name. Or a face. At the grocery store, you greet a man you met once, at a gas station, in 2009. He's thrilled. Then he's... a little scared. Downside: you never forget an embarrassment either. Seventh grade. The talent show. Your voice cracked on the high note. Most people would have forgotten it by now. You? You can still hear it. Every crack... in perfect quality. Downside: arguments. You win every single one. Have you ever tried to be friends with someone who wins every argument? Exactly. At work, your power is a quiet superpower. Court reporters already keep a record of every word. But you also remember what the record can't hold. Who looked at whom. Who paused before answering. Lawyers start bringing you coffee. Then the big case comes. A man is on trial for a burglary. The key witness swears he saw him clearly... at nine at night. You remember something different. Three weeks ago, in this same courtroom, the witness said the street light was broken that night. You checked. It's in your transcript. The defense lawyer reads it out loud. The jury gasps. The case... falls apart. Later, DNA from the scene points to someone else. You saved an innocent man... with a sentence nobody else remembered. And that's when Ben shows up. Ben is the county's most famous prosecutor. He has perfect hair... and a podcast. He wants you as his star witness. Not for one case. For every case. Imagine it, Rio. The human recorder. Juries will believe anything you say. You'll be on every news channel by spring. A publisher already wants your book. He hands you a business card. It's gold. Actually... gold colored. Who even does that? And there's a cost. Here's something scientists have learned. Forgetting isn't a failure... it's a feature. Your brain is always trimming. While you sleep, it strengthens some memories and lets others fade. That's how a bad day loses its sting. That's how grief slowly softens. You? Nothing fades... ever. The worst day of your life is as sharp as this morning. And there's another problem. Remembering everything doesn't make you right about everything. Memory isn't a video file. Each time you recall something, your brain rebuilds it. That's why eyewitnesses can be confidently wrong. If you're Ben's star witness, people will trust you completely. What happens the day... you make one mistake? Who pays for it? Your grandma lives with you now. She raised you after your parents moved for work. She taught you to read on her porch. She taught you to make biscuits. And she taught you a little song about the planets. You still sing it... in the shower. Two years ago, the doctors gave her memory loss a name. Alzheimer's disease. More than six million Americans live with it. It usually starts in a small curved part of the brain called the hippocampus. That's where new memories... are made. So Grandma forgets this morning... but she can still tell you about 1965. That's the year she got married. Right here, in this courthouse. In the clerk's office on the second floor. She tells you the story almost every day. Every time, it's the same. Your grandpa wore a borrowed tie. It was too short. She waited for him on the wooden bench under the big stained glass window. The one... with the eagle. She held one yellow rose. And every time she finishes, she squeezes your hand and says the same thing. You remember for me, okay? And you always answer. I'll remember for both of us. That's your line. Some days she knows exactly who you are. Some days she calls you by your dad's name. You never correct her. You just... remember. One night she asks you something that keeps you awake. Does it hurt, Rio? Remembering everything? You don't know how to answer. Because the truth is... yes. You remember the first morning she didn't recognize you. Every second of it. You replay it more than you'd like. Trial day. The biggest case of the year. Ben's star witness debut. Cameras outside. A news van on every corner. And Grandma's day program is closed for a water leak. So she's here, sitting on a bench outside the courtroom with a deputy and a crossword. You take the stand. Ben smiles at the cameras. Then, halfway through, a court officer hands the judge a note. The judge looks at you. Your grandmother has left the hallway. Nobody saw where she went. Your heart... stops. Experts say about six in ten people with dementia will wander at some point. Many don't remember where they meant to go. The courthouse has five floors, four stairwells, and two exits onto a busy road. It's January. Nineteen degrees outside. And Grandma... isn't wearing her coat. You close your eyes. You jump to this morning. You replay the car ride. She was talking. What did she say? You listen. Real time. One minute... two. Traffic. The radio. Her humming. Nothing yet. Three minutes... four. Ben leans close. Rio, stay focused. Deputies will find her. The jury is waiting. If you walk out of this courtroom now, the whole city sees it. You'll never get this chance again. He's right about one thing. You can't replay the whole day in time. Twenty-two minutes of driving. Forty more in the halls. You have all the memories. But not... the time to watch them. Your power is almost enough. Almost... It all comes down to one choice. Stay on the stand and become famous... or ask for a recess and go find Grandma. You stand up. Your Honor, I need to go. I'm sorry. The judge nods. Recess. Go. You run. And as you run, you stop replaying. You don't need the car ride. You don't need a billion seconds. You need... one story. The one she tells you every day. A borrowed tie. A yellow rose. A wooden bench. The stained glass eagle. Second floor. You take the stairs two at a time. There's a long hallway. And there, at the end, golden light pours through a tall window shaped like an eagle. On the old wooden bench under it, sits Grandma. Hands folded. Waiting. She looks up. She doesn't quite know your name today. But she smiles... Oh, there you are. I'm waiting for my husband. He's late. He always is... You sit down beside her. Your breath is shaking. Is he? Tell me about him. And she does. The tie. The rose. The eagle. You've heard it hundreds of times. You listen like it's... the first. A deputy finds you there. Then another. Then the court clerk. Then, quietly, half the jury. The judge had extended the recess. Word traveled fast. Nobody says much. A clerk brings Grandma a cup of tea. A juror, an older man with kind eyes, takes off his scarf. He wraps it around her shoulders. She thanks him like he's a prince. Ben is there too, at the end of the hall. His podcast microphone is off. He watches for a long time. Then he walks over. Rio, I'll find another witness for the next one. You should be here. Grandma pats his hand. Such a nice young man. Is he your friend? You look at Ben. He shrugs. Maybe... I am. You finish your testimony that afternoon. Simple. Honest... no headlines. You turn down the book. You turn down the podcast. You keep your job, typing every word. And the memory that used to hurt? The morning she didn't know you? It's still there. You can't forget it. But now, it has company. Golden light. An eagle in the glass. Her hand in yours. When the bad memory plays, you jump to this one instead. That's the trick. You can't erase a memory. But you can choose... which one you visit. That night, Grandma squeezes your hand. You remember for me, okay? I'll remember for both of us. So is any of this real? Partly. In 2006, researchers Elizabeth Parker, Larry Cahill and James McGaugh described a woman with an astonishing memory... for her own life. The condition is now called highly superior autobiographical memory. Only a small number of people have been confirmed to have it. They can often name the weekday of a date... and what they did. But they don't remember everything. Not every page of every book. And later studies found they can still form false memories, just like everyone else. Memory scientist Elizabeth Loftus showed how easily memories can be bent. In 1974, she and John Palmer showed people a film of a car crash. Changing one word in a question changed how fast people remembered the cars going. The Innocence Project reports something sobering. Mistaken eyewitness identification played a role in roughly seven out of ten of its DNA exoneration cases. So would perfect memory make us wiser... or just more certain? What do you think? And here's a mystery scientists still chase. Old songs often survive dementia longer than names do. Some people who can't remember breakfast can sing every word of a song from their teens. Why does music hide so deep? What's your take? Let us know below, and suggest the next power for us to try. Hit like, and subscribe to Rio Animation for more fascinating videos!

long.title: What If You Felt Zero Pain?
long.rel: younger brother who idolizes Rio (Eli, 17)
long.rule: You still feel touch and temperature but the pain alarm is gone, while damage happens at normal human speed.
long.plant: Eli draws a zero-to-ten pain face scale inside the brim of Rio's hard hat and rates Rio's injuries every night.
long.choice: Keep digging alone as the hero on live TV... or climb out and trust your brother's alarm.
long.script: The ground just... drops. One second, your little brother Eli is grinning up at you from the bottom of the trench. The next, the wall beside him slides in like a wave of brown sugar. It hits him at the chest. Eli! You're already moving. You jump down and start digging with your bare hands. Your gloves rip. A rock slices your palm. A fingernail tears clean off. You don't slow down. You don't even flinch. Up on the edge, a TV camera is rolling. A producer is yelling. Best footage ever! Eli stares at your hands. At the red on your knuckles. His voice is tiny. Rio... doesn't that hurt? You look down. And the honest answer is... you have no idea. But let's go back. Your name is Rio. You're twenty-eight. You run a framing crew on a big construction site outside Columbus, Ohio. Steel, concrete, mud... and lots of coffee. Here's how pain normally works. Your skin is packed with nerve endings called nociceptors. Their whole job is to scream when something is wrong. Touch a hot pan? Your hand jumps away... before your brain even catches up. Some pain signals crawl up your nerves at about two miles an hour... slower than you walk. The fast ones? About as quick as a car on the highway. The message is always the same. Stop. Now. You? You get... nothing. Here's the rule. You still feel touch. You still feel warm and cold, rough and smooth. But the alarm is gone. And the damage? It happens at exactly the normal human speed. So what if you felt zero pain? What if the alarm just... never rang? Monday morning. You kick a bundle of rebar with your bare toe. Nothing. Not even a hop. Upside: you will never fear a Lego in the dark again. At the dentist, you skip the numbing shot. She drills. You ask about her weekend. She stops drilling. Wait... you didn't feel that? On the job, you're a machine. You haul plywood all day. Your back never complains. Your foreman, Omar, squints at you over his clipboard. Nobody's back feels that good, Rio. Nobody. Then the downsides show up. The problem? Your coffee. It tastes hot. Just hot. You burn your tongue every morning and never notice. Your shower is scarier. Water at one hundred forty degrees can give an adult a serious burn in about five seconds. So you turn your water heater down to one hundred twenty, the setting safety experts recommend. You test your shower with a thermometer. Like a baby's bath. At lunch, you bite your cheek. Hard. You only find out when Omar points at your sandwich. Uh... are you okay? Kids born without pain often chew their own tongues and lips without realizing it. Now you know why. Wednesday, a nail gun kicks. A nail goes straight through your glove. You keep working for ten minutes before a guy on your crew yells, Dude, your hand! You look down. Huh. Is that... my hand? Thursday, pickup basketball. You land on someone's foot and roll your ankle. You keep playing. The next morning? Your ankle is the size of a grapefruit. Pain would have benched you after one play. Instead, you played on a sprain... for an hour. Friday, somebody films you on a phone. You're leaning on a scorching truck exhaust pipe. It feels warm. Just warm. You keep chatting. The video gets millions of views. Then your phone rings. It's a TV network. They want you for a new live stunt show called 'Feel Nothing.' Fifty thousand dollars an episode. You read the email three times. Is this real? It is. Scientists have spent years studying people born without pain, hoping to build better painkillers. Your body is suddenly... interesting. Amazing. And terrifying. Because the most dangerous moment of your summer hasn't happened yet. Here's what nobody tells you. Pain isn't just a feeling. It's information. And your body was built to run on it. Ever stand in line at the grocery store? Every few minutes, you shift your weight. You don't decide to. A tiny ache decides for you. You? You never shuffle. You stand like... a statue. People born without pain often wear down their joints, because nothing ever tells them to ease up. Your knees are twenty-eight. They feel fifty. Your doctor gives you a list. Check your skin every night. Check your eyes, because a scratch won't sting. Watch for fever, because an infection inside might never hurt. A burst appendix is an emergency. Normally, the pain drags you to the hospital. For you, the first warning might come way too late. Chest pain is a main warning sign of a heart attack. Your warning? It never comes. Your life becomes... a checklist. And there's one more cost. It's quieter. When Omar gets a migraine, you tell him to walk it off. A sprained wrist? Dramatic. You've forgotten what pain feels like. Which means... you've forgotten how to believe other people's pain. And on a construction site, the thing that saves your life is usually the thing that hurts first. Your little brother Eli is seventeen. He has your old hoodie, your old skateboard... and your habit of midnight cereal. This summer, he joined your crew. He follows you everywhere. If you skip your water break, he skips his. He watches your viral video every night. In the truck, he finally says it. I wish I was like you, Rio. Nothing hurts you. Why can't I be like that? So you sit him down on the tailgate. Pain is the alarm, Eli. Not the enemy. He rolls his eyes. Then he grabs a Sharpie, takes your hard hat, and draws something inside the brim. A row of little faces. A smiling face for zero. A crying face for ten. The same kind of scale nurses use in hospitals. Under it, he writes, 'How bad is it? Ask Eli.' You laugh. But every night after that, Eli checks your hands. He turns them over under the truck's dome light. He finds the splinters. The cuts. The bruise you never noticed. And he gives each one a number. That's a two. That's a five. That one's a seven, dude, go wash it. Silly? Maybe. But it works. Your brother has become your alarm. And the TV show's first big episode? It's filming right here. On your job site. Friday. Friday comes. The TV crew is everywhere. A producer in spotless white sneakers wants a shot of you walking the edge of a fresh trench. Eight feet deep. But the steel trench box is blocking his camera. So someone moves it. Just for ten minutes. Just for the shot. Omar's face goes gray. Who moved my box? Trenches five feet deep or more need a protective system. That's the law. Too late. Eli is at the bottom, laying pipe like you showed him. Then the wall moves. One cubic yard of soil can weigh about as much as a car. Way more than that just came down. It pins Eli to the chest. He can still breathe... barely. Every breath pushes against all that weight. You jump in. You don't think. You dig. Scoop. Scoop. Scoop. No burning palms. No screaming fingers. Nothing slows you down. This is what your power is for... isn't it? One minute. Two minutes. Eli's chest comes free. He gulps air. Three minutes. You hear a crack. You look at your left hand. Your ring finger is pointing the wrong way. The skin on both palms is shredded. You can't grip the dirt anymore. It just slides through your fingers. How bad is it? You honestly... can't tell. Then Omar's voice, sharp as a whistle. The other wall is cracking! Rio, get out! You look up. A long, thin line is opening in the dirt above your head. Rescue crews know that a second collapse can bury the people trying to help. Omar is already calling for help. The fire department's trench rescue team is six minutes out. They'll bring shoring panels. Safe... but slow. Up on the edge, the producer is waving his arms. Don't stop! Keep digging! This is the finale! Eli grabs your wrist with his free hand. He turns your palm over. Just like on the tailgate. His voice is shaking. That's a ten, Rio. That's a ten. Get out. So there it is. Keep digging alone as the hero on live TV... or climb out and trust your brother's alarm. You climb out. The producer groans. You don't care. You lie flat on a sheet of plywood, far from the edge. And you talk to Eli the whole time. About cereal. About the time he broke his arm at eight... and you carried him home. Six minutes later, sirens. The rescue team braces the walls with metal panels... and digs with care. Forty minutes. That's how long it takes to free Eli the right way. When they lift him out, he's muddy, bruised, and laughing. Nothing broken. The whole crew claps. The producer jogs over. That footage is gold! Sign for the full season tonight? You hold up your hands. Two broken fingers. No thanks. I'm done feeling nothing on camera. At the hospital, a doctor sets your fingers. Eli sits beside you with the hard hat on his lap. He points to the row of little faces. Then to your hands. That's still a ten. You nod. Yeah. I believe you. Pain is the alarm, Eli. Not the enemy. He smiles. He doesn't want to feel nothing anymore. He wants to feel things... and be brave anyway. A week later, Omar tapes a new sign on the site trailer. 'No box, no dig. Camera or not.' And you change too. When a guy on your crew says his back hurts, you don't tell him to walk it off. You ask, Zero to ten? And you believe the number. You still can't feel pain. But for the first time... you understand it. So... is any of this real? Yes... and that's the wild part. People born without pain really exist. It's called congenital insensitivity to pain, and it's extremely rare. In 2006, scientists studying families in northern Pakistan traced one form of it to a single gene called SCN9A. Their work began with a young street performer who did stunts that should have hurt... and didn't. In 2019, doctors described a woman in Scotland named Jo Cameron. She barely felt burns, cuts or even surgery. The cause? A rare change in a gene researchers nicknamed FAAH-OUT. The fiction? Zero pain and a perfectly healthy body. Real people with these conditions often get hurt a lot, especially as kids... because nothing warns them. Pain is a terrible feeling... and one of the best tools your body has. So here's the question. If a doctor could switch off your pain for one day... would you say yes? But what if it went the other way? What if you felt everything... ten times stronger? A hug. A sunrise. A paper cut. Would the world be too beautiful... or just too much? Do you buy it? Sound off in the comments, and tell us which ability we should push to the limit next. Hit like, and subscribe to Rio Animation for more fascinating videos!

long.title: What If Your Wounds Healed In One Minute?
long.rel: Rio's old high school coach (Coach Riley)
long.rule: Every heal burns body fuel, and when the fuel runs out the healing stops cold.
long.plant: Coach Riley's cooler of orange slices on the sideline, tied to his rule 'Nobody plays on an empty tank.'
long.choice: Protect the body worth twenty million dollars... or empty Coach's cooler and go back in.
long.script: You get a paper cut at work. You say ouch... and by the time you grab a bandage, there's nothing to cover. You burn your tongue on the first bite of pizza. By the third bite? Fine. You trip on the curb, skin your elbow, and keep walking. A minute later... the scrape is gone. Smooth. Pink. Like it never happened. At the pharmacy, you get a flu shot. The nurse turns to grab a bandage, turns back, and frowns. Wait... where did the needle go in? You shrug. Honestly? No idea. Your name is Rio. You're thirty-one. You teach science at the same high school you graduated from. And on Friday nights, you help coach football. Oh, and the ear piercing you got in 2011? It closed... while you were still standing at the mall kiosk. Here's how healing normally works. Get a cut, and your blood starts clotting within minutes. Tiny cells called platelets pile up like sandbags. Then comes swelling, then new tissue, then months of slow repair. A shallow cut usually takes a week or two to close. A broken bone? Often six to eight weeks. You? Any wound... one minute. Done. But here's the rule. Healing isn't magic. It's work. Your body still has to build every new cell from food. Every heal burns fuel, and big wounds burn a lot of it. Run out of fuel? The healing stops... cold. So what if your wounds healed in one minute? Monday. You slice your thumb chopping onions. You rinse it. And it's... gone. Upside: you will never own another box of bandages. Tuesday, you touch a hot baking sheet. A burn that would normally blister for days? Healed... before the cookies cool. Your students love it. One of them, a sophomore linebacker named Mason, keeps asking you to do it again. Can you heal a paper cut on command? Can you heal a sunburn? Mason... please sit down. Then the downsides creep in. The problem? Your body doesn't check what it's healing around. You step on a piece of glass at the beach. Before you can limp to a towel, your skin closes right over it. Now there's glass inside your foot... sealed in. A doctor has to cut you open to dig it out. And then you heal again... around her stitches. Upside, though: you're never sore after the gym. Muscles grow after workouts partly by repairing tiny tears in their fibers. That repair normally takes a day or two. For you? About a minute. You get stronger fast. Your gym buddies are suspicious. Steroids, dude? Downside: your stomach. You're hungry. All... the... time. The average adult eats around two thousand calories a day. You? After a bad scrape, you'd eat a whole pizza for a snack. Your grocery bill doubles. Your fridge looks like... a team locker room. Then the big one. Thursday, you slip on ice in the school parking lot. You land wrong. Your wrist snaps. You feel it. Oh man, the pain is real. You pull out your phone to call for help. But by the time the ambulance arrives? The bone has already healed... crooked. Bones heal in whatever position they're in. That's why doctors set them first. Now your wrist bends at a strange angle. A surgeon has to re-break it and line it up. Twice. You learn your lesson. Doctor first. Everything else... later. Word gets out. A woman in a gray suit shows up at football practice. Her name is Priya. She works for a private lab in California. She doesn't waste time. Twenty million dollars, Rio. Five years. You live at our facility. We study everything. Exclusive rights. You'd never have to teach again. Twenty million? Is she serious? You laugh. Then you stop laughing. Because that's a lot of zeroes... for a science teacher. And here's what keeps you up at night. When you heal, you're not just patching skin. Your cells are dividing. Copying themselves. Over and over, as fast as they can. Now... what is cancer? Cells dividing that won't stop. Your doctor doesn't say you'll get it. She just says nobody knows... because nobody has ever healed like you. And there's another cost. Scars. Normal scar tissue is never quite as strong as the skin it replaced. It's a patch... not a copy. You heal so fast, the patching never gets a chance to finish properly. Some of your old wounds feel tight. Stiff. Like your body is wearing... a tape job. Then there's the fuel. Your body doesn't have an unlimited tank. If you get hurt three times in one hour, you shake. Your vision goes gray. You feel dizzy, like your blood sugar has crashed. Because it has. Healing is fast. But free? Not even close. Coach Riley is sixty-eight. He's been coaching at your high school for forty years. This is his last season. He's the reason you're a teacher. Senior year, your dad lost his job, and you almost quit the team to work nights. Coach Riley drove you home every day that winter. He never made a speech about it. He just... showed up. Coach Riley has one rule, and he's said it a thousand times. Nobody plays on an empty tank. That's why there's always a cooler of orange slices on the sideline. Every practice. Every game. Forty years of oranges. Funny old-guy thing? You used to think so. Now, with your power, it's your survival plan. Coach is the only one you tell. You show him your thumb. You cut it with a pocketknife, and he watches it close. Does he say wow? Nope. He just reaches into the cooler and hands you an orange slice. Then he asks, Who's taking care of you, Rio? Nobody asks you that. Everybody asks what you can do. Coach asks how you're doing. So you tell him about the lab. About the twenty million. Coach Riley chews on that for a while. Then he says, Money's a scoreboard, kid... It's not the game. What does that mean? You don't know yet... but you will. Homecoming. Friday night. The stands are packed. The marching band is warming up in the old field house behind the end zone. Mason's little brother is in there. So are thirty band kids. And Coach Riley, who went in to grab extra jerseys. Then you smell it... smoke. A space heater in the equipment room has tipped over. The field house is old. Wood floors. Piles of padding. The American Red Cross says a home fire can leave you as little as two minutes to escape. This building is a lot bigger. And a lot older. You sprint. The doors are jammed with panicked kids. You pull them out two at a time. A beam drops and burns your arm. One minute later, healed. Smoke stings your eyes. Healed. Glass cuts your hand. Healed. You go back in. Again. And again. Twenty-six kids out. Twenty-eight. Thirty. Then you count. Where's Coach? He went back in for Mason's little brother. You start to run. And your legs... just stop. You fall to your knees on the grass. Your hands are shaking. Your burns are still raw. They're not healing anymore. Your tank is... empty. Behind you, someone grabs your arm. It's Priya. She came to watch you. She's on the phone with her boss. Rio, listen to me. If you go back in like this, you won't heal. You could die. The contract is ready. Twenty million dollars. Don't throw that away on one more trip. She's not wrong about the danger. Smoke is the real killer in most fires. And healing can't fix the biggest problem. Carbon monoxide grabs onto your blood about two hundred times more tightly than oxygen does. You can heal a burn in a minute. You can't heal your way out of breathing poison. The fire trucks are still three minutes away. You look at the doors. Then at the sideline. And you see it. The cooler. So there it is. Protect the body worth twenty million dollars... or empty Coach's cooler and go back in. You crawl to the cooler. You eat orange slices by the handful. Ten. Twenty. Sugar hits your blood. Your hands stop shaking. Your burns start to close. Nobody plays on an empty tank. You pull your shirt over your mouth. You stay low, where the air is cleaner. Coach Riley is on the floor by the back door. He's wrapped around Mason's little brother... like a shield. You drag them both out, one in each arm. Just as you hit the grass, the sirens arrive. Paramedics put oxygen masks on Coach and the boy. Mason is crying and hugging his brother. Coach coughs, pulls the mask off, and looks at you. You look terrible, kid. Me? You're one to talk, Coach. The whole stadium is on its feet. Not cheering. Just clapping. Slow and loud. Two days later, Priya calls again. The offer is still open. Twenty million. You thank her. And you say... no. Instead, you volunteer for a study at the state university hospital. For free. On one condition. Everything they learn gets shared with every doctor, everywhere. Maybe one day, a burned kid heals a little faster because of you. On his last game day, Coach Riley gives you a gift. It's the cooler. Taped to the lid is a note in his crooked handwriting. 'Who's taking care of you, Rio?' And underneath, a new line. 'Everybody. That's who.' Because the whole town has your back now. Neighbors drop off food. The band kids bake you cookies. Mason makes you a sandwich every Friday. And for the first time, you don't feel like a science experiment. You feel like... a person. Here's what you still can't answer, though. Your cells keep copying. Over and over. And one morning, in the mirror, you notice something strange. A small gray hair. Then another. Is healing this fast... making you age faster? So what would you do with a body that heals in one minute? Would you take the twenty million? Tell us in the comments. And if you've ever had a coach who showed up when nobody else did... tell us their name. Hit like, and subscribe to Rio Animation for more fascinating videos!

long.title: What If You Could Hold Your Breath For An Hour?
long.rel: Rio's 10-year-old daughter (Jenna)
long.rule: The hour only holds while sitting calm and still; every kick, sprint or panicked heartbeat burns oxygen faster.
long.plant: Jenna's green glow stick bracelet from the county fair, tied on Rio's wrist so she can always find him.
long.choice: Stay still and win the money on live TV... or swim to the boat and burn your last oxygen.
long.script: Forty-one minutes. That's how long you've been underwater. It's dark down here... murky green. Above you, a pontoon boat floats upside down, rocking in the storm. And somewhere under it, you hear a voice. Small. Echoing. Daddy? Is that you? It's your daughter, Jenna. She's ten. She's trapped in a pocket of air under the hull with three other kids. You grab the rail... and pull yourself in. Your chest is tight. Your vision is starting to sparkle... at the edges. For forty minutes, you were fine. Now? You're running... low. And on the dock, a TV camera is still waiting for you to come up a hero. But let's go back. Your name is Rio. You're thirty-six. You fix air conditioners in a little lake town in Minnesota. Summer is your busy season. And this summer? Something strange happened. Here's what normally happens when you hold your breath. Most adults can last about a minute, give or take. That burning feeling in your chest? It's not your body running out of oxygen. It's carbon dioxide building up in your blood. Your brain reads that and starts yelling. Breathe. Breathe! Your brain is greedy, too. How greedy? It's about two percent of your body weight... but it burns around twenty percent of your oxygen. Cut it off for about four to six minutes... and brain cells start dying. You? You can hold your breath for an hour. Sixty... full... minutes. But here's the rule. That hour is an hour sitting still. Calm. Quiet. Every kick, every sprint, every panicked heartbeat spends your oxygen faster. Swim hard? Your hour can shrink... to minutes. So what if you could hold your breath for an hour? First week. You're at the town pool with Jenna. You sink to the bottom... and read a whole comic book. The lifeguard blows her whistle three times. You give her a thumbs up. She does not... give one back. Upside: you are unbeatable at the kids' game of who can stay under longest. Downside: the kids stop inviting you. Can you blame them? You fix a leaking pipe in a flooded basement. No pump. No snorkel. You just... wade in and work. Your boss calls it the fastest job in company history. You drop your keys off the end of the dock. Twelve feet of water. Gone forever? For most people, sure. You? You have time for a snack down there. The problem? Shaving. Brushing teeth. Long phone calls. You keep forgetting to breathe. Because your alarm, the carbon dioxide alarm, almost never goes off. One night, your smartwatch buzzes you awake. It says your blood oxygen is low. You've been sleeping... without breathing. For how long? Eleven minutes. Is that dangerous? Your doctor doesn't know. Nobody does. Then the deeper problem. Water pressure. Every thirty-four feet of fresh water adds one full atmosphere of pressure. You dive to the bottom of the deepest part of the lake. Over one hundred feet. Your ears scream. Your lungs squeeze down... like a fist. Holding your breath doesn't fix pressure. Who knew? You do now. And the cold? Deep lake water stays cold even in July. Down where the sun can't reach, it can sit in the forties. Water pulls heat out of your body many times faster than air. You might have an hour of oxygen... but not an hour of warmth. Then the world... finds out. Somebody posts a video of you napping on the bottom of the pool. It gets millions of views. A TV network calls. They want a live world record attempt. Right here, in your lake. Prime time. Fourth of July weekend. One hour underwater. A prize of five hundred thousand dollars. Five hundred thousand dollars? Really? You do the math. That's college for Jenna. That's a new roof. That's... everything. Amazing. And terrifying. Because the one person in town who won't go near that lake... is your daughter. Here's the cost nobody sees. Jenna is scared of the water. She always has been. When she was little, she slipped off a dock and went under for a few seconds. Just a few. But did she forget it? Never. Now her dad lives underwater. Every afternoon, you dive. Every afternoon, she sits on the dock, hugging her knees. Staring at the spot where you went down. Counting. Cute? You think so. It isn't. One day you come up after thirty minutes, and she's crying. I counted to a thousand, Dad. Why were you gone so long? I thought you weren't coming back. So you make her a promise.
