You teach her the trick that keeps your oxygen lasting. You put your hand on her chest. Slow heart. Long breath. You say it together. Slow heart. Long breath. She tries it every night at bedtime. Does it work? It actually... does. Then she gives you something. A glow stick bracelet from the county fair. Bright green. She snaps it, and it lights up. She ties it around your wrist. So I can always find you, Dad. You laugh. But you keep a pack of them in your truck. And every time you dive, she snaps a new one. Green on your wrist. Green on hers. Two little lights... in a big dark lake. Fourth of July. Storm clouds roll in at sunset. Cancel? The TV crew says the show must go on. They've built a platform thirty feet down, with lights and an underwater camera. A host in a bright blue suit is counting down. Ten. Nine. Eight. You dive. You sit on the platform. Calm. Still... waiting. Your heart slows down. Cold water on your face triggers a real trick. It's called the diving reflex. Your heart rate drops. Blood shifts toward your brain and heart. Every mammal has some version of it. Seals have it big. Ten minutes. Twenty. Thirty. Forty. Upstairs, the crowd is cheering. Then the wind hits. A pontoon boat full of families is heading back to shore. A gust catches it broadside. It tips... and flips. Forty-one minutes. The host's voice is in your earpiece. Rio! Stay down! Nineteen more minutes and you're a champion! You hear me? We've got rescue boats! The rescue boats are four minutes away. Under that hull, there's a pocket of trapped air. It can keep kids alive for a while. But how long? Not forever. And then you see it. Through the green murk, under the boat. A tiny green light. Jenna's bracelet. Wait... she was on that boat? So there it is. Stay still and win the money on live TV... or swim to the boat and burn your last oxygen. You kick off the platform. Every stroke costs you. You can feel it... Your hour is draining... like a bathtub. You swim to the green light. You pull yourself under the rail and come up in the air pocket. Four kids. Four faces in the dark. Jenna grabs your arm. Daddy! The other kids are screaming. Splashing. Breathing way too fast. Panic burns air. And that pocket? It's all the air they have. Here's the hardest part. Real drowning doesn't look like the movies. It's... quiet. No waving. No yelling. A person can slip under in less than a minute. You can't take all four kids at once. You have to dive out, swim under the rail, surface, and come back. Four trips. Each one costs you oxygen you don't have. Your head is pounding. Your fingers are numb. You can't think. You start to panic... too. Then a small hand lands flat on your chest. Jenna. Her voice is shaking. But she says it anyway. Slow heart. Long breath. You look at her. You nod. You say it with her. Slow heart. Long breath. Your heart slows down. Then she turns to the other kids, and she says it to them. Slow heart. Long breath. They copy her. The splashing stops. The fast breathing stops. They wait. One trip. Two. Three. On the third trip, a rescue boat pulls up. A lifeguard grabs the kid from your arms. Last trip. Jenna. She's terrified of the water. And you're asking her to go under. Hold my wrist, you tell her. Follow the light. You go under together. Three seconds. Four. You come up into the rain. Gasping. Both of you. The rescue boat pulls you in. Your vision goes sparkly... then clear. You breathe. Big, ugly, wonderful gulps of air. On the dock, the host is still staring at a clock. The record is gone. So is the five hundred thousand dollars. And does anyone on that shore care? Not even a little. Moms are crying. Dads are hugging soaked kids. The whole town is clapping in the rain. A week later, the TV network calls. They want a rematch. You say no. Instead, you start teaching swim lessons at the town pool. For free. Drowning is the leading cause of death for American kids ages one to four. Can you fix that alone? No. But you can help. And the first kid in your first class? Jenna. She's still scared. But now she puts her face in the water. She counts. She comes up smiling. Slow heart. Long breath. She doesn't sit on the dock counting anymore. She swims out next to you. Two green lights. Same lake. So... is any of this real? Some of it, yes. Trained free divers really can hold their breath for many minutes. The Guinness world record for a breath hold is over twenty minutes. But there's a catch. The record holder breathed pure oxygen before going under. Without that, records are closer to eleven or twelve minutes. Please don't try it at home. Practicing breath holds alone can cause blackouts, even in shallow water. In 2018, researcher Melissa Ilardo and her team studied the Bajau people of Southeast Asia. They've been sea divers for generations. The team found the Bajau have bigger spleens. That may help push extra oxygen-rich blood around during a dive. Some animals put us to shame. Weddell seals can dive for over an hour. One Cuvier's beaked whale was tracked underwater for nearly four hours. But a human holding their breath for a full hour? That's... fiction. So here's the question. If humans could evolve to stay underwater that long... what would we give up on land? And here's a stranger one. What if you never needed to sleep? No dreams. No naps. Twenty-four hours a day. Would you get more done... or slowly come apart? So what would you do with one hour underwater? Tell us in the comments. And if someone ever taught you to slow down when you were scared... tell them thank you. Hit like, and subscribe to Rio Animation for more fascinating videos!

long.title: What If You Were 10 Times Stronger?
long.rel: dad, a retired mover with a bad back
long.rule: Only Rio's muscles got ten times stronger; bones, tendons and joints stayed normal human.
long.plant: Dad's old frayed two-man leather carrying strap with his and Rio's uncle's initials, and his line 'Nobody lifts alone.'
long.choice: Lift it alone and become a legend on camera... or grab Dad's old strap and lift together.
long.script: You open a pickle jar for your neighbor... pop. The lid flies across the kitchen. The jar? Still in one piece... barely. You carry a couch up three flights of stairs. Alone? With one hand... while texting with the other. A car is parked too close to your driveway, so you... gently scoot it over a foot. Is that legal? You're honestly not sure. At the grocery store, a kid asks if you can pick up his dad's truck. You smile and say, Not today... buddy. And then you go home and shake hands with your landlord. Very, very carefully. He still... winces. Your name is Rio. You're thirty-three. You work at your family's moving company outside Pittsburgh. The sign on the truck says 'Two Guys and a Big Blue Truck.' There used to be two guys. Who? Your dad and your uncle. Now it's mostly you, your Aunt Bev on the phones, and a dolly with a squeaky wheel. Here's how strength works. You have more than six hundred muscles. They pull on your bones through tough cords called tendons. A muscle's strength depends mostly on how thick it is. Why do bodybuilders look like that? Thick muscle. The heaviest deadlift ever recorded is a little over eleven hundred pounds. A trained strongman, years of work. You? You could lift a lot more than that... before breakfast. But here's the rule. Only your muscles got ten times stronger. Your bones didn't. Your tendons didn't. Your skin, your joints, your spine? All regular. Human. So every time you go all out... something has to give. So what if you were ten times stronger? First week on the job. A client has an upright piano. Most uprights weigh somewhere between three hundred and five hundred pounds. Normally? Four guys, two straps... and a lot of grunting. You? You carry it down the porch steps like a laundry basket. The client faints... just a little. Upside: jobs that took a whole day now take two hours. Aunt Bev books three moves a day. Then four. Her new name for you? The forklift. Downside: everything you own is... breaking. Doorknobs snap off. Car doors bend. You've gone through five phone screens in a month. You hug your aunt... and she says something cracked. Was that her back? Thankfully, no. Just her reading glasses... in her shirt pocket. Then the hungry part. Muscle is expensive. It burns energy even when you're resting. More muscle? More fuel. You eat like a teenager on a growth spurt. Six meals a day. Peanut butter... by the spoonful. Aunt Bev texts you a photo of the grocery receipt. Seriously, Rio? And there's a cost. Your hands are fine. But one morning, you yank a stuck truck door. You hear a pop in your elbow. Was it the door? Nope. It was... you. The doctor shows you... an x-ray. Your tendon pulled so hard... it ripped a tiny chip of bone right off. It has a name. An avulsion fracture. It happens to athletes sometimes. And to you? For you, it could happen every day. Here's the problem with ten times stronger. Your muscles can now pull harder than your skeleton can take. Your Achilles tendon is the strongest tendon in your body. During a run, it already handles several times your body weight. Now picture ten times the pull. What happens? Snap. So you learn to hold back. Every day. All day. Like driving a race car... in a school zone. Then a video goes viral. You, flipping a refrigerator onto a dolly with one finger. The next morning, a man in a shiny jacket shows up at the office. His job? He runs a pro wrestling league. He slides a contract across Aunt Bev's desk. Two million dollars... three years. Your own action figure. The Mover. You stare at the number. Two million? For a moving guy? That's more than your family's company has made... ever. Amazing. And terrifying. Because the wrestling promoter doesn't want you to hold back. That's the whole show. Who pays to watch a guy go easy? And your body... was never built to stop holding back. Here's the hidden part. Your dad is sixty-four. He hauled furniture for thirty-five years. Thirty-five years of fridges, pianos and sleeper sofas. Now his back is a mess. He walks with a cane. A bag of groceries? He can't lift it without a sharp breath. And here's the thing nobody says out loud. Your dad doesn't feel needed anymore. He used to run every job. Now you do it all alone. Faster. Bigger. Better. Every time you lift something he can't, you see it in his face. Pride. And something else... something sad. One night, he sits on the back step of the truck. He's holding an old leather strap. It's frayed. Dark with sweat. His initials are burned into one end, and your uncle's are on the other. A two-man carrying strap. The kind movers use so two people share the weight. Your dad hands it to you. He says, Thirty-five years, and I never once lifted alone. That's how you keep your back, Rio. Nobody lifts alone. You laugh. Dad, I don't need a strap anymore. Look at me. He doesn't laugh. He just says it again. Nobody lifts alone. Then he limps... inside. You hang the strap on a hook in the truck. And you forget about it... for a while. Saturday. Big job. An apartment move in an old brick building. The wrestling promoter is there too, with a camera guy. He wants a sizzle reel. Show us something huge, Mover. Something nobody's ever seen! Got it? Your dad came along... to supervise. Sitting on a folding chair. Cane across his knees. Then it happens. Behind the building, a delivery van's jack slips. The van drops. Was anyone underneath? Yes. A man changing a tire. Now he's pinned at the hips. A van like that can weigh around five thousand pounds. You're there in two seconds. You grab the bumper. You lift. And the van moves. One inch. Two inches. Then you hear it... pop. Your shoulder. A white-hot flash shoots down your arm. Your muscles could lift this van all day. Your joints can't. Another inch, and your arm could tear right out of its socket. The man under the van is groaning. His face is gray. A crush injury is a race against time. Firefighters train for this. They use air bags and wooden blocks. They lift slowly, inch by inch, so nothing slips again. The fire department is eight minutes away. Eight minutes? That's a long time to be pinned. Behind you, the promoter is shouting. This is it! Do it alone! One clean lift, and you're a legend! The camera is right in your face. Then you hear your dad's voice. Quiet. Steady. Rio. The strap. So there it is. Lift it alone and become a legend on camera... or grab Dad's old strap and lift together. You let go. The van settles back an inch. You run to the truck and pull the leather strap off its hook. Your dad is already up. Cane and all. And now he's doing what he did for thirty-five years. He's running the job. Bev, call the fire department back and tell them it's a crush. Kid with the camera, put it down and grab those bricks. You, sir, the guy in the jacket. Find me a two-by-four. Your dad loops the strap around the bumper. You take one end. Three neighbors take the other. A two-by-four slides under the frame as a lever. A lever trades distance for force. Archimedes supposedly said, Give me a place to stand, and I'll move the world. You? You only need to move one van. Your dad counts it off, the way he did a thousand times. Lift with your legs. On three. One. Two. Three. The van rises. Slow. Steady... no pop. Your shoulder holds, because the weight isn't all on you. Two inches. Four. Six. The kid with the camera shoves bricks under the frame. The van is blocked... safe. You and a neighbor slide the man out. Ninety seconds later, sirens. The paramedics take it from there. The man is going to be okay. The whole street is clapping. The neighbors are hugging. The camera guy is crying... a little. The promoter walks up to you. His jacket is covered in brick dust. That wasn't the shot I wanted. But honestly? That was better. Still want to sign? Do you? You look at your dad. He's leaning on his cane, out of breath, smiling like it's his first day on the job. You hand the contract back. No thanks. I've got a crew. Monday, you change the sign on the truck. The old name is gone. The new one says 'Nobody Lifts Alone.' Your dad comes back to work. Not lifting. Leading. He trains every new hire. He makes them practice with the strap. He tells them movers' backs aren't made of steel. The government's own safety lifting guide uses fifty-one pounds as a recommended limit for ideal conditions. Your dad says it's a good rule. You say it's a great rule. And you still carry pianos. But always with a partner on the other end of the strap. Even if they're not really doing... much. Your dad catches you one day, letting a new kid think he's carrying half. He grins. Nobody lifts alone, Rio. You grin back. Not even me. Here's what still bugs you, though. One night, you're carrying your sleepy niece up to bed. Light as a feather... nothing to it. And you notice something. Your heart is pounding. Hard. Your heart is a muscle too. If it got ten times stronger... what is it doing to your blood pressure? So what would you do if you were ten times stronger? Would you sign with the wrestling league? Tell us in the comments. And if someone taught you that you never have to carry it alone... tag them and say thanks. Hit like, and subscribe to Rio Animation for more fascinating videos!

long.title: What If Your Body Stopped Aging At 30?
long.rel: spouse who keeps aging (Ruth)
long.rule: Only Rio's body stops aging, and the power cannot be shared with anyone by any means.
long.plant: Ruth's anniversary height marks on the kitchen doorframe, with a smiley face drawn for each new wrinkle.
long.choice: Chase a forever that might not exist... or get Ruth the treatment that actually works, right now.
long.script: Snow is falling hard... on Maple Court. It's 2070. A black helicopter is circling over your street, its spotlight sweeping across the roofs. Your phone buzzes. A text. 'Landing in ten minutes. Come alone. This is your last chance.' On the kitchen floor, your wife Ruth is trying to say your name. She can't. The left side of her face is drooping. Her hand won't grip yours. Ruth is seventy-four. Her hair is... white. Her laugh lines are deep. And you? You look exactly thirty. Same face as your wedding photo on the fridge. Not one gray hair. Not one... wrinkle. A neighbor kid once asked if you were Ruth's grandson. You were seventy... at the time. The helicopter gets louder. Ruth squeezes your hand... weakly. But let's go back. Your name is Rio. It's 2026, and you just turned thirty. You're a paramedic in a quiet suburb outside Denver. You have a mortgage, a dog named Pickles... and a wife who steals the blankets. Here's how aging normally works. Most of your cells can only divide a limited number of times. Scientists call it the Hayflick limit, after Leonard Hayflick, who described it in the 1960s. Every time a cell copies itself, the caps on the ends of your chromosomes get a little shorter. Those caps are called telomeres. Over the decades... damage piles up. Skin thins. Muscles shrink. Eyes stiffen. You? On your thirtieth birthday, it all just... stops. Here's the rule. Your body stops aging. Not time. Not the world. Not the people you love. And you can't share it. Not with a pill. Not with a hug. Not with anyone. So what if your body stopped aging at thirty? Year one. Nobody notices. Why would they? Thirty-one looks a lot like... thirty. Year five. Your friends start buying reading glasses. Most people need them sometime in their forties, when the lens in the eye gets stiffer. You? You can still read a cereal box from across the room. Upside: you never need a new prescription. Downside: your best friend from the station hates you for it... a little. Year ten. Ruth finds her first gray hair. She laughs about it. You check your own head every morning. Nothing. Is that good news? It feels like it... at first. Year fifteen. You're forty-five. You run a marathon. A doctor checks your heart. A common rule of thumb says your max heart rate is two hundred twenty minus your age. Yours still beats like a thirty-year-old's. She checks your chart twice. Then she checks... your birth date. Then the problems start. The problem? Paperwork. Your driver's license photo looks like your son. A cashier refuses to sell you a senior discount coffee, even when you're sixty. A bouncer won't believe your ID. Your bank flags you for possible identity theft. Three times... in one year. And there's a cost. Your coworkers retire. You can't. How do you explain staying thirty? So you change jobs. Then you change towns. Then you change back... because Ruth refuses to leave Maple Court. Year twenty-five. A rumor starts. You've had surgery. You're on some secret cream. Someone on the internet makes a video about you. It gets millions of views. And that's when the billionaire calls. She owns one of the biggest cosmetics companies on the planet. Her offer is simple... and secret. Come to her private lab. Let her scientists study every cell in your body. She'll pay you two hundred million dollars. You'll have a new name, a new face on her billboards, and a new life. One catch. You leave tonight. You never come back. Two hundred million? For your skin? You hang up. She keeps calling. Every year... on your birthday. Here's the hidden cost. It's not your body. It's everything around it. Every year, Ruth gets a little slower on the stairs. Every year, you don't. You go to your best friend's retirement party. Then his seventieth birthday. Then... his funeral. You stand in the back... looking like his grandson. People whisper. Who is that young guy? And there's something worse. You start pulling away. Not on purpose. You just stop making new friends. Why would you? They'll all get old. They'll all leave. You? You won't. Psychologists know that lonely people tend to be less healthy. Your body doesn't age. But loneliness doesn't care. It can still make you sick... from the inside. Ruth notices first. She always... does. Ruth is a middle school art teacher. She's funny. Stubborn. Allergic to cats and to giving up. On your first anniversary, she grabbed a pencil. She marked a line on the kitchen doorframe, right at the top of her head. She wrote the date next to it. Then she made you stand there too. Every anniversary since, she does it again. Two lines. Two dates. At first, the lines look the same. Then, slowly, hers start to drop. Half an inch. Then... an inch. People really do lose height as they age, as the discs in the spine compress. Your line never moves. One year, you can't take it. You tell her you're sorry. Sorry you're stuck. Sorry she's not. Ruth just laughs. She pokes the wrinkle next to her eye. Every wrinkle is a year I got to keep, Rio. Then she points at you. You keep looking young. I'll keep looking... lucky. Every year after that, she draws a tiny smiley face next to her line. One for each new wrinkle. By year forty, there are dozens. A doorframe full of little faces. She calls it her trophy case. You call it... the best thing in the house. Now back to the snow. 2070. Ruth is on the kitchen floor. You've been a paramedic for most of your life. You know these signs. Face drooping. Arm weakness. Speech trouble. It's a stroke. Doctors have a saying. Time is brain. In a common type of stroke, the brain can lose almost two million nerve cells. Every minute. A clot-busting drug can help, but it works best when it's given fast. Usually within a few hours. Sooner is better. You call for an ambulance. The dispatcher's voice is calm. The roads are buried. The nearest ambulance is forty minutes out. Forty minutes. That's a lot of... brain. Then the helicopter lands. Right on your street. Snow blasts sideways. The billionaire steps out in a long white coat. She doesn't waste a second. Rio, my team has done it. We grew your cells. We made a serum. It might stop Ruth's aging too. It might even reverse this. Get in, both of you. Sign the contract on the way. Might? The word hangs in the cold air. Her serum has never been tested on a human. Not once. And here's the rule, the one you learned decades ago. Your power can't be shared. Not with a pill. Not with anyone. You know that. She doesn't. Or she doesn't care. So there it is. Chase a forever that might not exist... or get Ruth the treatment that actually works, right now. You look down at Ruth. She can't speak. But her eyes find yours. Then they flick up... to the doorframe. To the little faces. Every wrinkle is a year I got to keep. You turn to the billionaire. Your helicopter. Can it fly to a hospital? She blinks. What? Can it fly to the stroke center? Right now? If it can, I'll owe you a lot more than a contract. For a long moment, she just stares. Then something in her face... changes. Maybe it's the snow. Maybe it's the little faces on the doorframe she can see through the window. She waves to her pilot. Go. You carry Ruth out. Your thirty-year-old legs don't shake. Your thirty-year-old arms don't tire. For the first time in forty years, you're grateful for every bit of them. Seven minutes later, you land on the hospital roof. The stroke team is already waiting. You called ahead. Paramedic habit. Ruth gets a scan. Then the clot-busting drug. Then you wait. One hour... two. A nurse comes out. She's smiling. Ruth is moving her left hand. And she's asking for you. She's also asking, word for word, why her husband let her get on a helicopter in her bathrobe. Recovery takes... months. Speech therapy. Physical therapy. Walking again, one hallway at a time. You're there for every step. The whole street shows up too. Casseroles. Snow shoveling. A kid from next door draws Ruth a get-well card covered in smiley faces. And the billionaire? She never mentions the contract again. A year later, her company funds a stroke center for your county. No billboard. No name. When Ruth finally comes home, she walks straight to the kitchen doorframe. She picks up the pencil. She marks her line. It's a little lower than last year. And she draws one more smiley face. Then she hands you the pencil. And for the first time in forty-four years, you do something different. You stop marking how tall you are. You start marking what you did with the year. 'Learned to bake bread.' 'Called my sister.' 'Made a new friend.' Because your body stopped aging. But you didn't have to stop living. So... is any of this real? Parts of it are. Animals that barely seem to age really exist. The tiny jellyfish called Turritopsis dohrnii can turn back into an earlier life stage when it's stressed. Naked mole rats can live over thirty years, which is extreme for a rodent. In 2016, scientists estimated that some Greenland sharks live for centuries. In 2006, Shinya Yamanaka showed that adult cells could be reprogrammed back into stem cells. He won a Nobel Prize for it in 2012. Since then, researchers have used parts of that trick to make old mouse cells act younger. But a human who simply stops aging at thirty? Nobody has ever been confirmed. The oldest verified person, Jeanne Calment of France, lived to one hundred twenty-two. And she aged... the whole way. So here's the question. If you could stop at thirty... would you? Even if everyone you love kept going? Or flip it around. What if you could see exactly how much time you had left? A number. Floating over your head. Would you live better... or just count down? Where do you land on this one? Comment below, and name the power you want to see next. Hit like, and subscribe to Rio Animation for more fascinating videos!

long.title: What If You Could Focus For 100 Hours Straight?
long.rel: Nora, Rio's younger sister, a college sophomore with asthma; signature line: One thing at a time.
long.rule: Once Rio locks onto a task nothing else gets in until it is finished, and breaking the lock early causes hours of fog and slow legs.
long.plant: A tiny scratched brass bell Mom tied to Nora's backpack when she got lost as a kid, which she still keeps.
long.choice: Finish the game and win fifty thousand dollars... or let go right now and run into the dark half-blind.
long.script: Your alarm goes off at six. You dump a thousand-piece puzzle on the kitchen table. You blink... and it's done. Every piece. Your coffee? Still hot. Your little sister texts you a photo of her chemistry homework. Thirty problems. Hard? Not for you. You read them once. You solve them in your head... while brushing your teeth. At work, your boss drops a four-hundred-page report on your desk. By noon, you've read it, checked it, and found a typo on page three hundred eighty-one. Nobody else found it. Why? Nobody else got that far. Then you open your lunch bag. There's a sandwich inside. It's Monday's sandwich. Today is... Thursday. Huh. When you lock in... you forget everything else. Even lunch. Apparently, even three lunches. Your name is Rio. You work nights at a big university library. Old building. Marble floors. Two basement levels of books that smell like dust and rain. And you can focus... like nobody alive. Here's how normal works. During World War Two, the Royal Air Force had a problem. Radar operators kept missing things... late in their shifts. Why? So in 1948, a British psychologist named Norman Mackworth built a test. A clock hand that ticked forward... and every so often, jumped twice. The only job? Spot the double jump. How long did people last? Within about half an hour... they started missing it. Attention fades. That's just being human. You? A hundred hours. Four days and four nights without one wandering thought. But there's a rule. Once you lock onto a task, you can't let go until it's done. Nothing else gets in. Not sounds. Not hunger. Not even... your own name. And if you force yourself out early... you crash. Hours of fog. Heavy legs. Like a phone dying at one percent. So what if you could focus for a hundred hours straight? Day one. The library's rare book room is a mess. Ten thousand volumes, half of them in the wrong place. How big a job? Six months, normally. You start on Monday night. You finish... Tuesday morning. Your supervisor just stares at you. How? You shrug. One thing at a time. Upside: you're the best employee in the building. Downside: now every messy job lands on your cart. Next, you try chess. Here's why chess is hard. After just one move each, there are four hundred possible positions. In 1950, the mathematician Claude Shannon estimated about ten to the one hundred twentieth power possible chess games. That's more than the number of atoms in the observable universe. Most players spend years learning patterns. You lock in for sixty hours... and come out playing like a machine. The campus chess club invites you to a casual game. You win... in fourteen moves. Then again. And again. Is this fun? Kind of. Is it fair? You're honestly not sure. And there's a cost. Your brain is about two percent of your body weight. But it burns about twenty percent of your energy. Run it at full power for days, and it eats through your fuel. You forget to eat. Water? You forget that too. Most people can only last about three days without water. During one marathon session, you stand up... and the floor tilts sideways. So now you keep a gallon jug taped to your desk. With a sign. 'DRINK, KHAI.' Does it work? Nope... you still forget. But at least the sign is judging you. Then the requests start. A grad student needs forty sources found by Friday. You find them by midnight. A professor needs a lost letter from 1890 in the archives. You find it in the wrong box, two floors down. Word spreads. People start calling you the Library Ghost. Then a flyer shows up on the bulletin board. The state chess championship. The final is held right here, in the great reading room. First prize? Fifty thousand dollars. You enter. You win round one. Round two. Round six. And now? Only one player stands in your way. His name is Vince. Reigning champion. Calm voice. Sharp eyes. He shakes your hand and says, I've watched your games. You never look up once. Do you even know I'm here? Honestly? Not really. Here's the part nobody sees. Every hour you're awake, a chemical called adenosine builds up in your brain. It's part of what makes you feel sleepy. It's the pressure that pushes you toward bed. Caffeine works by blocking adenosine from its receptors... but it doesn't make the adenosine go away. Your power works the same way. It doesn't erase the tiredness. It just hides it. In 1964, a high school student named Randy Gardner stayed awake for about eleven days for a science fair. By the end, he struggled with memory and concentration. You never go that long. But after every hundred-hour lock, the bill comes due all at once. You sleep fourteen hours. You wake up confused. Once, you put your shoes... in the fridge. And there's a cost that's worse than tired. While you were locked into the rare book room, you missed something. Your sister's nineteenth birthday. She left a cupcake on your desk with a little candle in it. You found it two days later. The candle? Burned all the way down. Your power hides everything that isn't the task. Which raises a scary question. What happens when the thing that matters most... isn't the task? Her name is Nora. She's your little sister. She's a sophomore here, studying biology, and she has asthma. When your parents moved back to Ohio, you made them a promise. I'll look out for her. She's loud and funny and always losing things. Keys. Gloves. Her inhaler... at least twice a week. When she was five, she got lost in a grocery store. So Mom tied a tiny brass bell to her backpack. So we can always find you. Nora is nineteen now. The bell is still there. Scratched. A little bent. She'd never admit she kept it on purpose. She brings you snacks at work, because she knows you forget. She sits on the floor between the shelves and reads while you work. And when you start to lock in, she always asks the same thing. One thing at a time, huh? And you always say it. One thing at a time. And she always answers. Cool. When's it my turn? She laughs when she says it. But you can tell she means it. The night of the final, she squeezes your arm. I'll be downstairs studying. Basement two, by the old atlases. I'll cheer through the floor. Then she jingles the bell, just to annoy you, and walks away. Saturday night. Thunder rolls over campus. The reading room is packed. Cameras. A live stream. A giant check on an easel. You sit down across from Vince. You lock in. The world goes silent. Two hours pass... like two seconds. You're ahead. Checkmate in four moves. You can see it as clearly as your own hands. Then lightning hits a transformer down the street. The lights go out. The emergency lights snap on upstairs. But in basement two... they flicker once. And die. Nora is down there. In total darkness. Dust shakes loose from the old shelves. Her chest tightens. Her airways swell and squeeze. She drops her bag. Her inhaler is inside it. Where? She can't see it. She can't find it. She can barely whisper. She texts you with shaking hands. 'cant breathe. dark. help.' Your phone lights up on the table. Right next to your elbow. And you... don't see it. The rule. Nothing gets in. Vince sees it. He reads it upside down. His face goes pale. Rio! Rio! Nothing. What now? Vince does something smart. He picks up your phone. And sets it down... right on top of your king. Now it's part of the board. Now it's part of the task. You read it. And time slows. Your clock shows eleven minutes. Four moves to win. Maybe ninety seconds. The stairwell to basement two drops forty feet. Down there, three hundred feet of shelving, row after row, no windows. Human eyes need about twenty to thirty minutes to fully adjust to the dark. Do you have twenty minutes? No. If you break the lock now... the crash hits. Fog. Slow legs. You'll be stumbling, nearly blind, through a maze. If you stay locked in, you win in ninety seconds... and then you run. Ninety seconds doesn't sound like much. Unless you're the one who can't breathe. Finish the game and win fifty thousand dollars... or let go right now and run into the dark half-blind. You stand up. The chair falls over. Cameras swing toward you. Vince stares. One thing at a time, you whisper. And right now... the one thing is her. You let go. The crash slams into you like a wave. Your head goes thick. Your legs feel like sandbags. You grab the railing and take the stairs two at a time anyway. Basement two is pure black. You can't see your own hand. Nora! Nora, where are you? Nothing. Only rain on the walls and the silence of a dead building. Your brain is foggy. You can't remember which row the atlases are in. You've walked this floor a thousand times... and right now, it's all gone. Then you hear it. Ding. Tiny. Far to the left. Ding. Ding. Sound travels about eleven hundred feet per second. It finds you instantly. Nora can't shout. But she can shake her bag. And that little brass bell... rings. You follow it. Left. Left again. Row nineteen. Your foot hits her backpack. You dig through it and find the inhaler by feel. You press it into her hand. She breathes in. Albuterol relaxes the muscles around the airways, and it usually starts working within minutes. One breath. Two. Her shoulders drop. Then a beam of light sweeps the aisle. Who? It's Vince, phone flashlight held high, with campus security right behind him. He already called nine-one-one. The paramedics check Nora on the library steps. Is she okay? She's going to be... just fine. Upstairs, the tournament director announces it. Vince wins by forfeit. But Vince shakes his head. Not like this. Rematch next month. No clock. No cameras. The crowd starts clapping. For him. For you. For the girl on the steps wrapped in a blanket, holding a bent brass bell. Two days later, you show up at Nora's dorm with a cupcake. One candle. You light it. Happy very late birthday. She rolls her eyes. But she's smiling. One thing at a time, huh? You nod. One thing at a time. You first. But something strange happened that night. You were locked in. Nothing should have gotten through. And yet, somehow... that bell did. So maybe the rule isn't a wall. Maybe it's a door. And if one tiny sound can get through... what else can? So what would you do with a hundred hours of perfect focus? Tell us in the comments. And if you've got someone whose bell you'd hear through anything... call them tonight. Hit like, and subscribe to Rio Animation for more fascinating videos!

long.title: What If One Minute Felt Like One Hour?
long.rel: Pops, Rio's dad, a retired ramp worker with hearing loss flying home from Arizona; signature line: 'See you on the ground' / I'll be the one waving.
long.rule: Only Rio's mind speeds up sixty times; the body still moves at normal speed, so there is always more time to think but never more time to act.
long.plant: Pops taught Rio airport ramp hand signals as a kid, including both arms crossed high above the head for emergency stop.
long.choice: Stare into the camera and win a million dollars... or drop the phone and talk to Pops with your arms.
long.script: A raindrop slides down the airport window. You watch it fall. Slowly... like it's thinking about it. A hummingbird hovers outside the food court glass. Its wings beat about fifty times a second. Most people see a blur. You? You can count every flap. A man in a suit tries to sneak into the boarding line ahead of you. You notice him... about three steps before he notices himself. Your coworker throws a pen at your head as a joke. You have time to sigh, think about lunch, and step aside. The pen sails... right past. Your coworker groans. How do you always do that? Then the barista hands you your coffee. Enjoy your flight! You've had what feels like forty-five minutes to plan your answer. And you say... you too. You don't even have a flight. Why? You work here. Your name is Rio. You're a gate agent at one of the busiest airports in the country. Fifty gates. Thousands of strangers. Everybody... late. And for you... every minute lasts an hour. Here's normal. Something surprises you. How fast do you react? About a quarter of a second. A single blink takes about a third of a second. Most people don't even notice their own blinks. You? You watch your eyelids come down like a garage door. Twenty slow seconds... of darkness. Every. Single. Blink. Your mind runs sixty times faster than everyone else's. But there's a rule. Only your mind speeds up. Your body? Normal speed. Normal legs. Normal arms. Normal voice. You get an hour to think... but only a minute to act. Fair? Not really. Plenty of time to think. Never more time to move. So what if one minute felt like one hour? At first, it's amazing. A passenger yells at you about a missed connection. Normally? You'd panic. Now you have twenty quiet minutes to plan the perfect calm answer. He leaves smiling. Upside: you're the best gate agent on the concourse. Downside: you've rebooked forty flights in your head before your coffee cools. Then you try rock, paper, scissors with Gabe, the guy at gate twelve. Gabe is a skeptic. He doesn't believe anything he can't see. A human hand takes a fraction of a second to change shape. You see it forming... like clay. Rock? Paper? You always know. You win nine times in a row. Gabe throws up his hands. You're a cheater, man. Or a wizard. Probably... a cheater. Then you try trivia. On the quiz show Jeopardy, the final round gives players thirty seconds of think music. For you, thirty seconds is a half-hour study session. You sign up for 'Sixty Seconds to a Million', a TV quiz show. Every round, the host calls you on video. Ten questions. Sixty seconds. You answer all of them. Every... single... time. A producer from the show calls you personally. You're our first finalist ever. One more round, Rio. One live call. One million dollars. Are you ready? And there's a cost. Because your mind doesn't just think faster. It lives longer. One day of yours holds about sixty days of thinking. A week feels like more than a year. Waiting in line? A five-minute line feels like five hours. A delayed flight... is a prison sentence. And then there's talking. People speak about a hundred fifty words a minute. To you, that's a hundred fifty words an hour. Every word lands... like a slow drip from a faucet. You stop calling friends. You stop going to movies. Why sit through two hours that feel like a hundred twenty? Your brain is about two percent of your body weight. Its energy share? About a fifth. Run it at sixty times speed, and you're starving by ten a.m. You keep granola bars in every pocket. Gabe calls you the snack goblin. But the real cost is quieter. Life feels long. And lonely. Your thoughts have nobody to keep up with them. And somewhere deep inside, you start to worry. What if one day, you see something terrible coming? All the time in the world to watch it... and no time to stop it? His name is Pops. He's your dad. Thirty years on the airport ramp, waving jets into their gates with orange wands. He taught you the signals when you were six. Arms straight up means this way to me. Arms waving means slow down. And both arms crossed high above your head... means emergency stop. Stop everything. Right now. You practiced in the backyard until Mom laughed. Thirty years next to jet engines also cost Pops something. His... hearing. Noise above about eighty-five decibels, day after day, can damage tiny hair cells in the inner ear. Once they're gone, they don't grow back. Now Pops wears hearing aids. And in loud places, he mostly reads faces. Pops talks slow, too. Long pauses. For most people, it's charming. For you? Every pause feels like... ten minutes. Over the years, you started cutting his calls short. Gotta go, Pops. Work stuff. He never complained. Now he's been in Arizona for six months, helping your aunt after her surgery. And he's finally... flying home. Today. Before every flight, he texts the same thing. 'See you on the ground.' And you always text back. 'I'll be the one waving.' The terminal is packed. Holiday weekend. You're on break, standing at the top of the long escalator down to baggage claim. Pops's flight just landed. You can see him far below, by the carousel, in his old orange ramp jacket. Then your phone buzzes. It's the show. It's the live call. The host's big grin fills the screen. Rules, Rio! Eyes on the camera. Look away, you forfeit. Ten questions. Sixty seconds. For one million dollars. Starting... now. Question one. You answer instantly. Question two. Easy. And then you see it. Just below you on the escalator, a little girl in soft rubber clogs. Her mom is busy with a stroller. The girl's foot drifts against the side of the moving step. Soft rubber can grab the edge... and pull. Her shoe catches. She tugs. It doesn't come loose. She starts to cry. And she's riding straight down. Toward the bottom. Where the steps fold flat... under the metal comb plate. Your mind kicks into full speed. A typical escalator moves about a hundred feet per minute. She's about twenty feet from the bottom. Twelve seconds. In your head... twelve minutes. Plenty of time to think. You think. There's a red emergency stop button at the bottom of every escalator. Right next to the handrail. Right next to Pops. Can you run down? The steps are packed with suitcases. Can you shout? The terminal roars. And Pops can barely hear anyway. Can you call him? He'd have to find his phone, unlock it, answer it. Too slow. The rule. Your mind has all the time in the world. Your body has twelve seconds. And the host is still talking. Question three, Rio! Eyes on the screen! Stare into the camera and win a million dollars... or drop the phone and talk to Pops with your arms. You drop the phone. It clatters on the floor. Somewhere, a host is yelling. You don't hear him. You climb onto the steel ledge so your whole body is above the crowd. Pops! He can't hear you. But you knew he wouldn't. You throw both arms high above your head. And you cross them. Hard. Emergency stop. Way down at the bottom... Pops looks up. Thirty years on the ramp. His body knows that signal before his brain does. He doesn't ask why. He just... moves. One step. Two. His palm slams the red button. The escalator jolts. And... stops. The girl's clog is still stuck, eight feet from the comb plate. Eight feet. Her mom wraps her arms around her. A janitor works the shoe free. Her toes? Wiggling. Not a scratch. People start to clap. First one. Then dozens. Somebody yells, Who's the guy in the uniform? Gabe yells back. That's Rio! He's a wizard! You pick up your phone. The screen says 'Call Ended.' Forfeit. One million dollars... gone in three seconds. You don't feel sad. Not even... a little. Because Pops is walking up the stopped escalator. Slowly. One step at a time... in his orange jacket. He reaches the top. He's breathing hard. He smiles. Still remember the signals, huh? You nod. I'll be the one waving. He pulls you into a hug. A normal hug. Three seconds long. But for you... it lasts three minutes. Three whole minutes of his old jacket, his aftershave, his slow, steady heartbeat. And for the first time in your life, you're glad time is slow. That night, you sit at his kitchen table. He tells a long story about Arizona. Long pauses. You don't check your phone. You don't cut him off. You just let every second stretch. Two weeks later, the producer calls back. The video of you went everywhere. The show wants you back for a special episode. You say maybe. First, you've got a dinner with Pops. Is any of this real? Kind of. In 2007, neuroscientist David Eagleman and his team ran a wild experiment. Volunteers dropped about a hundred feet, backward, into a net. Terrifying. Afterward, they said their fall felt about a third longer than other people's falls looked. But here's the twist. During the fall, they wore a wrist display. It flashed numbers too fast to read. If time truly slowed down for them, they should've been able to read it. Could they? No. So scared brains don't think faster. They remember more. More memory feels like more time. Meanwhile, some animals really do see the world in finer slices of time. A house fly can detect flickers several times faster than you can. That's part of why it's so hard to swat. But a human mind running sixty times faster? That's... fiction. At least for now. Would you even want it? So here's the strange part. Ever since the escalator, something has changed. Sometimes, when Pops laughs... the slow time switches on all by itself. No danger. No adrenaline. Just joy. So what's really controlling your clock? Could you handle it? Tell us in the comments, and tell us what we should crank up next. Hit like, and subscribe to Rio Animation for more fascinating videos!

long.title: What If Your Heart Beat Only Once A Minute?
long.rel: Dr. Kim, chief of cardiology and Rio's mentor who paid for Rio's first certification; signature line: Slow is not stopped.
long.rule: Rio's heart beats exactly once a minute and can never speed up, not for exercise, fear or emotion.
long.plant: Dr. Kim's old wooden metronome set to 110 beats a minute, used for her free Saturday CPR classes and kept in her car's cup holder.
long.choice: Get in the car and fly toward the stars... or stay on this cold concrete and be someone's heartbeat.
long.script: Snow blows sideways into level four of the hospital parking garage. You're on your knees. Your hands are locked together on the chest of the woman who taught you everything. Push. Push. Push. Two inches deep. Over... and over. Behind you, a black SUV idles. A man in a gray coat taps his watch. Rio. The plane leaves in forty minutes. You don't answer. Why? You can't. Because inside your own chest, your heart beats. Once. And then... nothing. For a whole minute. The edges of your vision start to go dark... like someone closing a curtain. How did you end up here? And why can't your heart just... speed up? But let's go back. Your name is Rio. You're an EKG technician on the cardiology ward. You glue little stickers on people's chests and read the squiggly lines their hearts make. Every day, you watch hearts. Fast ones. Tired ones. And sometimes... broken ones. Here's normal. A healthy adult heart at rest beats about sixty to a hundred times a minute. That's roughly a hundred thousand beats a day. Each squeeze pushes out about a third of a cup of blood. You? You get one beat a minute. One giant squeeze. Roughly five liters. Basically your entire blood supply... in one push. Sound efficient? Wait for it. But there's a rule. Once a minute. Never faster. Not when you run. Not when you're scared. Not when someone you love walks into the room. Your heart has one speed... and it's slow. So what if your heart beat only once a minute? Day one at work. You hook yourself up to the EKG machine, just to see. The screen shows a long... flat... line. Then one huge spike. Then flat again. A nurse runs in with the crash cart. Code blue! Then she sees you sipping coffee. Oh. It's just Rio. Never... mind. Upside: you are the calmest person alive. Spider on your pillow? Your heart doesn't jump. Job interview? Steady... as a rock. Bad news? You deliver it gently, without a tremble. Patients love you. You make waiting rooms feel quieter. Downside: stairs. Hard exercise? A healthy heart pumps several times more blood than at rest. It speeds up to feed your muscles. Yours? It can't. So you climb one flight... and stop. Climb another... and stop. Your coworker passes you carrying two coffees and a bagel. Need a hand, grandpa? Very... funny. So how does your blood keep moving between beats? Here's a real trick of your body. Your aorta, the biggest artery you have, is stretchy. Every time your heart squeezes, it balloons out a little. Then it slowly springs back, pushing blood forward between beats. How often? Normally, about once a second. Yours has to stretch... and hold... for sixty seconds. When your heart does beat, it's a thump. A big one. How big? People can see your shirt jump. But in 2019, scientists strapped a sensor to a blue whale. On deep dives, its heart dropped to about two beats a minute. Your closest relative? Apparently, it's a whale. And there's a bonus. He doesn't smile... much. In space, Rio, we worry about stress. Panic. Oxygen. You barely use any of them. Then he slides a folder across the counter. 'Deep Space Candidate Program.' A trip to Mars could take about seven months, one way. We need someone calm for every one of those days. Training starts in Houston. The car leaves Friday night. Will you be on it? But the slow heart has a price. Stand up fast from a chair. Gravity pulls blood down into your legs. In most people, the heart instantly speeds up to push it back to the brain. Doctors call the drop orthostatic hypotension. For most people, it's a quick head rush. For you? There's no speeding up. You stand... and the room spins. Twice this month, you've ended up on the floor of the supply closet. Your fingers? Always cold. Your toes are always numb. And there's a quieter cost. Your brain uses about a fifth of your body's oxygen. If blood stops reaching it, a person can pass out in about ten seconds. So every single minute... you're living on one beat. One. If that beat ever comes up short? There's no backup. And then there's the part that stings. Your last date ended early. She said, Your heart doesn't even race around me. Do you feel anything at all? Did you feel anything? You did. You just couldn't... prove it. People see your calm and call it cold. You start to wonder if they're right. And one fear keeps coming back. What happens on the day someone needs you to be fast... and all you have is slow? Her name is Dr. Kim. Sixty-four years old. Chief of cardiology. Reading glasses... on a chain. Sneakers with her suit. Ten years ago, you were a nervous kid pushing a mop down this hallway. She saw you staring at the heart monitors one night. You like hearts? Then learn them. She paid for your first certification course. When your own weird heart showed up, you were scared. You thought you were broken. She looked at your EKG for a long time. Then she said it. Slow is not stopped, Rio. You wrote it on a sticky note. It's still on your locker. Every Saturday morning, Dr. Kim teaches a free CPR class in the hospital lobby. She uses an old wooden metronome. It ticks a hundred ten times a minute. Push to the beat, she tells everyone. Every heart needs a beat to follow. The metronome rides in the cup holder of her little blue car. She refuses to buy a new one. But lately, she's been rubbing her chest. Just heartburn, she says. Is it? You ask about her checkup. She waves you off. I'm the cardiologist. Who's going to tell me? Friday night. Your last shift. The car to Houston is waiting on level four of the garage. Dr. Kim insists on walking you out. She hugs you by the elevator. She's proud. You can tell. Go see the stars, she says. Then she takes three steps toward her car... and drops. You're beside her in a second. You shake her shoulders. Dr. Kim! No answer. She's making slow, strange gasps. That's not real breathing. You know that from her own class. You check her pulse. Nothing. Sudden cardiac arrest. You yell for help and call the hospital operator. Code team, level four, east garage! The team has to cross the sky bridge and come down the ramps. Three minutes. Maybe four. Without blood flow, brain cells start dying within about four to six minutes. You lock your hands. You start pushing. Hard and fast. A hundred to a hundred twenty compressions a minute. At least two inches deep. And here's the rule. CPR is brutal work. Your arms burn. Your muscles scream for oxygen. A normal heart would race to feed them. Yours? Thump. And then a minute of nothing. After about ninety seconds, your vision tunnels. Your hands tingle. Your rhythm starts slipping. A hundred ten... a hundred... ninety. If you pass out now, nobody's pushing at all. Theo leans out of the SUV. Rio, the plane won't wait. If you're not on it... the seat goes to the backup. Get in the car and fly toward the stars... or stay on this cold concrete and be someone's heartbeat. You look down at Dr. Kim's face. Slow is not stopped. You stay. But you can't do it alone. So you do the one thing your slow heart is perfect for. You stay calm. You look up. A pizza delivery guy is frozen by his car. A teenage girl stands with her phone out. And Theo. You! Pizza guy! Kneel here. Hands right here. Push when I say push. Then you yank open Dr. Kim's car door. You grab the wooden metronome. You set it on the concrete. Tick. Tick. Tick. A hundred ten. Every heart needs a beat to follow. Push to the beat! The pizza guy pushes. You count out loud in a steady voice. You point at the girl. The red box by the elevator. It says AED. Run! She runs. And you turn to the gray coat. Theo. You're next. He stares. Then he takes off his coat... and kneels. Two minutes. Switch. long.title: What If You Never Felt Cold Again?
long.rel: Grandpa, a 79-year-old fisherman in an orange wool hat who warmed Rio's hands as a kid; signature line: Cold is a warning, kid. Listen to it.
long.rule: Rio's internal furnace runs on food fuel with no cold warning signs, and when the fuel runs out it shuts off all at once.
long.plant: Grandpa made Rio practice tying a bowline one-handed with eyes closed every Sunday, because someday the other hand will be busy holding on.
long.choice: Finish the swim and win the Arctic... or turn back and spend your heat on Grandpa.
long.script: Black water. Snow falling into it. You're swimming hard toward a white shape in the dark. It's an overturned boat. And clinging to it... an old man in an orange wool hat. Grandpa! Sixty feet to go. Then... fifty. And then, without any warning at all, something inside you clicks off. Like a furnace at three in the morning. For the first time in four years... the water feels cold. Not cool. Cold. How cold? It slams into your chest like a door. You gasp. Your arms go stiff. Forty-one degree water, and you're dressed for summer. Grandpa is shouting something. You can barely... hear him. How did you get here? And why didn't you feel it coming? But let's go back. Your name is Rio. You live in a small fishing town on the Alaska coast. One road. One diner... and one stoplight that nobody obeys. Two hundred boats in the harbor. You work the dock at the seafood plant, unloading salmon and halibut in the rain. And you haven't felt cold... in four years. Here's normal. Your body works hard to stay near ninety-eight point six degrees. Drop below ninety-five, and doctors call it hypothermia. Your thinking slows. Your hands fumble. Your speech... slurs. And here's the scary part. Water versus air, same temperature? Water steals your heat about twenty-five times faster. That's why falling into Alaska's water is so dangerous. You? You could float in it all afternoon. Your body runs like a furnace. Your core never drops. Not even... one degree. But there's a rule. Your furnace runs on fuel. Food. Every minute in freezing weather burns through it. And because you never feel cold... you never feel the warning. No shivers. No numb fingers. No chattering teeth. When the fuel runs out, the furnace doesn't fade. It just... shuts off. All at once. Scary? Very. So what if you never felt cold again? Upside: no more winter coat. It's ten degrees on the dock, and you're in a T-shirt. Your coworkers wear... four layers. They look at you like you're a polar bear in disguise. One of them asks, Aren't you freezing? Nope. Want my gloves? Anyone? Downside: you can't tell when anything is cold. You hand a customer a frozen fish with your bare hands. She... shrieks. Your fridge breaks, and you don't notice for three days. The milk? The milk notices. Upside: you save a fortune. Your heating bill drops to almost nothing. Neighbors start dropping their kids at your place on snow days. Why? Nobody whines about the cold there. Mostly because... you keep the heat off. Then it gets bigger. A crab boat gets its propeller tangled in a line. In normal people, cold water triggers something called cold shock. The first minute brings a huge involuntary gasp. If your head is underwater during that gasp... you can breathe in seawater. Divers usually need a thick suit to work down there. You? You dive in... with a mask and a knife. Ten minutes later, the propeller is free. The captain just stares at you. Dripping. Smiling. In a T-shirt. What are you? Then a video of you swimming in the harbor in January goes viral. Two million views... in a weekend. Comments pour in. Is this guy real? And one of those comments is from a woman named Hailey. She works for a big outdoor gear company. We want to sponsor you, Rio. An Arctic expedition. You'd swim and trek across sea ice, wearing almost nothing, on camera. Gear. Salary. A documentary. But first, a test. One mile across the bay. At night. In December. Live. Can you do it? You say yes before she even finishes. And there's a cost. Your furnace burns a lot. How does a normal body make heat? Shivering is a big one. And hard shivering burns energy fast. Your body skips the shiver and goes straight to the burn. So you're always hungry. You eat breakfast. Then... second breakfast. Then a third one, standing over the sink. You lose eight pounds in a month without trying. The real danger is quieter. Cold is your body's alarm. It tells you to get out, go inside, put on a hat. Without it, you have no idea how much fuel you have left. Twice this year, the furnace has flickered. Once on the dock. Once on a hike. Each time, you felt the wind for one second... and then it was gone. Both times? You'd skipped lunch. And there's one more cost. Nobody can warm you up anymore. Hot cocoa? Just brown water. A blanket is just weight. And the one thing you used to love most... doesn't work anymore. You'll see why. Grandpa is seventy-nine. Fifty years on fishing boats. Hands like old baseball gloves. He never goes anywhere without the orange wool hat Grandma knit for him in 1982. It's faded now. Patched... twice. When you were little, he'd take you out on his skiff before school. When your fingers turned red, he'd take your hands in his. And rub them hard. Then he'd breathe on them, like a little campfire. Better? Better. And every single time, he'd say the same thing. Cold is a warning, kid. Listen to it. He also taught you a knot. The bowline. Sailors call it the king of knots, because it doesn't slip, and it doesn't jam. Grandpa made you tie it with one hand. With your eyes closed. Every... Sunday. Why one hand, Grandpa? Because someday your other hand will be busy holding on. These days, the sea is mostly done with Grandpa. His knees are bad. But he still takes the skiff out to check his last crab pot. Your mom wants him to stop. Will he? Nope. Commercial fishing is one of the most dangerous jobs in America. And Grandpa? He's done it longer than most of these boats have existed. When you tell him about the sponsorship, he's quiet for a long time. Then he says it. Cold is a warning, kid. Listen to it. And you feel your chest tighten. Because you can't. Not... anymore. And deep down, you know that's the problem. December. Nine p.m. The night of the test. Snow drifts down over the bay. The water is forty-one degrees. A sponsor boat follows you with lights and cameras. Hailey is on deck, watching the live chat explode. You dive in. You swim. Half a mile. Three-quarters. Easy. The furnace is roaring. But you were so nervous today... you barely ate. Then the radio on Hailey's boat... crackles. It's the harbormaster. Skiff flipped by the breakwater! One man in the water! Orange hat! Your stomach drops. Grandpa. He went out to pull his last pot before the storm. The breakwater is a quarter mile behind you. The finish line is a quarter mile ahead. Here's what you know. In water like this, there's a rule rescuers use. One minute to get your breathing under control. About ten minutes of useful movement before your arms and legs stop cooperating. And maybe an hour before you pass out. Grandpa is seventy-nine. He's already been in for two minutes. Rescue boats from the harbor? Maybe ten minutes out. And your furnace? You can feel nothing. That's the whole problem. It could have twenty minutes left. Or two. Hailey shouts from the boat. Rio! You're almost there! Finish, and the expedition is yours! Turn back, and the sponsor walks. The cameras are rolling. Two hundred thousand people are watching live. Finish the swim and win the Arctic... or turn back and spend your heat on Grandpa. You turn around. You swim harder than you've ever swum in your life. A quarter mile. Every stroke burns fuel. You can't feel how much. Sixty feet. Fifty. And then... click. The furnace dies. And the cold hits all at once. The gasp rips out of your chest. Your heart pounds. Your breath comes in short, wild bursts. Every instinct says thrash. Fight. Then you hear his voice... cracked and stubborn. Not in your memory. For real. Across the water. Rio! Float! Breathe! One minute! Cold is a warning, kid! Listen to it! You listen. You stop fighting. You lie back. You breathe. In. Out. Slower. Slower. One minute. Then you swim the last forty feet. Grandpa's hands are shaking. Yours are going numb fast. You can't climb up the hull. Neither can he. And in a few minutes, neither of you will be able to hold on. So you grab the loose rope trailing off the skiff. One hand on the boat. One hand free. You loop it around both of you. Eyes stinging. Fingers clumsy. The king of knots. One-handed. Just like every Sunday. It holds. Now even if your grip fails... the rope won't. You press against him, chest to chest. You share what little heat you have. Rescuers call that huddling. It slows heat loss. A light sweeps across the water. It's the sponsor boat. Hailey told the captain to turn around. Right behind it, the harbor boat, horn blaring. And two fishing boats from the dock. Hands grab you. Blankets. A deck... under your back. Somebody cuts the rope. Somebody yells, The knot held! In the ambulance, you're wrapped in a warming blanket. Your teeth are chattering. Loud... very loud. For the first time in four years, you're shivering. And it feels... wonderful. Grandpa sits across from you, gray-faced but grinning, his orange hat soaked. He reaches over. He takes your hands. He rubs them hard. Then he breathes on them. Like a little campfire. Better? You can't stop smiling. Better. Back on shore, the whole town is waiting at the dock. Coffee. Soup. Applause. Hailey walks up, shaking her head. The sponsor pulled out. But my phone won't stop ringing. People want to help you. Maybe something bigger. You shrug. Cold is a warning. I listened. Is any of this real? Partly. In 2007, endurance swimmer Lewis Pugh swam one kilometer at the North Pole. The water was below freezing. It took him about nineteen minutes. Afterward, he said his fingers stayed numb for months. In 2009, several research teams confirmed that adults still carry brown fat. It's a special tissue that burns energy just to make heat. And regular cold water swimmers? Over time, their bodies can soften the cold shock gasp. But turning off the feeling of cold completely? That's... fiction. And honestly, it would be dangerous. Cold is how your body keeps you alive. So would you really want to lose it? Weeks later, a doctor at the clinic runs a scan. Your brown fat isn't just big. It's glowing. And it seems to be... growing. Into what? Believe it or not? long.title: What If You Could Taste Every Single Ingredient?
long.rel: Mom, who opened the roadside diner 22 years ago and wears the same yellow apron; signature line: Good food tells the truth.
long.rule: Light tasting is always on, but a deep read naming every ingredient in a dish leaves Rio's tongue completely blank for one hour.
long.plant: Mom keeps a bag of lemon drops in the torn pocket of her yellow apron to reset Rio's overloaded tongue.
long.choice: Taste the stolen sauce and save the diner... or keep your tongue clear and follow your warning.
long.script: You take one sip of coffee. Colombian beans. Roasted three days ago. A little too long. And the water? It came through an old copper pipe. You set the mug down. How do you know all that? You just... do. A trucker at the counter bites into a burger and frowns. Something's off. What is it? You take one tiny bite. The pickles came from a new supplier. Too much vinegar. A little girl in a booth won't eat her pancakes. You taste the syrup. It's not maple. It's corn syrup... with a fake maple label. You switch it. She grins. The cook brags that his famous chili has eleven secret spices. Eleven? You taste it. It has nine. And one of them... is ketchup. He looks at you like you just read his diary. Then Dottie, the waitress, sets down your lunch. You take a bite. How long did it sit under the heat lamp? Eleven minutes. Thanks, Dottie. Your name is Rio. You work the counter at your mom's roadside diner on a two-lane highway in Ohio. Twelve stools. Six booths. And one pie case... that people drive forty miles for. And you can taste every single ingredient in everything. Here's normal. Your tongue has thousands of taste buds. Each one is a tiny cluster of cells. They wear out and get replaced... about every couple of weeks. Most people can pick out the five basic tastes. Sweet. Salty. Sour. Bitter. And umami, that savory taste in broth and cheese. Who named umami? A Japanese chemist, Kikunae Ikeda, in 1908. He was studying a seaweed soup. Most people taste a stew and say... it's good. You? You taste a stew and read it like a list. Every herb. Every pinch of salt. Even the brand... of the broth. But there's a rule. Light tasting is always on. That part is free. But a deep read, naming every single ingredient in a complicated dish, costs you. After one deep read, your tongue goes blank for a full hour. No taste at all. Your food? Wet cardboard. One deep read... then sixty minutes of nothing. So what if you could taste every single ingredient? Upside: you're a human food inspector. The milk truck shows up a day late. Is it safe? You taste one drop. Sour... by tomorrow. Mom sends it back. Downside: can you enjoy a candy bar? Not really. You taste the factory. You taste the wax on the wrapper. Mmm... wax. Upside: the old recipes come back. A widow down the road misses her late husband's pot roast. Nobody could ever copy it. She brings you a frozen leftover from 2019. You do one deep read. Mustard. Coffee. One cinnamon stick. She cooks it that Sunday... and cries into the gravy. Good tears. Then the internet finds you. A customer films you naming all fourteen ingredients in a stranger's casserole. Three million views. Is this guy real? Food bloggers show up. A TV crew. A man with homemade hot sauce. Why does his wife hate it? You taste it. Too much garlic. And then a black car pulls into the gravel lot. A man in a crisp white chef's jacket walks in. You know his face. A TV chef. Frozen dinners with his face on the box. He orders pie. Does he eat it? No. Instead, he sets a small glass jar on the counter. Dark red. It's barbecue sauce. From a tiny family rib shack two states away. Sixty years old. The recipe has never been written down. How did he get it? He doesn't say. Do you really want to know? I need you to read it, Rio. Every ingredient. Every amount. I'll bottle it, and I'll pay you one hundred thousand dollars. And there's a cost. Some people are born with far more taste buds than others. Supertasters. For them, bitter things taste much more bitter. Broccoli. Black coffee. Grapefruit. You? A supertaster times a thousand. Does food still taste delicious? Not anymore. It tastes like a report. Too much salt. Not enough acid. A burned spot on the bottom of the pan. Even Mom's cooking. Her chicken and dumplings used to taste like coming home. Now? Flour. Thyme. Chicken stock. Black pepper. A list. Just a list. You eat less. You smile less. Does Mom notice? Of course she does. And the blank hours are scary. Bitter taste is one of the body's oldest warning systems. Many poisonous plants taste bitter. Ever wonder why kids spit out bitter things? That's part of it. During a blank hour... you have no warnings at all. You could eat anything. Spoiled. Burned. Dangerous. Would you know? Never. Her name is Mom. Everybody calls her Mom. Even the truckers. Even people... older than her. She opened this diner twenty-two years ago. A loan. A used griddle. And you, in a car seat on the counter. She still wears the same yellow apron. Torn pocket. A grease stain... shaped like Florida. And in that pocket, she always keeps a little bag of lemon drops. Whenever your tongue gets overloaded, she hands you one. Here, baby. Reset your tongue. The sour hits fast and wipes everything clean. Like hitting refresh. Why has her diner lasted so long? Mom always gives the same answer. Good food tells the truth. You say it too. It's on a sign above the pie case. 'Good food tells the truth.' But lately, the truth is ugly. The landlord raised the rent. The diner is three months behind. Mom hides the letters under the register. You find them anyway. A hundred thousand dollars? It would fix everything. You tell Mom about the TV chef. She goes quiet. Then she says, That sauce belongs to somebody's grandma, Rio. You know that, right? You do. So why don't you say no? There's one more thing. The smoke and carbon monoxide alarm by the storeroom has been chirping for a week. Low battery. Mom pulled the battery out to stop the noise. I'll grab one Tuesday, she says. Tuesday never comes. Saturday night. A huge storm rolls across the cornfields. The diner is packed. It's the volunteer fire department's pie night fundraiser. Seventy people. Every booth full. Then lightning hits a pole. The power dies. Candles come out. People cheer, because it feels like a party. The cook drags the old gas generator into the back storeroom. The freezers need power. Too much rain to put it outside, he says. He props the door open a crack. And at seven sharp, the black car pulls in. The TV chef walks right up to the counter. He sets down the jar. He opens a laptop. His investors are on a live video call. Read it now, Rio. On camera. Tonight, or the deal is gone. Then something tickles your tongue. Faint. Strange. What is that? Sour metal. Like licking a battery... but in the air. Here's the thing. Carbon monoxide has no color. No smell. No taste. For everyone else, it's invisible. It comes from burning fuel, like a generator engine. In the United States, more than four hundred people die from accidental carbon monoxide poisoning every year. It grabs your hemoglobin over two hundred times more tightly than oxygen. So your blood carries less and less oxygen... and you don't even notice. The first signs? Headache. Dizziness. Feeling sick. Confusion. And Mom? She went back to the storeroom ten minutes ago... for more pie. And here's your rule. Deep read the sauce, and your tongue goes blank for an hour. That faint sour metal taste? Gone. The only alarm in this building that works... is your tongue. And the TV chef is holding a spoon right in front of your face. Taste the stolen sauce and save the diner... or keep your tongue clear and follow your warning. You push the spoon away. You walk toward the kitchen. The taste gets stronger. You pass the storeroom door. Stronger. Your head starts to throb. Your thoughts go fuzzy. Your own blood is soaking up the gas. Are you walking right into it? Yes. Mom! Silence. The storeroom is dark. The generator roars. The air tastes like a mouthful of pennies. Your eyes water. The kitchen is spinning. And now your tongue is overloaded. Too much. Coffee, grease, smoke, sugar, rain, metal. It's all noise. You can't tell which way the gas is coming from. Your power is almost enough... but not quite. Then your hand finds it. Mom's yellow apron, hanging on the hook. You dig into the torn pocket. A lemon drop. Reset your tongue. You crunch it. Sour floods your mouth. And everything goes clean. The noise drops away. Now you can taste it... again. Clear and sharp. The metal is strongest... down low. By the floor. You drop to your knees. There. Behind the flour sacks. Mom is sitting on the floor, slumped against the shelf. Her eyes are half-open. I just... got a little dizzy. You try to lift her. But your legs are jelly. Your arms won't work right. Dottie! Dottie! The whole diner hears you. Dottie comes running with three volunteer firefighters still holding paper plates. Gas! Generator! Get her out! Big hands grab Mom. Somebody kills the generator. Somebody kicks open the back door. Fresh air pours in like cold water. Out under the awning, in the rain... Mom breathes. Deep. Again. Again. The firefighters know exactly what this is. Oxygen masks. One for her... one for you. An ambulance takes you both in, just to be safe. Mom's going to be fine. So are you. At the hospital, you check your phone. The TV chef is gone. The deal is gone. But his laptop was still live when you walked away. And his investors saw everything. Two days later, the rib shack family hears what happened. They call the police. The TV chef? He has a lot of explaining to do. And then the town does something you'd never expect. The fire department's pie night video gets shared everywhere. People start mailing you checks. Truckers leave twenty-dollar tips... under your coffee cups. The rib shack family drives two states with a hundred bottles of their real sauce. They sell them in the gravel lot. Every dollar goes to the diner's rent. By the end of the month, the diner is caught up. Mom puts a new battery in the alarm... just to make a point. Then she installs... two more. Never run a generator inside. Not in a storeroom. Not in your garage. Not even with the door cracked. A week later, Mom sets a slice of cherry pie in front of you. You brace yourself for the list. Cherries. Butter. Sugar. Flour. But this time... it doesn't come. It just tastes like pie. Warm. Sweet. A little too much cinnamon. Like home. You laugh. Your eyes sting. Mom smiles and taps the sign over the pie case. Good food tells the truth, baby. You nod. And the truth is... it's perfect. But something strange has started. Your tongue isn't just tasting food anymore. Last night, you held a stranger's hand. And you tasted... salt. Like tears. So what is your tongue really reading? And what else can you taste?
