long.title: What If Your Fingertips Were 100 Times More Sensitive?
long.rel: Ray, Rio's best friend since fourth grade and partner in the locksmith shop
long.rule: The power only works when Rio's heart is calm, because a racing pulse thumps inside the fingertips and drowns out every other sensation.
long.plant: Ray taps the counter once a second when he thinks, a habit that quietly calms Rio, and repeats his dad's saying 'Slow hands, slow heart.'
long.choice: Drive to the bank and crack Dante's vault to save the shop, or follow a panicked mom and open the floor safe her son is trapped in.
long.script: Your morning coffee cup is talking to you. Not out loud. The barista wrote your name on it in marker, and you feel every letter... through the cardboard. K. H. A. I. Your name is Rio. You run a tiny lock and key shop with your best friend. And lately, your fingers have been acting strange. A customer slides a five dollar bill across the counter. You feel the raised ink of the portrait... and the fibers woven inside the paper. Your phone buzzes in the back room. You feel it through the floor... before you hear it. A woman hands you a house key to copy. You run your thumb along the teeth and frown. Somebody already copied this one. Badly. The third cut is a hair too shallow. She blinks. How could you possibly know that? Honestly? You just... know. Then the shop cat hops onto the counter. You pet her... and you can count every single whisker... with your knuckles. Okay. That part is just weird. Here's the thing. Your fingertips were already amazing. Press two toothpicks against a fingertip, about two millimeters apart. Most people feel two separate points. Try the same thing on someone's back? The points need to be around forty millimeters apart. That's more than an inch and a half. Fingertips are packed with tiny touch sensors. Some, called Pacinian corpuscles, love fast vibrations, around two hundred fifty buzzes per second. A normal person can feel a grain of salt on a smooth table. You? You can feel which way the grain is facing. Everything you touch is turned up one hundred times. But there's a rule. Your fingertips feel your own heartbeat. A tiny thump inside every finger. When you're calm, your heart beats maybe sixty times a minute. The thumps are soft and far apart. The world speaks in the quiet between them. When you panic? An adult heart can race past one hundred twenty. The thumps blur into a drumroll... and the power drowns. Calm heart, super hands. Scared heart... nothing. So what if your fingertips were one hundred times more sensitive? Start with the obvious. Locks. Most front doors use a pin tumbler lock with five little pins. Push each pin to just the right height, and it turns. The idea is old. Ancient Egyptians built wooden pin locks about four thousand years ago. Linus Yale Junior patented his famous pin tumbler designs in the 1860s. A skilled locksmith can pick a basic lock in a few minutes. You? You feel every pin like a row of piano keys. Click. Click. Click. Click. Click. Six... seconds. Ray, your best friend and business partner, drops his sandwich. Did you just... do that blind? Upside: lockouts are your new specialty. A dad locked out with a baby inside? You're in before the baby finishes crying. A grandma who lost the key to her late husband's toolbox? Open... and now she's the one crying. Downside: clothes. Every shirt tag feels like a cactus. Every seam... feels like a rope. You start wearing your T-shirts inside out. Ray notices. Is that a fashion choice? It is... now. Downside two: rain. Each drop lands like a flicked pebble. You buy the biggest umbrella in the store. Upside: you learn Braille in one afternoon. Louis Braille invented his raised dot system in the 1820s, as a teenager. Each dot is only about half a millimeter tall. You read a whole page with your eyes closed... and start volunteering at the library. Then comes the video. A customer films you opening a rusty padlock in three seconds. By morning, it has more views than your town has people. A museum calls. They have a safe from an old train station that nobody has opened in decades. Can you try? Experts call it manipulation. No drilling. You turn the dial and feel for tiny bumps called contact points. Real safe technicians train for years to feel them. A dial with one hundred numbers and three wheels? That's a million possible combinations. You? Four minutes. Inside, there are old train tickets... and a love letter nobody ever mailed. The museum director hugs you. You flinch. Because hugs... hurt now. And then a man in a nice gray coat walks into your shop. He doesn't need a key. He just smiles. My name's Dante. I hear you can open anything. Here's the hidden cost. Your brain has to read all of it. In the 1930s, a neurosurgeon named Wilder Penfield mapped the strip of brain that handles touch. The hands take up a huge share of it. Now feed that strip a hundred times more signal. It never stops. Sheets. Socks. Wind. Your own hair on your neck. You stop... sleeping well. There's a real medical condition called allodynia. A gentle touch feels painful, because the nervous system is turned up too high. That's you... all day. So you start avoiding people. No handshakes. No high fives. When your mom visits, you hug her with your elbows. She laughs. Her eyes don't. And remember the rule? The moment you're scared, the power disappears. So the one time you'll need it most... it might not show up. Ray has been your best friend since fourth grade. He taught you to pick your first lock. His dad's old practice padlock. Scratched brass, with a little dent on the side. It still hangs on a nail behind the register. Ray's dad had a saying, and Ray repeats it every time a job gets hard. Slow hands, slow heart. Ray has a habit, too. When he's thinking, he taps the counter with one finger. Tap. Tap. Tap. Once a second, like a clock. It used to drive you crazy. Now it calms you down. You've never told him that. But the shop is in trouble. The landlord just raised the rent. Ray shows you the letter, and his taps get faster. Two months, Rio. Maybe three. Then we're done. You look at the padlock on the nail. You think about the man in the gray coat. Dante left a card. Just a phone number. And a promise. One bank vault. One night. Half a million dollars. Nobody gets hurt, he said. You're just opening a box. You don't call him... but you don't throw the card away, either. Friday. Eight forty at night. Dante texts. Tonight. Nine fifteen. The bank on Fifth Street. Last chance. Your hand is on your car keys when the shop door bangs open. A woman, out of breath. My son, she gasps. He was playing hide and seek. He climbed into his grandpa's old floor safe... and the door swung shut. Nobody knows the combination. Grandpa passed away last spring. The fire department is coming, but they'll have to cut through steel. How long does that take? Too long. And a small sealed box doesn't hold much air. Your phone buzzes. Dante. Twenty minutes, or the deal is off. Ray is out on a job across town. It's just you. So here it is. Drive to the bank and save the shop... or follow this mom and save a kid you've never met. You grab your tools. You follow the mom. Her basement is cold. The safe is the size of a mini fridge, sunk into concrete. A tiny knock from inside. Then crying. Hey, buddy, you call. I'm right here. You put your fingertips on the dial. And... nothing. Just your heartbeat. Thump thump thump thump. Way too fast. One hundred thirty? One forty? The contact points are in there somewhere... a fraction of a millimeter wide. And your own pulse is drowning them out. The dial is three inches across. One number is a sliver of an inch. Your hands are shaking. The knocking gets slower. You can't do this. Not like this. You call Ray. First ring. Rio? What's wrong? You tell him. He doesn't waste a word. Put me on speaker. Set the phone on the safe. You set it on the steel. And through the speaker... you hear it. Tap. Tap. Tap. Ray's finger on a counter, miles away. Once a second. Like a clock. Slow hands, slow heart, he says. You breathe with the taps. In for four. Out for four. Your pulse drops... One twenty. One hundred. Eighty. Sixty-five. And there... the world comes back. The dial whispers. A bump at twelve. A bump at forty-seven. The last wheel drops into place... like a pebble into sand. You turn the handle. The door swings open. A little boy, maybe six, blinks up at you, sweaty and red faced. His mom pulls him out. And then he does something you're not ready for. He grabs your hand. And holds on tight. You wait for it to hurt. It doesn't. With your heart this slow, it just feels... warm. The fire truck pulls up while he's laughing. You never make it to Fifth Street. The next morning, you walk into the police station and hand over Dante's card. Real lesson here: if a stranger offers you a fortune to just open a box... it's never just a box. The bank changes its vault lock that same week. Then something you don't expect. The boy's mom tells her neighbors. The neighbors tell theirs. On Monday, there's a line outside your little shop. Lockouts. Rekeys. A teacher who wants a mailbox lock just so she can shake your hand. By the end of the month... the rent is paid. Ray tapes the boy's drawing above the register, next to the old brass padlock. Two stick figures holding hands beside a giant box. 'Thank you, lock man.' One evening, closing up, Ray holds out his arms. You haven't hugged anyone properly in months. You take a breath. He taps your back. Once a second. And it doesn't hurt at all. Slow hands, slow heart. So... is any of this real? Partly. Your fingertips really are packed with sensors, and they're sharper than most people think. In 2013, researchers in Sweden found people could feel wrinkles on a surface only about thirteen nanometers tall. That's thousands of times thinner than a hair. Safe technicians really do open locks by feel and sound. Braille readers really do glide across those tiny dots. And slow breathing really can help calm a racing heart. What's not real? Turning touch up one hundred times. Your skin can only hold so many sensors. Your brain can only process so much. Allodynia hints that a nervous system turned up that high would feel like pain, not a superpower. And modern high security locks are built to resist manipulation. So... would you still want to feel everything? But here's something stranger. Your fingertips wrinkle in the bath. People assumed that was just skin soaking up water. It isn't that simple. Those wrinkles need working nerves to form. Some scientists think they help you grip wet things, like treads on a tire. So why would your body build grip treads... and only switch them on underwater? What would you have done? Share it in the comments, and vote for the next power we try. Hit like, and subscribe to Rio Animation for more fascinating videos!

long.title: What If You Could Never Lose Your Balance?
long.rel: Sofia, Rio's younger sister, a nurse afraid of heights since a childhood fall
long.rule: Rio's perfect balance runs through the eyes, so in total darkness Rio is an ordinary person with a lazy inner ear.
long.plant: A yellow star-shaped keychain flashlight Rio gave Sofia in the hospital after letting go of the treehouse ladder, which she still clips to her bag.
long.choice: Walk the wire on 'Skyline Live' and become a legend, or climb down and go get your sister off the broken fire escape.
long.script: Seven stories up, the rain is flying sideways. You're clinging to a rusty fire escape in the middle of a storm. Across the street, a TV crew is shouting your name. And just above you, on a tilted metal landing, your little sister is holding on with both hands. She hates heights. She has hated them since she was eight. Then... every light in the city goes out. All of them. At once. And for the first time in a year... your knees start to shake. Your name is Rio. And until this exact second, you could not lose your balance. Not on ice. Not on a rope. Not on anything. So why are you about to fall? But let's go back. One year earlier, you're a delivery driver with a bad back and a worse apartment. Then one Tuesday, you trip on a curb... and don't fall. Your body just tilts, holds, and comes back. Like a bobblehead. Weird, right? Then you notice it... everywhere. So how does balance normally work? Your brain is juggling three sources at once. Your eyes. Your inner ear. And sensors in your muscles and joints that tell you where your body is. Inside each inner ear, there are three tiny loops filled with fluid, called semicircular canals. When your head turns, the fluid sloshes... and tiny hairs bend. There are also little crystals of calcium carbonate that tell you which way is down. Yes. You have rocks in your head. Everybody does... so don't feel bad. Try standing on one foot with your eyes open. Plenty of adults start wobbling well before a minute. You? You can stand on one foot on a moving bus... while drinking soup. But there's one rule. Your power runs through your eyes. As long as you can see, even a little, your balance is perfect. In total darkness? You're just a regular person. Maybe... worse. So what if you could never lose your balance? Beat one: the bus. Your morning commute? Now it's your favorite part of the day. Everybody grabs the rails. You just... stand. Hands in your pockets. A guy watches you through the whole ride. At his stop, he whispers, How? You shrug... core strength. Beat two: the ice. Did you know falls are a leading cause of injury for older adults? In the US, about one in four adults over sixty-five falls each year. Your downstairs neighbor broke her wrist last January. This January, you walk her to the mailbox every morning. She calls you... her handrail. Beat three: the job. You quit driving and start washing windows on tall buildings. Real window washers work from platforms hanging hundreds of feet in the air, clipped into safety lines. You clip in, too. Always. But you never... need it. Upside: the view. Downside: pigeons have zero respect... for personal space. Beat four: boats. Seasickness happens when your eyes and your inner ear disagree. Your eyes say the cabin is still. Your ear says you're tipping. Your brain panics. You? You go fishing with your uncle. Everybody else is green. You're the only one on board... eating a sandwich. Beat five: the skateboard. You've never skated in your life. You step on a board and ride a handrail on the first try. A group of teenagers stares. One of them asks if you're a stunt double. Are you? You say... sort of. Then the internet finds you. A video of you walking a steel railing, twenty stories up, gets millions of views. Comments pour in. Fake. It's a green screen. Nobody's that steady... right? Beat six: the history lesson. In 1974, a French high wire artist named Philippe Petit walked a cable between the Twin Towers in New York. About thirteen hundred fifty feet up. He crossed back and forth eight times, for about forty-five minutes. In 2012, Nik Wallenda walked a wire right over Niagara Falls. Those men trained for decades. You? You trained for... zero days. And then the call comes. A TV producer in a shiny jacket wants you for a live show. 'Skyline Live.' A wire between two towers downtown. Six hundred feet up. Prime time. No net? No net. They're offering more money than you've made in five years. Pretty tempting, right? So what does it cost? Plenty. Here's the hidden cost. Your brain is constantly deciding which balance sense to trust most. Scientists call it sensory reweighting. Stand in the dark, and your brain leans harder on your inner ear and your joints. But your brain has stopped bothering. Why would it bother? Your eyes handle everything now. So your other balance senses are getting lazy. Doctors have a simple balance check called the Romberg test. Stand still with your feet together, then close your eyes. Most healthy people barely sway. You try it one night in your kitchen. You close your eyes... and fall straight into the fridge. Twice. Your inner ear is like a muscle you stopped using. And there's a second cost. What is fear of heights, really? A warning system. It keeps people away from edges. You don't feel it anymore. Not even a little. You stop understanding why anyone would. And that's going to be... a problem. Because of Sofia. Your little sister Sofia is twenty-six now. A nurse. Smart, funny and brave about everything... except heights. And it's your fault. When she was eight, you were twelve. She climbed the ladder to your treehouse, and you were supposed to hold it. You said it, too. I've got the ladder. Then the ice cream truck came around the corner. You let go. She fell. A broken arm. Six weeks in a pink cast. That night in the hospital, she was scared of the dark. So you gave her your keychain flashlight. A plastic yellow one, shaped like a star. She still has it. Clipped to her bag. Every single day. Now she won't take an elevator past the tenth floor. When you show her your rooftop videos, she covers her eyes. Rio, please stop. You laugh. What's the big deal? It's totally safe. She doesn't laugh back. You can't feel her fear anymore. So you can't understand it. Earl is the old window washer who trained you. Forty years on the ropes. He watches you walk the edge of a roof one afternoon, and he frowns. The sky doesn't care how good you are, kid. Just how careful. Dramatic much? You think he's just being... dramatic. The night of the show, a storm rolls in early. The producer doesn't care. Rain looks great on camera... apparently. Sofia promised she'd come watch, from the roof of an old apartment building across the street. Facing her fear. For you. You're on the platform, sixty seconds from going live, when you see her. A gust of wind slams the rooftop door shut behind her. So what does she do? She tries the old fire escape instead. Halfway down, a rusty bolt snaps. The whole landing tilts. Now she's eight stories up, on a slanted grate, gripping the rail. Frozen. Fire trucks are coming, but traffic downtown is jammed. The producer grabs your arm. Thirty seconds, Rio. Millions of people are watching. So here it is. Walk the wire and become a legend... or climb down and go get your sister. You unclip from the show. You take the stairs down, three at a time. You cross the street. And you climb. Up the fire escape. Rung by rung. Your balance is perfect. Five stories. Six. Seven. And then... the storm takes out the power grid. Every light... gone. No streetlights. No windows. No moon. Total dark. And your power? Gone... like someone flipped a switch. Suddenly, the metal is slippery. The wind hits you at maybe forty miles an hour. Your stomach drops. Your knees lock. And for the first time in a year... you feel it. Pure fear. Your lazy inner ear spins. Up and down swap places. You grab the rail and you can't let go. Is this what Sofia has felt this whole time? Above you, a small voice. Rio? Is that you? Then... a tiny circle of light. Yellow. Shaped like a star. Sofia, who covers her eyes at rooftop videos, lets go with one hand. Unclips that little flashlight from her bag. And points it straight down... at your feet. Her hand is shaking. But the light holds. I've got the ladder, she says. And with that tiny beam, your eyes find the steps. Your balance snaps back. You climb the last fifteen feet in seconds. You wrap one arm around Sofia and one around the rail. You can't fly her down. But you can be the steadiest thing on that fire escape. Ready? you say. Look at the light. Not the street. One step. Then another. She holds the flashlight. You hold her. Together, you inch down the stairs. Seven. Six. Five. At the fourth floor, red lights flood the alley. A ladder truck. Firefighters reach up, and Sofia steps onto their ladder. She makes it to the street. She's crying. So are you... obviously. Back on the tower, the show goes on without you. Someone filmed the whole thing with a phone. By morning, it's not a wire walk people are sharing. It's a shaky video... of a tiny yellow star shining down a fire escape. Your downstairs neighbor prints a picture of it and tapes it to her door. Earl sends one text. That's careful. You turn down the next TV offer. And the one after that. And then you start training the boring way. Every night, you practice standing in the dark with your eyes closed. Waking up your lazy inner ear. Falling into the fridge... a little less each week. And you start to feel your fear again. Which means you finally understand Sofia's. A month later, she visits your apartment with a box of string lights. She wants them on the ceiling. She looks at the stepladder. Five feet tall. She takes a deep breath. You put your hand on the ladder. I've got the ladder. She climbs. All the way to the top. Those tiny calcium crystals in your ears? Sometimes they break loose and drift into the wrong loop. When they do, the whole room spins every time you roll over in bed. It's one of the most common causes of dizziness. Doctors often fix it with a simple series of head turns. Strange, right? But think about it. If a few loose crystals can flip your whole world... what else is quietly holding you upright? So what would you do if you could never lose your balance? Tell us in the comments. And if you've ever held the ladder for someone you love... this one's for you. Hit like, and subscribe to Rio Animation for more fascinating videos!

long.title: What If Your Metabolism Was 10 Times Faster?
long.rel: Lucy, Rio's roommate of six years who runs the orange food truck 'Lucy's Little Kitchen'
long.rule: Rio's body has no energy savings, so reserves burn out in about an hour and a skipped meal means a crash.
long.plant: Every morning Lucy slips a peanut butter and honey bar labeled 'Eat me, Rio.' into Rio's jacket pocket, and about six uneaten bars pile up there.
long.choice: Stay at the table and win the pancake prize for Lucy's truck, or run onto the ice for a kid you've never met.
long.script: It's nine degrees outside, and you're wearing a T-shirt. Your neighbor stares at you from his driveway. Aren't you freezing? Nope. You're... toasty. Snowflakes land on your arms... and vanish before they can melt properly. Your roommate's car? Buried in ice. You put both palms on the windshield. Thirty seconds later... she can see through it. You cut your thumb slicing bagels. By lunch... it's a pink line. By dinner, it's gone. You eat a large pizza. Then another one. Then you open the fridge... and ask if there's anything else. And when you step out into the cold, steam rolls off your head... like a boiling kettle. A kid on a sled points at you. Mom! That man is cooking! Your name is Rio. And you're not cooking. You're just... burning. How much energy does a normal adult burn? Somewhere around two thousand calories a day, give or take. Most of that just keeps you alive. Your heart. Your lungs. Your brain uses about one fifth of your energy... all by itself. You? Twenty thousand calories. Every single day. Your body runs ten times faster than everyone else's. But there's a rule. Your body has no savings account. Normal people store energy as fat, and as sugar in the liver. Enough to survive a skipped meal. You burn through your reserves in about an hour. Miss a meal... and you don't get grumpy. You crash. Shaking. Confused. Then... you're down. So what if your metabolism was ten times faster? Beat one: heat. A resting person gives off about one hundred watts of heat, roughly like an old light bulb. That's why a crowded room gets warm. You? About a thousand watts. You're a walking... space heater. Upside: your roommate Lucy hasn't turned on the heater all winter. Downside: in July... nobody will sit next to you on the bus. Beat two: healing. Paper cuts? Gone... in an hour. A sprained ankle from a pickup basketball game? Fine by dinner. Your doctor looks at your chart and says a word doctors aren't supposed to say. Whoa. Beat three: growth. Your hair grows so fast that you need a haircut every week. Your fingernails? You trim them every morning... like brushing your teeth. Beat four: the grocery bill. A pound of plain pasta is around seventeen hundred calories. You need about twelve pounds of it a day. Lucy watches you carry home four bags of rice. Are we opening a restaurant? Beat five: speed of thought. Your brain is burning fuel faster, too. Crosswords take you five minutes. Then you fall asleep at the table. Why? Because thinking... used up lunch. Beat six: animals. Small animals already live like this. A hummingbird's heart can beat more than a thousand times a minute. Some shrews have to eat almost constantly just to stay alive. Scientists noticed long ago that smaller animals burn energy faster for their size. A mouse lives fast and dies young. An elephant lives slow and lives long. Which one are you now? Beat seven: sweat. Your body cools itself mostly by sweating. When sweat evaporates, it carries heat away. You sweat through three shirts a day. Your gym locker smells... legendary. Beat eight: the internet. Lucy films you eating breakfast. Two dozen eggs. A loaf of toast. And a whole melon... for dessert. The video goes viral. Fake! Nobody eats like that! And then the email arrives. It's from the Frost Fest Food Truck Festival down by the lake. They're hosting a pancake eating contest. Grand prize? Ten thousand dollars. And a gold trophy shaped like a syrup bottle. You have to admit... that trophy is beautiful. Here's the thing about pro eating. Ever seen the famous Nathan's hot dog contest in New York? In 2021, Joey Chestnut ate seventy-six hot dogs and buns in ten minutes. Those eaters train their stomachs to stretch. You? You don't need to stretch. You need to... refuel. You could eat pancakes all day. But there's a hidden cost. Real people can have a version of this. It's called hyperthyroidism. The thyroid is a little butterfly shaped gland in your neck. When it makes too much hormone, the body speeds up. People lose weight without trying. Their heart races. They feel hot all the time. Their hands shake. They have trouble sleeping. That's you... turned up to ten. Your heart is pounding all day, even when you sit. Sleep comes in short, jumpy naps. You wake up starving at three in the morning. Every time you crash, the rule bites harder. One afternoon at work, the vending machine eats your dollar. Twenty minutes later, you're on the break room floor. Your coworker finds you, shaking. Low blood sugar is serious. It can make anyone dizzy, confused and weak. For you? It hits like a train. You realize something cold and uncomfortable. Your power isn't strength. It's... a countdown. Lucy is the reason you're still standing. She's been your roommate for six years. She also runs a tiny food truck called 'Lucy's Little Kitchen,' painted bright orange. She sells grilled cheese and tomato soup. Her grandma's recipe. Lucy is the kind of person who feeds strangers for free when they look sad. Great for strangers. Not so great... for business. Every morning, before you leave, she slips something into your jacket pocket. A little peanut butter and honey bar, wrapped in wax paper. She writes on every single one. 'Eat me, Rio.' Same words. Every time. And every time, she says the same thing. Feed the furnace. You laugh. You always forget about the bar. It just sits there. How many are in that jacket pocket now? About six. But the truck is in trouble. The engine is dying, and the repair is going to cost more than eight thousand dollars. If she can't fix it, she's out. Lucy doesn't say it out loud. She just stands at the window of her orange truck, staring at the lake. So when you see that ten thousand dollar prize... you see Lucy's truck. Saturday. Frost Fest. Thirty food trucks line the edge of the frozen lake. The air smells like fried dough and cinnamon. There's a stage. There's a long table. There's a mountain of pancakes. And there's your rival. Quinn. Three time regional champion, wearing a headband that says 'Stack Attack.' Quinn leans over. Good luck, rookie. You'll need it. The host lifts the whistle. And that's when you hear it. A crack. Then a scream. Out on the lake, past the warning signs, a kid has gone through the ice. A boy, maybe ten, chasing a runaway hockey puck. He's in the water up to his chest. His dad is running toward him. Stop! The ice won't hold you! Rescue crews are on the way. But how long? The festival is on the far side of town. So here it is. Stay at the table and win Lucy's truck back... or run onto the ice for a kid you've never met. The whistle blows. You run. You flatten yourself on the ice to spread your weight, the way rescuers do. Crawl... don't walk. Behind you... the crowd is yelling. You reach the hole. The water is about thirty-three degrees. In water that cold, the first minute is the worst. A gasping shock. Then a person has maybe ten minutes of useful movement before their arms stop working. The boy has been in for four. His lips... are blue. He can't grip anything. You grab his jacket. You pull. He slides halfway out... and your arms go soft. Because you skipped breakfast. Because you were saving room for pancakes. The cold is pulling heat out of you faster than ever. Your body is burning everything it has. And now? It's... empty. Your hands shake. The world tilts. You can't let go of him. But you can't pull him out either. Then your hand brushes your jacket pocket. Wax paper. Six bars. 'Eat me, Rio.' You tear one open with your teeth. Peanut butter, honey. Then another. Then another. Your body grabs that sugar like a fire grabs paper. Ninety seconds later... warmth floods back into your arms. You pull. The boy slides out onto the ice. You wrap yourself around him, chest to chest, and stay flat. He's freezing. You're a thousand watts. For once, your curse is exactly what someone needs. You're his heater... until the rescue crew arrives. The boy's dad is crying. The paramedics wrap him in blankets. And one of them looks at you, steaming in the snow. You kept him warm? With what? You just smile. Feed the furnace. The contest? You lost. Quinn won. You missed the whole thing. But then Quinn walks over, still wiping syrup off that headband. Quinn holds out the gold syrup bottle trophy. Turns out, everybody on stage stopped eating to watch the rescue. Including Quinn. I didn't win anything today, Quinn says. You did. And then something better happens. The boy's dad owns an auto repair shop. Two days later, he tows Lucy's orange truck in and fixes the engine. The bill? Zero. The festival crowd comes to find the truck that belongs to the steaming hero. Lucy sells out of grilled cheese by noon. Then again the next day. And the doctor finally helps you, too. You get bloodwork. A plan. Food on a timer every forty-five minutes, like medicine. No more crashes. No more break room floors. The next morning, Lucy hands you a bar. You don't laugh this time. You eat it right in front of her. Feed the furnace. So... is any of this real? Some of it is. Hyperthyroidism is real. It really can make people hot, shaky and hungry, with a racing heart. Hummingbirds really do live on a knife's edge. On cold nights, many drop into a deep state called torpor... slowing way down to survive until morning. Cold water shock is real, and lying flat on ice really does spread your weight. What's impossible? A human body running ten times faster. You'd need to breathe in about ten times more oxygen. Your heart would have to pump far harder than it's built for. And a thousand watts of heat inside one body would be extremely hard to get rid of. You might overheat... on a mild spring day. So here's the question. Would a body this fast be a gift... or a fuse? But here's a bigger mystery. Black bears can sleep through the winter for months. They barely eat or drink. Their metabolism drops way down. And somehow, they wake up in spring without losing nearly as much muscle as you'd expect. A human stuck in bed for that long would get very weak. How do bears do it? And could we ever learn their trick? So, real or not? Drop your verdict in the comments, and pick the power we should test next. Hit like, and subscribe to Rio Animation for more fascinating videos!

long.title: What If You Could Feel Every Emotion Around You?
long.rel: Rio's 12-year-old son, a seventh grader who has gone quiet
long.rule: Rio feels every emotion within about a hundred feet, and inside that range the biggest feeling always wins.
long.plant: The childhood code word 'Pickles' that Rio's son can text when he feels scared or stuck, plus Rio's private truth that his feelings are the only ones never 'not mine'.
long.choice: Stay on stage and help Ms. Harper win the room, or walk away from the cameras and find your son.
long.script: Six hundred people are packed into a middle school gym. Somebody smells rotten eggs. Somebody else yells... gas. And then it hits you. Not a smell. Not a sound. A wave. Six hundred people's fear, all at once, slamming into your chest like cold water. Your heart pounds. Your hands go numb. You can't tell which panic is yours... and which belongs to the man behind you. Your phone buzzes. One word on the screen. 'Pickles.' That's the code. That's your son, telling you he needs you. Right now. Somewhere in this building. Your name is Rio. You can feel every emotion around you. And right now, every emotion is screaming... so how are you supposed to hear his? But let's go back. Three months earlier, you're a school bus mechanic and a single dad. Rent is late. Life is... normal. Then one morning, a cashier smiles at you... and you feel how tired she is. Not guess. Feel. Here's the thing. Humans already catch feelings from each other. Scientists call it emotional contagion. Without noticing, people copy the faces and voices around them. And copying a face can nudge the feeling... too. Newborn babies often start crying when they hear another baby cry. How do most people read emotions? Faces. Your face has more than forty muscles. Some expressions flash by in under half a second. You? You don't need faces. You feel it directly... like weather. But there's a rule. Your range is about a hundred feet. And inside that range, the biggest feeling wins. One angry guy in line? You're angry... too. A room full of nervous people? You're a wreck. Can you block it? No. Turn it off? Also no. So what if you could feel every emotion around you? Beat one: the grocery store. The man in the checkout line is smiling. But underneath? He's terrified. He just came from the hospital. You let him go ahead of you... and pay for his milk. Why? He doesn't know. You do. Beat two: work. The bus garage is full of grumpy mechanics. Turns out, they're not grumpy. They're tired. And one of them is... lonely. You start bringing donuts on Fridays. The whole garage... softens. Upside: you're suddenly the best coworker in the building. Downside: you know exactly who ate your sandwich. And how guilty he feels. Beat three: dating. You go on a first date. She says she's having a great time. Is she? Nope. You feel her checking the clock. Honestly? That's a gift. You both laugh... and split the check. Beat four: lies. Your landlord says the heater will be fixed next week. You feel the shrug behind his words. Will it? Nope. You buy a space heater. Beat five: movie night. Two hundred people cry at the same scene. One sad wave. You walk out sobbing... over a cartoon robot. And now, the big one. The election. Your town is picking a new mayor. Ms. Harper is a candidate. Sharp suit. Perfect smile. A speech for everything. She hears about you, the guy who always knows what people feel. She finds you at the bus garage. I need someone who can read a room, she says. Tell me what voters feel before they know it themselves. Tell me what scares my opponent. I'll say exactly the right words. You stand there holding a wrench. She offers a salary three times what you make. A real office. A future. And underneath her smile? Not kindness. Hunger. But it's so much... money. Here's the hidden cost. Feeling everyone, all the time, is exhausting. Real nurses, doctors and firefighters can develop something called compassion fatigue. It comes from absorbing other people's pain, day after day. They get worn out. Numb. That's you... times a thousand. When you're stressed, your body releases a hormone called cortisol, and your heart speeds up. Your body doesn't care whose stress it is. If the room is stressed, you get the cortisol. And there's something worse. You're losing track of your own feelings. Are you happy? Or is the guy next to you happy? Are you angry... or is it the lady on her phone? You start saying the same thing under your breath, all day long. Not mine. Not mine. Not mine. It's the only way to stay yourself. And then there's your son. Your son is twelve. Seventh grade. He used to talk the whole ride home. Now he wears his hood up and answers with one word. Fine. Good. Whatever. Sound familiar? The brain is under construction at that age. The prefrontal cortex, which helps with planning and calming down, keeps developing into the mid twenties. Your power should help, right? But it doesn't. Because his feelings are small and quiet... and the world is so loud. School pickup is the worst. Five hundred kids, all excited, all stressed. His feelings just... disappear. When he was five, you two made up a code word. If he ever felt scared or stuck, he just had to say one word. Pickles. Because he hated pickles. And you would drop everything. He hasn't used it in years. Forgot it? Probably. Here's what you never told him. The only feeling in the world you'd never call 'not mine'... is his. Ms. Harper calls again. Big night, she says. The town hall debate... in your son's middle school gym. Stand side stage. Tell me what the crowd feels. If tonight goes well, the job is yours. You say yes. Your son comes along. He'll be fine, he says. Fine. Good. Whatever. Six hundred people. Folding chairs. News cameras. You stand side stage, and the room pours into you. Hope. Boredom. A teacher who just wants to go home. Ms. Harper leans back between questions. What do they feel? you hear her whisper. Your son was in the bleachers. Now he isn't. Do you notice? No. You're too busy reading the room. Your phone buzzes. You ignore it. Then a janitor sniffs the air and frowns. Rotten eggs. Here's a real fact. Natural gas has no smell on its own. Gas companies add a chemical so a leak smells like rotten eggs... so people know to get out. Someone yells. And six hundred people stand up at once. The panic hits you like a truck. Your heart rate jumps past one hundred forty. In real emergencies, people often rush to the door they came in through. Even when other exits are closer. You can feel it happening. A huge knot of fear jamming the main doors. You check your phone. 'Pickles.' Sent eleven minutes ago. Your son needed you. And you didn't even... look. Ms. Harper grabs your arm. Her eyes are bright. This is it, Rio. Tell me what they feel, and I'll calm them down. They'll remember who saved them. Stay. Please. So here it is. Stay on stage and help Ms. Harper win the room... or walk away from the cameras and find your son. You pull your arm free. You do one thing first. You point at the side doors and shout. Exits on the left! They're open! The crowd tilts. The knot loosens. People start moving the right way. Then you run. Out of the gym. Into the dark hallway. The panic is still crushing you. It's too big. You can't feel your son. Not anywhere. And then you remember the rule. A hundred feet. The biggest feeling wins. So what do you do? You get out of range. Past the lockers. Past the cafeteria. Eighty feet. A hundred. One twenty. The crowd's fear fades... like a radio losing signal. And in the quiet, there's something tiny. Small. Scared... alone. You know that feeling. You'd know it anywhere. Mine. You follow it. Down the stairs. To the band room. The door is jammed. Old door. Swollen frame. Inside, your son is sitting on the floor, hood up, hugging his knees. You pull the door with everything you have. It pops open. He looks up. You came, he says. You didn't answer. I thought... I thought you were too busy. You kneel down. I'm here. I'm so sorry. You walk him out the back door into the cold night air. The firefighters are already there. The gym empties safely. The leak? A cracked pipe near the kitchen. Small. Fixable. Scary anyway. Later, sitting on the curb, your son finally talks. Kids at school have been teasing him for weeks. Seeing them in the bleachers was too much. So he hid. Then the alarm went off, and the door wouldn't open. He texted the code word... and waited. You listen. All of it. No crowd. No firefighters. Just him. And your own heart. For the first time in months, you know exactly which feeling is yours. It's love. Huge, stubborn, embarrassing love. Not mine, you whisper... except this one. This one's mine. You turn down Ms. Harper's job the next morning. Does she take it well? Nope. You feel that, too. But a week later, the news posts the video. Not of the debate. Of a bus mechanic, shouting about the side doors. Parents start calling you. Teachers thank you in the pickup line. The school asks you to help plan clearer exit routes. You keep your old job. You keep your Friday donuts. And every day at pickup, your son pulls his hood down... and talks the whole ride home. So... is any of this real? More than you'd think. Emotional contagion is real. People really do catch moods from the people around them. In the 1990s, a team in Parma, Italy, led by Giacomo Rizzolatti, studied monkey brains. They found cells that fired when a monkey grabbed something. The same cells fired when it watched someone else grab. They're called mirror neurons. How much they explain about human empathy is still debated. There's also mirror touch synesthesia. Some people feel a touch on their own body... just watching someone else get touched. Compassion fatigue is real. And natural gas really does get that rotten egg smell added on purpose. What's not real? Feeling emotions through walls, with no face, no voice and no body language. Feelings aren't radio signals. Your brain reads clues... it doesn't receive broadcasts. So if you can read a face... how sure are you that you're reading it right? And here's something stranger. Yawning is contagious. Just reading about it might make you... yawn. Some studies suggest even dogs can catch a yawn from their humans. Why would a yawn jump between two completely different species? Your turn. Tell us in the comments what you believe, and which power we should explore next. Hit like, and subscribe to Rio Animation for more fascinating videos!

long.title: What If You Could Learn Any Skill In One Day?
long.rel: Grandma June, 79, who left school at fourteen and is studying for her GED
long.rule: Rio must watch someone do the skill once, then sleep a full night, and can lock in only one new skill per night.
long.plant: Grandma June's yellow sticky note from her CPR class, 'Push hard. Push fast. Count out loud.', tucked in Rio's wallet, plus Rio's habit of saying 'Give me one day.'
long.choice: Ride the elevator to the corner office, or stay on this floor and fight for a stranger.
long.script: Sunday night, you watch a street performer juggle on your phone. Three oranges. Round and round... and round. You go to bed. Monday morning, you grab three oranges from the fruit bowl... and juggle them perfectly. Monday night, you watch a barista pour latte art. Tuesday morning, there's a swan in your coffee. A real swan. With a little... curled neck. Tuesday night, you watch a video of a man playing the piano. Wednesday morning, you sit down at your neighbor's old upright piano... and play the whole song. Your neighbor drops her laundry basket. You've lived here three years, she says. You can't even whistle. That's true. Why can't you whistle? You never watched anyone teach it. Your name is Rio. You work in a gray cubicle on the twenty-second floor of a downtown office tower. And you can learn any skill... in one day. How long does it normally take to get good at something? Forever. In 2008, Malcolm Gladwell's book 'Outliers' made the ten thousand hour rule famous. It was based on research by psychologist Anders Ericsson. Ericsson later said the number was oversimplified. Still, real mastery takes years... of focused practice. London taxi drivers spend around three to four years memorizing the city's maze of streets. It's called 'The Knowledge.' You? One video. One night... done. But there's a rule. You have to watch someone do it once. Then you have to sleep. A full night. And your brain can lock in only one new skill per night. No sleep... no skill. Simple, right? So what if you could learn any skill in one day? Beat one: work. Your boss asks if anyone knows spreadsheets. Not the basic kind. The scary kind... with pivot tables. You watch a tutorial at lunch. Next morning, you build a budget model that makes the finance team gasp. Upside: your boss learns your name. Downside: so does everyone... with a spreadsheet problem. Beat two: typing. How fast does the average person type? Around forty words a minute. You watch a speed typist once. Now you're at one hundred fifty. Your keyboard sounds like... popcorn. Beat three: languages. The US State Department rates Japanese as one of the hardest languages for English speakers. It has three writing systems. Hiragana, katakana and kanji. Diplomats study it full time for well over a year. You? You sleep on it. Wake up. Order breakfast in Japanese at the sushi place downstairs. The chef asks where you studied. Where? You say... my pillow. Beat four: the car. Your check engine light comes on. You watch a mechanic video, sleep, and fix it yourself. Two hundred dollars saved. Your dad would be... proud. Beat five: the dog park. Your friend's dog refuses to sit. Ever. You watch a trainer once. The next day, that dog sits, rolls over, and fetches your friend's slippers. Beat six: the city. You watch a guitar lesson, and on Saturday you play by the fountain downtown. People throw dollar bills into your open case. Can you believe it? Somebody films it. Then somebody films you rewiring a lamp. Then speaking Spanish. Then doing a backflip. Wait... a backflip? Okay. That one took two nights. And then? The big one. The vice president of your company calls you into her corner office. Glass walls. A view of the whole river. We're closing a deal with a company in Tokyo, she says. Friday morning. Eight a.m. sharp. Lead the pitch, and you're the new director of global sales. A corner office? Triple your salary? Your heart jumps. How could you say no? Here's the hidden cost. Fast learning fades fast. In the 1880s, a German psychologist named Hermann Ebbinghaus tested his own memory with lists of nonsense syllables. He found that new memories drop off steeply in the first day or so, unless you review them. Scientists call it the forgetting curve. They also found the fix. Spread your practice out over time. It's called the spacing effect. Cramming works for a test. Spaced practice works... for life. Your power? It's the ultimate cram. Everything you learn in one night starts slipping away within weeks... unless you keep using it. So what happens? You're re-learning things every night. Spreadsheets. Japanese. Guitar. All your nights are booked. Sleep is when your brain replays the day and decides what to keep. And there's only so much room on the shelf. Something old has to fall... off. Little things start to go. Where you parked. Your best friend's birthday. The words to the song your grandma used to sing while she made biscuits. You can't remember them anymore. And that one... really hurts. Grandma June raised you. She left school at fourteen to work in a peach cannery, so her little brothers could eat. She never went back. Now she's seventy-nine, and she's studying for her GED. That's the high school equivalency test. Four subjects. Math, science, social studies, and language arts. She has passed three. Math? She has failed it... twice. Grandma June learns slowly. Carefully. She writes everything on yellow sticky notes in big round letters. They're all over her fridge. She doesn't just study math, either. Last spring, she took a six week CPR class at the senior center. Six weeks? You laughed. Grandma, I could learn that in one day. She just peeled off a fresh sticky note, wrote on it, and pressed it into your hand. 'Push hard. Push fast. Count out loud.' You stuck it in your wallet to be nice. And then you never thought about it again. Every time she asks you to help with her math homework, you have the same answer. Give me one day. You'll learn it tomorrow, then explain it to her. But tomorrow is always booked. Japanese. Spreadsheets. The Tokyo pitch. Her fourth try at the math test is on Friday morning. You promised you'd drive her. You'll squeeze it in. Somehow. You always do... right? Thursday night, you sleep on Japanese business etiquette. Friday morning, seven forty-five, the lobby of your tower is packed. Grandma June is with you. You're dropping her at the test center right after the pitch. She's holding a brown paper lunch bag. She packed one for you, like always. Then... a crash. Near the coffee cart, an older man in a security uniform falls straight to the marble floor. He isn't moving. He isn't breathing right. Someone screams. Someone calls nine one one. Where are the paramedics? And everyone else just... stares. Your phone buzzes. The vice president. Elevator doors close at eight. If you're not upstairs, the job goes to someone else. You kneel next to the guard. You know a thousand things now. Japanese. Guitar. Backflips. But CPR? You never learned it. You were always going to learn it... someday. Give me one day. He doesn't have one day. When the heart stops, the brain starts running out of oxygen fast. After about four to six minutes, damage can begin. Paramedics downtown are maybe eight minutes away. You pull up a CPR video on your phone. You watch. You put your hands on his chest. And it's just... not there. The power needs a night. You don't have a night. You have seconds. Your hands are on his chest, but you have no idea how hard to push. How fast? How deep? Upstairs, the elevator is waiting. Downstairs, a stranger is dying. So here it is. Ride the elevator to the corner office... or stay on this floor and fight for a stranger. You stay. You open your wallet. Your fingers are shaking. And there it is. A wrinkled yellow sticky note. Big round letters. 'Push hard. Push fast. Count out loud.' Grandma June is already kneeling beside you. Her knees crack on the marble. Her arms are seventy-nine years old. She can't push deep enough for long. But you can. Lock your elbows, she says. Center of the chest. Push about two inches. A hundred to one hundred twenty times a minute. Like the song. You know the song? And then your grandma starts singing. 'Stayin' Alive.' The Bee Gees. Its beat is right around one hundred beats per minute. That's exactly why CPR instructors teach it. Ah, ha, ha, ha... You push. On every beat. One. Two. Three. Four. Your arms burn. Your shirt sticks to your back. Grandma doesn't stop singing. She doesn't stop counting. A woman from the coffee cart runs over with the AED from the lobby wall. It talks. It tells you where the pads go. Stand clear. A shock. Then... back to pushing. Grandma never misses a beat. Two minutes. Four. Six. Seven. Then... the paramedics come through the revolving door. One kneels and takes over. The other checks the screen... and nods. He has a pulse. You sit back on the marble. Your arms are jelly. Grandma is holding your hand. Who is he? Everyone in the building knows him. The guard has said good morning to every single person here for nineteen years. Today, the whole lobby is crying for him. And then they start clapping. For you. And mostly... for her. You check your phone. Eight twenty-two. The elevator doors closed long ago. Someone else got the job. You're okay with that. Because Grandma's math test starts at nine. You drive her yourself. She walks in nervous, clutching her pencil. Three hours later, she walks out with a grin you haven't seen in years. She passed. Barely. And barely is plenty. Two weeks later, the guard comes back to work. He brings you a coffee. He brings Grandma a dozen roses. And the building manager asks Grandma June to teach a CPR class. For the whole tower. She says yes. Then she looks at you. You'll help? It takes six weeks. You don't sleep on it once. You learn it the slow way. Practice after practice. Every week, Grandma brings biscuits. And one Saturday, at her kitchen table, she starts humming. That song. The biscuit song. You don't remember the words. So she teaches you. One line at a time. Over and over. Slowly. And this time... it stays. That night, she hands you her new study book. Algebra. She wants to take a community college class next. Can you help? You don't say one day anymore. You hand her a pencil. Take all the days you need. Here's something strange about your brain. While you sleep, the brain seems to replay what you learned during the day. Scientists have watched it happen in rats. Cells that fired while a rat ran a maze fired again in the same order... while it slept. Like a rehearsal. So every night, while you're dreaming, your brain might be practicing without you. But what exactly is it practicing? And what is it deciding to forget? So what would you do with the power to learn any skill in one day? Tell us the first skill you'd learn in the comments. And if someone ever taught you the slow way... this one's for them. Hit like, and subscribe to Rio Animation for more fascinating videos!

long.title: What If You Could Do Math Faster Than A Computer?
long.rel: Rio's old math teacher, Dr. Bennett (signature line: Show your work.)
long.rule: The power only works while Rio is holding a plain wooden pencil, and the biggest problems burn it out for about an hour.
long.plant: Dr. Bennett always keeps a yellow pencil tucked behind her right ear 'for math emergencies'.
long.choice: Make the call and earn ten million dollars... or hang up and spend your whole brain on that boy.
long.script: The ice cracks under your elbow. A thin white line shoots out from your arm... like lightning trapped in glass. You stop breathing. You're lying flat on a frozen pond behind your old middle school. Twenty feet ahead, there's a hole. Black water. And a boy in a red hat, clinging to the edge with both hands. He's nine. And his fingers are slipping. Your phone buzzes in your coat pocket. Again. And again. You know who it is... A trading firm in Manhattan. Ten million dollars... and they want you back on the line. On the shore, an old woman in a purple scarf is shouting your name. Rio! Rio, use your head! You want to. You really do. Because your head can do math... faster than any computer on Earth. But right now... it can't do anything. Why not? Because ten seconds ago, your pencil slipped out of your glove. It skittered across the ice... and dropped into the water. Gone. But let's go back. Your name is Rio. You're thirty-one. You keep the books for a tire shop in New Jersey. Rent, a used Honda, a cat named Decimal. Normal life. Then one Tuesday... numbers get slow. Like they're waiting for you. Here's normal. Ask most adults to multiply two four-digit numbers in their head. They need paper. A few minutes. Maybe... an apology. A cheap laptop does it in about a billionth of a second. You? You have the answer... before the person finishes asking. But there's a rule. The power only works with a pencil in your hand. Not a pen. Not a keyboard. A plain wooden pencil. You don't have to write. Just... hold it. Drop it... and you're back to counting on your fingers like everybody else. So what if you could do math faster than a computer? First stop? The grocery store. The cashier starts scanning. You already know the total. Eighty-four dollars and seventeen cents. The last item beeps. Eighty-four seventeen. She stares at you. Have we... met? Saturday, dinner with eleven friends. One giant bill. Tip, tax, and one guy who only had soup. You hold up your pencil. Done. Everyone owes thirty-one dollars and forty cents. Except the soup guy. He owes nine. He has never loved you more. Monday, at the tire shop, you check five years of receipts... in four minutes. And you find a problem. Somebody's been rounding up. For years. It adds up to sixty thousand dollars. Your boss is thrilled. Then he asks how you did it. What do you tell him? I held a pencil? Then a coworker films you at lunch. Seven digits times seven digits. You beat the calculator every time. By Friday, the video has two million views. The comments? 'Fake.' 'Edited.' 'Please do my taxes.' Upside: a weekend in Las Vegas. Blackjack. You track every card in the shoe. You win. And win... and win. Card counting isn't illegal. But a casino can ask you to leave. Two very large men in suits ask you... very politely. Downside: you do the math on the lottery. The odds of hitting the Powerball jackpot are about one in two hundred ninety-two million. You stop buying tickets. Your mom keeps buying hers. Some things, math can't fix. Then the big one. Wall Street. Trading computers buy and sell in millionths of a second. Speed is money. How much? One company spent hundreds of millions of dollars on a fiber-optic cable from Chicago to New Jersey. The goal? Shave a few thousandths of a second... off each trade. And now there's you. Her name is Claire. She recruits for a trading firm in Manhattan. Sharp blazer. Sharper smile. She saw the video. She invites you up to the trading floor. Forty-third floor. Hundreds of screens. Numbers pour down like rain. Most people see chaos. You see... patterns. Little ones. Everywhere. Claire slides a contract across the table. The salary has more zeros... than your zip code. Want to change your life, Rio? Who wouldn't? Then she tests you. One of the fastest supercomputers in the world is called Frontier, in Tennessee. It can do more than a quintillion calculations every second. That's a one with eighteen zeros. Claire's engineers race you against their best machine. You win. By a hair. Then you need a sandwich. Two... sandwiches. And there's a cost. Your brain is only about two percent of your body weight. But it burns about twenty percent of your energy... just sitting there. Yours isn't just sitting there. It's a race car... with the gas pedal glued down. You're always hungry. A granola bar in every pocket. After a hard problem, your head pounds. And after the biggest ones? Something scarier. The numbers go dark. For about an hour, you can't add two plus two. Like a fuse blowing. One giant problem... then nothing. You'll just pick your problems carefully. Right? But there's a quieter cost too. You've stopped calling people back. People are messy. Numbers aren't. And there's one person you haven't called in four years. Her name is Dr. Bennett. She has a PhD in mathematics. She could have worked anywhere. She chose... seventh grade. Room twelve, Lincoln Middle School. That's where you met her. You were twelve. You were failing. You'd scribble an answer, get it wrong, and crumple the paper. She'd uncrumple it. Every time. Then she'd tap the page and say the same three words. Show your work. Why? Because a wrong answer isn't the enemy. Hiding is. She's seventy-four now. Retired. But every winter break, she runs a free math camp. Room twelve. For kids who hate math. And she still has one strange habit. There's always a yellow pencil tucked behind her right ear. Always. Why? For math emergencies, she says. So the morning before you sign Claire's contract, you drive to Lincoln Middle. Room twelve looks smaller now. The radiator still clanks. Dr. Bennett looks up. She doesn't say hello. She says, Show your work, Rio. What have you been up to? You laugh. And you tell her everything. Then she asks one question. And who are you going to help with all that? You don't have an answer. Not yet. She just smiles... and taps the pencil behind her ear. Outside, the kids take a snack break by the pond. The pond is frozen. Mostly. Your phone rings. It's Claire. Rio, we've got a situation. The market opens at nine thirty. We need your number now. Call it right... and your signing bonus is ten million dollars. You grab your pencil. The numbers start lining up. And then you hear it... A crack. A splash. A scream. The boy in the red hat. One of the camp kids. He chased a hockey puck onto the ice. Now he's in the water. Twenty feet from shore. Dr. Bennett is already dialing nine-one-one. The fire department is minutes away. Does he have minutes? Here's what rescuers teach. Reach or throw... don't go. But there's nothing long enough to reach. Nothing to throw. And cold water is brutal. Experts call it the one-ten-one rule. About one minute of gasping. About ten minutes before your arms and legs stop working. About an hour before the cold knocks you out. He's already used his one. Here's the thing about ice. Experts want at least four inches of clear, solid ice... just to walk on. White, cloudy ice is only about half as strong. This pond has both. Patches everywhere. If you calculate it all... thickness, weight, every crack... you'll know exactly where to crawl. But that's one giant problem. And you only get one. Claire is still on the line. Rio? Are you there? Fifty seconds. Make the call and earn ten million dollars... or hang up and spend your whole brain on that boy. Sorry, Claire. Wrong problem. You hang up and shove the phone in your coat pocket. You get down flat. That spreads your weight. You crawl. One inch. Another. Then the ice cracks under your elbow. That thin white line. Your glove jerks. And the pencil skitters away... into the water. Your head goes quiet. Just you now. Just normal. The boy is crying. I can't hold on! Your phone buzzes. Again. And again. On the shore, Dr. Bennett is shouting. Rio! Rio, use your head! You try. Nothing. Then her voice changes. Steady. Like the first day of school. Rio! Math emergency! Something comes spinning across the ice. Yellow. Bouncing. It stops against your sleeve. Dr. Bennett's pencil. The one from behind her ear. You grab it. And the world... slows down. Every crack lights up like a map. The thick ice runs in a curve. Left, then right. You can see it. But he can't. So you do what she taught you. You show your work. You scratch arrows into the frost as you go. A path anyone could follow. You reach him. Hey, buddy. Listen to me. Kick your legs like you're swimming. Flat. Arms on the ice. He kicks. You pull. He slides out... like a seal. Now roll. Don't stand up. Roll. You roll together, following your own arrows, all the way back to shore. Then... sirens. Paramedics wrap him in a silver blanket. His lips are blue. But he's talking. Is he okay? He's going to be... just fine. The camp kids go wild. Somebody's crying. Maybe... you. Later, you call Claire back. You missed the trade. She's quiet for a long time. Then she says... I saw the news. Is that boy okay? He's okay. Good. Then, softer. Does that math camp take volunteers? Back in Room twelve, you hand Dr. Bennett her pencil. She shakes her head. Keep it. Then she pulls out a new one and tucks it behind her ear. Of course she has a spare. Now you're in Room twelve every Saturday. Kids shout out problems. You answer. Then you show them how. Step by step. Because the answer was never the point. You call people back now. And when a kid crumples up a wrong answer? You uncrumple it. You tap the page. Show your work. So... is any of this real? Partly. Some people really are astonishing at mental math. In 1980, in London, Shakuntala Devi multiplied two thirteen-digit numbers in her head. It took her twenty-eight seconds. In 2004, Daniel Tammet recited pi from memory to more than twenty-two thousand digits. But faster than a computer? No. Not even close. Your nerve signals top out around two hundred seventy miles per hour. A computer chip flips its switches billions of times every second. And the pencil rule? Pure fiction. Still, your brain is amazing. It runs on about twenty watts. Less than a bright light bulb. And it gets to decide which problems are worth solving. So which problem would you pick? But one thing still bugs you. With your own pencils, the math comes fast. With Dr. Bennett's pencil... the answer shows up before you even ask the question. Every time. Same wood. Same graphite... So why is hers different? And why does she always have a spare? What's your take? Let us know below, and suggest the next power for us to try. Hit like, and subscribe to Rio Animation for more fascinating videos!

long.title: What If You Could See In Total Darkness?
long.rel: Rio's 10-year-old daughter Zoe on a scout trip (signature lines: Are you still there? / Right here, kiddo. / I'll always find you back.)
long.rule: Real light blinds Rio completely for ten full minutes, so any flashlight or floodlight in the face takes the power away.
long.plant: Zoe's small purple headlamp with a red-light button (the 'Dad Light'), which she drops in the cave.
long.choice: Wait for the floodlights and keep your fortune safe... or turn off every light and walk into the flood.
long.script: Water is pouring past your knees. Ice cold. And it's... rising. In your arms, your daughter is shivering. You can't see her. You can't see anything. Not because it's dark. Because it's... bright. A floodlight just hit your face. Now the whole world is... a white blur. Somewhere behind you, people are shouting. Rio! Rio, don't move! You don't. One wrong step in this water... and you both go under. Then a tiny voice, right by your ear. Dad? Are you still there? Here's the strange part. Ten seconds ago, in pitch black, you could see every pebble in this cave. Every drop of water. Every crack in the ceiling. Then somebody... turned on a light. But let's go back. Your name is Rio. You're thirty-six. You work nights, stocking shelves at a big-box store outside Louisville. You share custody of a ten-year-old named Zoe. Three months ago, you had a fever for four days. Then you woke up at midnight... and the bedroom was bright. Not lamp bright. Silver bright. Like moonlight on snow. The lights were off. The curtains were closed. And you could read the tiny print... on your pill bottle. How? Here's how normal works. Your eye has two kinds of light sensors. About six million cones for color and detail. And about one hundred twenty million rods for dim light. Walk into a dark room, and your rods need time. About twenty to thirty minutes... to fully wake up. Even then, they need some light. A cat can see in about one sixth of the light you need. But in a sealed cave, with zero light? Even a cat is blind. You? You see... everything. In total darkness. Instantly. But there's a rule. Your eyes are tuned so high... that real light hurts. A candle? Fine. A phone screen? Squinting... A flashlight in your face? You're blind. Completely. For ten full minutes. No exceptions. So what if you could see in total darkness? First, the small stuff. The power goes out in your apartment building. Neighbors stumble around with phone flashlights. You walk down three flights of stairs... carrying groceries. And a cake. Your earring has been missing for a year. You find it under the couch. In the dark. Next to a dime... from 2009. Then the drive home from your shift. Four in the morning. No streetlights. A deer steps onto the road a quarter mile ahead. You see it... before your headlights do. You slow down. It walks away. Fine. Not a story. Except... it is. Drivers in the US hit more than a million deer every year. And about three out of four pedestrian deaths happen after dark. Darkness hides things. But not... from you. At work, your manager needs someone to walk the warehouse when the lights fail. You find a man stuck behind a fallen pallet... before anybody hears him. He shakes your hand for a full minute. Upside: you start stargazing. About eighty percent of North Americans can't see the Milky Way from home. Too much light pollution. You? You lie on the roof and see it every night. Rivers of... stars. Downside: a neighbor flips on a porch light. Ten minutes of blindness. You spend them lying on the roof. Saying whoa. And oh man. A lot. Then a man named Wes shows up at your store. He runs a private security company. Ports. Warehouses. Rail yards. Places that stay dark all night. Somebody posted a video of you finding that man in the warehouse. He watched it... forty times. I don't need cameras, Wes says. I need you. Three hundred thousand dollars a year. Nights only. You'd walk a huge shipping port on the East Coast. And see what the cameras... miss. Do you know what that kind of money means for a single parent? College. A house. A yard for Zoe. One catch. You'd move to Virginia. Next... month. And there's a cost. The power isn't just in the dark. It's in the daylight too. Here's the real science. In bright light, a pigment in your rods called rhodopsin gets bleached. It takes time to rebuild. That's why a dark movie theater feels so black... after a sunny parking lot. Your eyes now run on almost nothing but rods. So daytime isn't just bright. It's painful. You wear wraparound sunglasses at noon. You can't drive in the day. You miss things. Zoe's soccer games are on Saturday mornings. Bright fields. White sky. You've been to two this season. You sat in the car for both. She waved anyway... You could barely see her wave. And there's something else. Every time a light blinds you, the ten minutes feels a little longer. Your eye doctor frowns at the scans. Whatever you are, she says... you're not built for flashes. So be careful. Zoe is ten. She's brave about almost everything. Roller coasters. Spiders. Math tests. But not... the dark. She sleeps with the hallway light on. She checks under the bed twice. And every night, the same little ritual. She whispers, Are you still there? And you whisper back. Right here, kiddo. The dark can't hide you from me. Then she always answers. And I'll always find you back. Last month, you bought her a headlamp. A small purple one, with a little button on the side for red light. Why red? Because your rods are barely sensitive to red. That's why astronomers and pilots use red lights at night. It doesn't wreck your dark vision. For you, it doesn't hurt at all. So now Zoe sleeps with her red light on. And you can still see her, without pain, when you check on her. She calls it the Dad Light. This weekend, her scout troop is going to Mammoth Cave National Park in Kentucky. It's the longest known cave system on Earth. More than four hundred miles of passages, mapped so far. And she asked you to chaperone. Me? Why me? Because, she says, if the lights go out... you won't be scared. Wes calls the night before. Final offer. I need your answer by Monday. And Rio? Protect those eyes. They're worth a fortune. Saturday afternoon. Forty scouts and parents walk into the cave. The air is cool. About fifty-four degrees, all year round. The ranger leads the way with electric lights strung along the trail. Zoe holds your hand. Tight. Then a summer storm rolls in... up top. Thunder. A power line goes down. And the cave lights... die. Forty people. Total darkness. Kids scream. The ranger stays calm. Flashlights click on. Everyone counts off. Thirty-nine. Who's missing? You already... know. Zoe let go of your hand when the lights flickered. She'd dropped her headlamp. She went back to grab it. In the dark, she turned the wrong way. Into a side passage. Down toward the old stream bed. And the storm is sending water into the cave. Parts of the cave can flood. When it rains hard, underground streams can rise fast. Cave water is cold. Fifty-something degrees. Hypothermia starts when your body drops below ninety-five. For a skinny ten-year-old, soaking wet? That can happen in under an hour. Zoe's fear of the dark? It isn't small right now. The ranger radios for a search team. They'll bring floodlights. They're forty minutes away. Forty minutes... How high will the water be? You could see her. Right now. In this dark, you could walk straight to her. But the passage is full of flashlights. Every beam is a wall. Wes's voice in your head. Protect those eyes. Your doctor's voice too. You're not built for flashes. Wait for the floodlights and keep your fortune safe... or turn off every light and walk into the flood. You turn to the group. Please. Everybody. Lights off. They stare at you. Are you crazy? The ranger hesitates. Then she looks at your face. And clicks hers off. One by one, so does everyone else. Total black. And for you... it's sunrise. You run. Down the side passage. Over rocks you can see perfectly. The water is at your ankles. Then your shins. Zoe! Then you see her. Sitting on a ledge, knees to her chest. Right where she got lost. She remembered the rule you taught her. If you're lost, stay put. Stay put, and someone will find you. Dad? Are you still there? Right here, kiddo. You scoop her up. She's shivering. You turn back. The water is at your knees now. Thirty feet to dry rock. And then the search team arrives early. A huge floodlight snaps on at the far end of the tunnel. Straight into your eyes. White. Everything... white. You're blind. Up to your knees in rushing water. Holding your kid. Ten minutes until you can see. Do you have ten minutes? You don't move. One wrong step and you both go under. Then you feel Zoe reach into her jacket. Click. A soft red glow. Her headlamp... She found it after all. She can see now. Just a little. Just enough. And she's terrified. You can feel her heart pounding through her coat. But she talks anyway. Dad, left foot. There's a rock. Okay, step. Now right. Slow. Slow. Step by step, a ten-year-old who's afraid of the dark leads you through it. Thirty feet. Twenty. Ten. Your boots hit dry stone. Hands grab you. Rangers wrap you both in silver blankets. Zoe is cold. But she's laughing. Through chattering teeth. Dad. I found you back. Your eyes are wrecked for a week. Bandages. Dark rooms. Cold soup. And when the bandages come off, something has changed. The silver light is fainter now. Your dark vision is mostly gone. Gone? Mostly. But the daylight... doesn't hurt anymore. Monday, you call Wes. You tell him no. He's quiet for a while. Then he says... I heard what you did. Do you need anything? Yeah. Forty red headlamps. One for every scout. They arrive on Thursday. Saturday morning, you sit in the bleachers at Zoe's soccer game. No sunglasses. Bright white sky. And for the first time all season... you see her wave. That night, you check on her. The red light glows. Are you still there? Right here, kiddo. And I'll always find you back. But something keeps bugging you. In that tunnel, the red light was dim. Way too dim to see a wet rock under rushing water. And yet Zoe called out every single step. Perfectly. Last night you asked her how she did it. She just shrugged. I don't know, Dad. It was weird. The dark looked... kind of silver. So what would you do if you could see in total darkness? Tell us in the comments. And if someone you love is scared of the dark... tell them you'll find them.
