long.title: What If You Never Forgot A Single Face?
long.rel: Mom, who has face blindness (signature lines: I may not know your face. But I'll always know you. / Two notes means home.)
long.rule: The face memory only works in person; on photos or video Rio can't recognize anyone, not even his own mom.
long.plant: Mom's two-note whistle (high, then low) that she teaches to every kid she sits next to on a plane, plus the rule 'stay put and whistle'.
long.choice: Stay on camera and become famous... or walk off live TV to find a girl you can't even see.
long.script: A woman in sunglasses walks past you at the farmers market. Hat. Scarf. New haircut. You smile... Hi again! She stops. Do I... know you? Third grade. You sat behind her for one week. Then her family moved to Ohio. That was twenty-six years ago. At the gas station, a man holds the door. You know him too. A minor-league ball game in 2013. Row K. He spilled nachos... on his shoes. You don't mention the nachos. At the dentist, the new dentist leans over you. Big mask. Bright light. Open... wide. You stare up at his eyes. Wait. Is that... the kid from first grade? The kid who stole your pudding cup... every Tuesday? He freezes. Okay. Yes. That was me. You still remember that? You remember every face. And he's holding a drill near your mouth. So you just say it... You still owe me... eleven puddings. Your name is Rio. You're thirty-three. You work security at one of the busiest airports in the world, in Atlanta. And you have never... ever... forgotten a face. Here's how normal works. Researchers at the University of York tested how many faces people know. The answer? About five thousand on average. Some people knew around one thousand. Some knew around ten thousand. And your brain spots a face fast. In about one hundred seventy milliseconds, part of your brain fires. Face! Pay attention! Even newborn babies prefer to look at face-like patterns. We're built for this. But most of us... still forget. You? Every face you've ever seen. Forever. But there's a rule. It only works in person. Photos? Nothing. Videos? Nothing. On a screen, a face is just a blob of pixels to you. You can't even recognize your own mom... in a picture. So what if you never forgot a single face? Start with work. The TSA screens more than two million people on a typical day nationwide. You check IDs at checkpoint south. A man hands you his license. The name looks fine. But you saw this face... eight months ago. Same lane. Different name. Different birthday. You call your supervisor. He's carrying three fake IDs. Your supervisor stares. How did you... You shrug. I never forget a face. Upside: you're amazing at parties. You greet everybody. Even people from one baby shower in 2017. Downside: they don't remember you. So you seem... a little intense. Then the lost and found. A woman leaves her wallet on a tray. No ID. Just cash and a library card. You picture every face from lane four. Her. Gate twelve. You hand it back... before she notices it's gone. A pilot asks for a selfie. Of course, you can't recognize yourself in it. Then the police call. A shoplifter has been hitting airport stores for months. They show you a video. Useless. Pixels. So they walk you through the food court. Fifteen minutes later? You point. Blue backpack. He sat at this table... three Fridays ago. Then it goes bigger. A clip of you catching the shoplifter goes online. Twelve million views. The comments? 'Human search engine.' 'Can he find my ex?' Then a woman named Tara calls. She produces TV shows in Los Angeles. Her new one is called 'Never Forget.' Live. Prime time. Every week, Rio finds a hidden suspect in a crowd... while America watches. A hundred thousand dollars an episode. Your face on billboards. Think about it, Rio. You'd be the most famous face in America. You laugh. A famous face? When you can't see faces in photos? But you think about it... And there's a cost. You can't forget. Not ever. Every face you've ever seen is stored. And each one comes with a small spark. That little feeling. Oh, I know you. Most people feel it a few times a day. You feel it constantly. A busy airport can move tens of thousands of faces past you every hour. Each one, a tiny tap on the shoulder. Tap. Tap. Tap. By evening, your head throbs. You eat lunch in a supply closet... staring at a blank wall. And some faces you wish you could lose. The driver who hit your bike when you were twelve. The doctor who gave your family bad news. They never... fade. And you've started to wonder. What happens in a really big crowd? Your mom is the opposite of you. Her name is just Mom. She has face blindness. Doctors call it prosopagnosia. It's real. Some research suggests it affects up to about one in fifty people. Mom can look right at you... and not know it's you. At school pickup, she never knew which kid was hers. So she made up a trick. Two whistled notes. High, then low. Like a doorbell. She'd whistle in the parking lot. And you'd whistle back. Wherever you were. That's how she found you. And she taught you something else. If you're ever lost, she said, stay put. Find a mom with kids, or someone in a uniform. And whistle. She'd always say the same thing after. I may not know your face. But I'll always know you. Two notes means home. She's a retired kindergarten teacher now. And she still teaches every kid she meets on a plane the two-note whistle. Every kid. Every flight. In case they ever get lost, she says. You've told her a hundred times. Mom, that's a lot of whistling kids. She just shrugs. Good. This Saturday, she's flying in for your birthday. And this Saturday, Tara is shooting the pilot of 'Never Forget'... live, inside your airport. Saturday morning. Thanksgiving weekend. The airport is packed. Cameras everywhere. Tara wears a headset and a big grin. The challenge is simple. One actor is hidden somewhere in the terminal. You saw him once, in person, last week. Find him in under an hour. A million people are watching... Ten minutes in, you're doing great. Then the speakers crackle. Attention. A child is missing. Six years old. Yellow raincoat. Light-up sneakers. Please contact any airport employee. A man pushes through the crowd. Her dad. He's shaking. He holds up his phone. This is her. Please. You look at the photo. Pixels. A blur. Nothing. How can you find a kid... you can't see? And the clock is ticking. Airports are huge. Kids move fast. Every minute, she could get farther away. Onto a train. Through a door marked 'Employees Only.' Then your head starts to pound. Tap. Tap. Tap. Thousands of faces. Every one a spark. Too many. Your vision swims. Tara grabs your arm. Rio. We're live in thirty seconds. Security will find the kid. You stay with the show. Stay on camera and become famous... or walk off live TV to find a girl you can't even see. You take off your microphone. You hand it to Tara. I'm sorry. Wrong search. You turn to the dad. Did she pass through security this morning? Checkpoint south? He nods. Seven forty. Lane four. You close your eyes. Lane four. Seven forty. You were there... A grandmother with a cane. A teenager with headphones. And a small girl in a yellow raincoat... missing one front tooth. Her. Now you just need to find her. You run. Concourse A. Gate after gate. Faces flood in... Tap. Tap. Tap. Your head feels like it's going to split. Not her. Not her. Not her. Then you see a yellow raincoat. A woman is leading a little girl toward the exit. Is that her? Not her. Different family. So where is she? Then you hear it. A voice from thirty years ago. Stay put... and whistle. You climb up on a bench. You put two fingers in your mouth. And you whistle. High, then low. Like a doorbell. The terminal goes quiet. People stare. You whistle again. And then, from somewhere past Gate nine... two tiny notes. High, then low. You run toward the sound. She's sitting under a row of seats... right where she stopped. Knees up. Raincoat dripping. You see her face... and you know it. Lane four. Seven forty. Missing front tooth. Hi. I'm Rio. Your dad is looking for you. Who taught you that whistle? She sniffles. A nice lady on the plane. She said if I get lost... stay put and whistle. And then someone will find me. Her dad scoops her up. Then a woman with a big purse comes hurrying across the terminal. She doesn't know your face. She never has. But she heard... the whistle. She hugs you hard. I didn't know your face. But I knew those two notes. And the little girl? Last spring, she sat next to your mom on a flight to Denver. Row eighteen. The clip goes viral anyway. Not the show. The bench... and the whistle. Tara calls that night. You cost me a show, she says. Then she laughs. Best five minutes of TV I've ever seen. So no show, Rio. How about a public service ad? Teach every parent the whistle. You say yes... to that one. On your birthday, Mom puts a framed photo on your table. It's you, holding that little girl, on the bench. You can't recognize the faces in it. Neither can she. You both... laugh. Then she whistles. And you whistle back. Two notes means home. So... is any of this real? Some of it, yes. In 2009, researchers Richard Russell, Brad Duchaine and Ken Nakayama described super-recognizers. People with extraordinary face memory. London's Metropolitan Police later used them to spot suspects... in crowds and on camera. Face blindness is real too. The famous neurologist Oliver Sacks had it, and wrote about it. But never forgetting a single face? No. Even super-recognizers make mistakes. And your brain doesn't store faces... like files. It rebuilds them, a little differently each time. The in-person rule? Pure fiction. And here's a strange one. Real super-recognizers often do well with photos too. So what is your brain really remembering... a face, or a person? But one thing still bothers you. That night, you look at the framed photo again. Still a blur. Except... one face. In the background. A man by the window, watching. For the first time ever, you recognize a face in a photo. And you've never seen him in your life. So who is he? Do you buy it? Sound off in the comments, and tell us which ability we should push to the limit next. long.title: What If You Could Think Ten Thoughts At Once?
long.rel: Older brother Isaac, who raised Rio and runs the coffee shop (signature lines: Eyes on me, kid. / Three taps: I'm here.)
long.rule: The ten thoughts only run in silence; the moment Rio speaks out loud, nine shut off for one full hour.
long.plant: The radiator-pipe tap code from childhood: two taps for 'Are you okay?', three taps for 'I'm here.'
long.choice: Stay silent and win twenty million dollars... or say your brother's name out loud.
long.script: Six in the morning. The coffee shop line is out the door. Twelve customers shout twelve orders. You don't write... a single one down. Oat milk latte. Double shot, no foam. Iced chai for the guy who always says please. While your hands pour, part of your brain is learning Spanish. Another is planning your brother's birthday. Another is reading about bridges. Another notices the cash register is about to jam. It jams. The fix? Already ready. Twelve drinks. Perfect. In... ninety seconds. A woman stares at you. How are you doing all that? You just smile. You can't explain. Not out loud. And thought number ten? It's been humming a mattress commercial jingle... since Tuesday. Your name is Rio. You're twenty-nine. You work at your big brother's coffee shop in Portland, Oregon. Upstairs is a co-working space. Laptops. Startup dreams. A lot of cold brew. And you can think ten thoughts... at the exact same time. Here's how normal works. Your brain doesn't really multitask. It switches. Back and forth. And every switch... costs you a little focus. In 1956, psychologist George Miller asked how many things we can hold in mind at once. His famous answer? About seven, plus or minus two. Later research suggests it may be closer to four. In 2010, Jason Watson and David Strayer at the University of Utah tested drivers in a simulator. Driving plus hard mental tasks. Almost everyone got worse. Only about two and a half percent didn't. They called them supertaskers. You? Ten full thoughts. Not switching. All at once... side by side. But there's a rule. The power only works in silence. The second you speak out loud... nine of the ten thoughts shut off. And they don't come back... for one full hour. So what if you could think ten thoughts at once? First, the small stuff. You read ten books in one evening. Skimming? No. Reading. You finish a puzzle while folding laundry... and watching baseball. You win trivia night without a word. Answers on napkins. They call you the Quiet Genius. Upside: you remember every customer's order, name and dog. Downside: you can't talk while you do it. Not even hello. People think you're rude. A first date ends after twenty minutes. She says you seemed... distant. Distant? You were thinking about her ten different ways. Then driving. Ten minds, perfect driver? Nope. You've still only got two eyes. Read a text for five seconds at fifty-five miles per hour? You've just crossed a football field... blind. Ten thoughts can't see the road. So you take the bus. Upstairs, a freelancer can't find a bug in her code. You tap the screen. Line four hundred twelve. Another guy is stuck on a logo. You sketch three. He cries... a little. Your brain has about eighty-six billion neurons. And now ten of you are using them. And then the ideas start. Thread number seven never stops inventing. A cup lid that doesn't leak. A bus app for seniors with giant buttons. You fill notebook after notebook. You post the bus app online for free. A transit office actually uses it. Older riders leave thank-you notes... at the shop. Then somebody else notices. A vice president from one of the biggest tech companies on Earth. Untouched cappuccino. She's read your notebooks. How? We'd like to buy your ideas, she says. All of them. Every idea you have... for the next ten years. Twenty million dollars. Twenty million? Even thought number ten? The jingle? She doesn't laugh. Just one thing... Next Friday, you'll do a live demo for our board. Upstairs. Ten problems, all at once. In total... silence. And there's a cost. Every waking minute, your brain burns energy. As it works, a chemical called adenosine builds up. The more it builds, the sleepier you feel. Caffeine blocks it. That's the whole trick of coffee. And your brain, running ten threads? It piles up fast. By noon, you're exhausted. By three... your hands shake. The FDA says about four hundred milligrams of caffeine a day is generally safe for adults. Roughly four or five cups. You're past that... before lunch. And there's a deeper cost. When you do talk, people only get a sliver of you. One thought out of ten. Your brother noticed first. You're here, he said. But you're not... here. Are you? His name is Isaac. He's eight years older than you. When your dad left, Isaac was sixteen and you were eight. He got a job. He made your lunches. He learned to cut your hair for picture day... badly. Now he runs the coffee shop. 'Isaac's Grind.' Seven days a week. Five in the morning to seven at night. It's behind on rent. He hasn't told you. But one thread read the past-due notice... upside down. Growing up, you shared a tiny bedroom. Bunk beds. Paper-thin walls. Nightmares? You couldn't yell. Mom worked nights. So Isaac made up a code. You'd tap on the radiator pipe that ran up the wall. Two taps meant, Are you okay? Three taps meant, I'm here. Every night for years. Tap tap. Tap tap tap. And whenever your brain starts spinning too fast, Isaac still does the same thing. He snaps his fingers. Hey. Eyes on me, kid. And all ten of you... look up. Thursday night, Isaac closes up. Twenty million, huh? That's great, Rio. Really. He means it. He's also stacking chairs... a little too hard. Then he taps the counter. Three times. I'm here. Okay? Friday. Demo day. The glass conference room. A giant screen. The board, live from California. Ready? Begin. Ten windows. Ten threads. Code. Math. A business plan. It's going perfectly. And then... thread number four catches something. A smell. Smoke. A grease fire in the shop's back kitchen. The alarm screams. The building empties... in seconds. The vice president doesn't move. Rio, the board is watching. Finish. Your phone buzzes. A text from Isaac. 'got the kid out. went back. basement. cant see.' The kid is the sixteen-year-old on the morning shift. Isaac got him out. Then went back for... what? Your threads light up. Thread one maps the building. The basement storeroom. One stairway down. Thread two texts nine-one-one with the exact address and location. Thread three pulls up what firefighters teach. In a fire, you may have as little as two minutes to escape. Smoke kills more people than flames. Near the floor, it might be one hundred degrees. At eye level? Six hundred. Stay low. Get out. Stay out. Thread four hears the sirens. Still blocks away. The basement is full of black smoke. You won't see one inch. The only way to find Isaac? Call his name. And... listen. But the second you speak, nine minds vanish. The demo dies. The deal dies. On the screen, ten windows blink. Waiting... Stay silent and win twenty million dollars... or say your brother's name out loud. You stand up. The vice president's eyes go wide. Rio, if you walk out... You're already gone. You hit the stairs. The smoke is thick and hot. You drop. You crawl. Then you open your mouth. Isaac! And nine thoughts... switch off. Like lights in a hallway. One. By one. By one. Silence. Just you now. One regular, scared brain. You can't see. Your eyes burn. Isaac! Isaac, where are you? Nothing. Just the roar of the alarm. Which way was the storeroom? A second ago, you knew. Now? Gone. Then you hear it. Faint. Metal. Tap tap... Tap tap tap. The water pipe. It runs along the basement ceiling. You reach up. Cold metal. You follow it, hand over hand. Closer. Your fingers hit a door. You test it with the back of your hand. Warm. Not hot. You open it... Isaac is on the floor, low, coughing. One hand taps the pipe with a soup ladle. In his other arm? A cardboard box. Your notebooks. He went back... for your ideas. He can't see you. He can barely breathe. So you grab his face. Hey. Eyes on me. I've got you. You crawl together. Low. Along the pipe. Then a flashlight beam. Firefighters. Big gloves pull you both up... into the gray morning air. Isaac gets oxygen on the curb. Is he okay? He's going to be... just fine. The kid won't let go of his arm. The kitchen is ruined. The rest? Smoke damage. Lots of cleaning. And the deal? The vice president calls that afternoon. Why did you walk out? You tell her. My brother was in there. She's quiet. Then... the board saw you go. One of them wants the bus app. Free. For their own city. No twenty million. But the next morning, people start showing up at the shop. Freelancers. Bus riders. Regulars. They bring mops. Paint. A donation jar... that fills by noon. Somebody makes a sign. 'Isaac's Grind. Smoke, but no mirrors.' It's a terrible pun. Isaac laughs so hard he coughs. You give him the cup lid idea. And all the rest. Not for sale anymore. For the shop. That night, you sit with Isaac on the curb. You don't run ten threads. You don't run nine. You give him one. All of you. Thank you for the notebooks. He shrugs. They're you, kid. I wasn't leaving you in there. Then he taps the curb. Three times. And you tap back... I'm here. But here's the strange part. After an hour, eight of your thoughts came back. Eight. Not nine. Thread number seven never returned. The inventor. And this morning, Isaac wrote something on a napkin. A design for a smoke alarm that taps on pipes. He's never invented anything in his life. And he's humming... a mattress jingle. So what would you do... with ten thoughts at once? Tell us in the comments. And if there's someone who'd tap on the pipes for you... tap back today. Hit like, and subscribe to Rio Animation for more fascinating videos!

long.title: What If You Could Hear Sounds Ten Miles Away?
long.rel: Elderly neighbor Uncle Frank, 87, with two hearing aids (signature line: Listen close, Rio. The land always tells you the truth.)
long.rule: The super-hearing only works while Rio stands perfectly still; any movement snaps it back to normal ears.
long.plant: Uncle Frank's beat-up harmonica and his rule 'three of anything means help'.
long.choice: Finish the test and get the job of a lifetime... or walk into the storm after one old harmonica.
long.script: Rain hammers the soybeans. Lightning splits the sky. You stand perfectly still in a field... holding your breath. Are you scared? Okay. Yes. But mostly, you're... listening. Somewhere past the creek... an old man is trapped. And he's playing a harmonica. Three short notes. Then nothing. Then three more. You can hear it. Barely. Under the rain. Under the thunder... that hits your ears like a slammed car door. Behind you, a man in a soaked gray suit yells. Rio! You've got four minutes left on the test! The government is waiting! You don't answer. You can't. If you move one muscle... the harmonica disappears. But let's go back. Your name is Rio. You're thirty-four. You deliver mail outside a farm town in Nebraska. One stoplight. One diner. Sixty miles of gravel road. You know every dog. And every dog... knows your truck. Then you got an ear infection that wouldn't quit. And one spring morning... the world got loud. Here's normal. A whisper is about thirty decibels. A normal conversation, about sixty. And every ten decibels means ten times more sound energy. Out in the open, sound also fades fast. Every time you double the distance, it drops by about six decibels. That's why your neighbor's voice vanishes across a field. Most people lose a conversation... within a few hundred feet. You? Ten miles. A screen door squeaking in the next town. A cow chewing... three farms over. But there's a rule. The power only works when you're perfectly still. Stand like a statue... and the whole county opens up. Twitch a finger? It snaps shut. Instantly. So what if you could hear sounds ten miles away? First, the funny part. Sound in air travels about eleven hundred feet per second. So a sound from ten miles away takes about forty-eight seconds to reach you. You hear the diner's lunch bell... almost a minute late. You always know the pie is out. You're just never... first in line. Upside: lost dogs. Your neighbor's beagle runs off in a snowstorm. You stand still on her porch. A whimper. Four miles north. Under a hay wagon. He's home... by supper. Downside: you hear everything. Every argument. Every snore. A man three miles away practices the tuba. Is he good? He is not. He practices... every night. Then the farm stuff. Old tractors can top ninety decibels. You hear one rattle wrong... two miles away. A loose bearing. You call the farmer. He shuts it down in time. Next week, there's sweet corn on your truck. Then something bigger. A tornado watch. The sky turns that weird green. The town siren is old. But you stand still on the post office steps... and hear the storm. Low. Heavy. A freight train... with no tracks. You call the sheriff. The siren goes off early. Nobody gets hurt. Ever heard of infrasound? It's sound below about twenty hertz. Too low for most humans to hear. Elephants use rumbles down there to talk across the savanna. Big storms make it too. And now... you hear it. Word spreads. Then a man in a gray suit shows up at the diner. His name is Gus. A government agency. Which one? He doesn't say. He slides a card across the counter. We could use ears like yours, Rio. Embassies. Borders. Ships. A big salary. A badge. A house anywhere you want. One test. Saturday. We park a van eight miles away. You tell us everything you hear. Pass... and you never deliver another letter. Who says no to that? And there's a cost. Inside each of your ears is a snail-shaped organ called the cochlea. It's lined with tiny hair cells. Around fifteen thousand per ear. Sound bends them... and your brain hears. But here's the bad news. In humans, those hair cells don't grow back. Birds can regrow theirs. We can't. Loud noise damages them. For good. Safety experts say long exposure above about eighty-five decibels can cause permanent hearing loss. And your ears? Turned all the way up? Ordinary noise hits you like a rock concert. A dropped pan. A slammed door. Each one... chips something away. You wear foam earplugs to the diner now. And there's a quieter cost. People stop talking near you. They whisper when your truck goes by. Does it help? Not at all. At the gas station, you hear a woman say it. Careful. Rio hears everything. It's not a compliment. His name is Uncle Frank. He's not your uncle. He's not anybody's uncle. He's eighty-seven, and the whole town calls him that. His is the last mailbox on your route. Shaped like a red barn. He used to farm four hundred acres. Now? A garden... and an old storm cellar in the hill behind his house. And he wears two hearing aids. About one in three Americans between sixty-five and seventy-four has some hearing loss. Frank's past that. He jokes about it. Between us, Rio, we've got... one normal pair of ears. Every sundown, he plays a beat-up harmonica on his porch. Badly. He knows three songs. They all sound the same. But you love it. Because he's the only person in town who never lowers his voice around you. He tells you everything. Out loud. On purpose. Years ago, when you got lost hunting, he taught you a rule. Three of anything means help. Three shouts. Three whistles. Three flashes. Remember that. And he always says the same thing when he waves goodbye. Listen close, Rio. The land always tells you the truth. You tell him about the job. He goes quiet. Then three silly notes. Well. Who's gonna bring my mail? Saturday. The test. You stand in a soybean field next to Gus. The van is eight miles away. You stand still. You hear them. The engine ticking. A man unwrapping a sandwich. Tuna. Gus stops smiling. That means he's impressed. Then the sky changes. A thunderstorm builds in the west. Fast. Gus checks his watch. Ten more minutes. Just... ten. Then lightning. Close. The thunder hits you at full power. Thunder near a strike can top one hundred twenty decibels. With your ears turned up? A jet engine... inside your skull. You flinch. The world goes muffled. You stand still again. Slowly, the county comes back. And then, under the storm... three notes. A harmonica. Three short notes. A pause. Three more. Frank. You'd know that harmonica anywhere. Three of anything means help. Where is he? You can't tell. And when you move... it's gone. Gus grabs your shoulder. Rio, they're starting the final round. Is this a dog thing? It's not a dog thing. Sirens wail in the next county. Roads are flooding. You dial nine-one-one. The deputies are swamped. Can Frank wait? You don't know. And every thunderclap... takes a little more of your hearing. Finish the test and get the job of a lifetime... or walk into the storm after one old harmonica. You hand Gus your earpiece. I'm sorry. I'm needed somewhere else. Then you run. To your mail truck. Seven miles of gravel. Rain so thick you can't see the road. Every mile, you stop. Engine off. Breath held. Three notes... closer. You drive. Stop. Listen. Thunder rips the sky. Your ears ring. Then... nothing. Is this it? The strike that takes your hearing for good? Then it comes back. Thinner. But back. Three notes. Up the hill. Behind the house. The storm cellar. The wooden door is shut. A big branch fell across it. Frank went down when the sirens started. And his hearing aids? Dead batteries. He can't hear anyone outside. Not even you. And the cellar is taking in water... You grab the branch. Way too heavy. You pull anyway. It slides. A foot. Another. You yank the door open. Frank is on the top step. Soaked to the knees. A dying flashlight... and a harmonica. He can't hear a word you say. So he grins... and plays three notes. Sorry, Rio. Lost my phone. But I figured you'd be listening. You help him into the truck. Heater blasting. The deputies arrive twenty minutes later. Is he okay? Cold. Grumpy. But okay. In the morning, people show up at Frank's place. Neighbors. The tuba player. The sweet corn farmer. They pump out the cellar. They bring casseroles. Lots of... casseroles. And they talk to you. Out loud. On purpose. One woman says it plainly. You could've had that big job. You heard Frank instead. And Gus? He sends a handwritten letter. 'You failed the test. You passed something bigger.' And your ears? The range shrinks. Ten miles... becomes two. You lost something. But for the first time in months, you sleep without earplugs. That evening, Frank sits on his porch. New hearing aids. A new harmonica. Still... terrible. He plays three notes. Not for help. Just for you. Listen close, Rio. The land always tells you the truth. So... is any of this real? Hearing ten miles away? Not for a human. But sound can travel that far. Thunder can often be heard around ten miles from a storm. That's where the saying comes from. When thunder roars, go indoors. In 1883, the Krakatoa volcano erupted in Indonesia. People heard it about three thousand miles away. And some people really do hear more than most. Daniel Kish, who is blind, gets around by clicking his tongue. He listens to the echoes. Real echolocation. Bats do it too. But the stand-still rule? Pure fiction. And super-hearing would probably hurt more than help. Your ears can already catch a whisper in a quiet room. So here's a question. Is the world too loud... or are we just not listening? But here's the strange part. Ten miles became two. Except... once. Last night, perfectly still, you heard three short notes. Not a harmonica. A whistle. Farther than ten miles. Farther than anyone could hear. So how did you hear it? Someone out there knows the rule too. Three of anything means help. Where do you land on this one? Comment below, and name the power you want to see next. long.title: What If You Only Needed One Meal A Week?
long.rel: grandpa, a farmer
long.rule: Rio must eat his one meal every Sunday before sundown, his energy drains all week like a battery, and if he misses sundown he has about one hour before he switches off.
long.plant: Grandma's old iron dinner bell on the porch, which Grandpa rings every evening at six.
long.choice: Ride to Des Moines and eat on live TV... or wade into that creek on an empty tank.
long.script: Five in the morning. The rooster hasn't even cleared his throat... and you've already fixed the fence on the north pasture. No coffee. No toast. Not even a granola bar. Noon. The whole county breaks for lunch. You keep stacking hay bales. Your stomach doesn't growl. Not once. Hungry? Nope... not even a little. Not all week. At the county fair, a guy waves a funnel cake under your nose. Come on, Rio. Smell that? You smell it. It smells amazing. You just... don't need it. Your fridge holds a jar of pickles, half a bottle of ketchup, and one sticky note. It says 'Sunday.' That's it. That's your whole grocery list. Your name is Rio. You're thirty-one. Last spring, you quit a desk job in Des Moines and moved back to your grandpa's farm. Two hundred acres of corn. One lazy creek. And forty calves who think you're... their mom. And you eat... once a week. Here's how hunger normally works. When your stomach is empty, it releases a hormone called ghrelin. Scientists call it the hunger hormone. It climbs before meals and drops after you eat. Your fat cells send a different signal, called leptin. Leptin says... relax, we have reserves. Most adults need around two thousand calories a day. That's the number printed on nutrition labels across America. Go a full day without food, and your liver burns through most of its stored sugar, called glycogen. Your body switches to burning fat. You get shaky. Grumpy. Hangry? That's real. You? One meal. Seven days. Totally fine. But here's the rule. The meal has to happen every Sunday... before the sun goes down. And your energy drains like a battery. Monday, you're a tractor. By Sunday afternoon? You're running on fumes. Miss sundown, and you get about one hour. Then you just... switch off. Like a phone at one percent. So what if you only needed one meal a week? Upside: time. Americans spend a little over an hour a day eating and drinking. That's about seven hours a week. You get almost all of it back. You use it to fix the barn roof. Then the chicken coop. Then the neighbor's chicken coop. Upside: money. Your grocery run drops to one cart a week. One very, very... full cart. Downside: lunch is social. At the feed co-op, the other farmers eat together at a picnic table. You sit there... with nothing. Not hungry, Rio? Nope. Weird. Yep. Some animals already live like you. A python can go months between meals. The neighbor's kid starts calling you Snake. Do you love it? You do... not. And Sundays? Sundays are intense. You eat for three hours straight. Pot roast. Mashed potatoes. Corn bread. A whole pie. Grandpa just watches, holding his coffee. Where does it all go? Great question. A normal person eats about fourteen thousand calories a week. You eat maybe three thousand. Your doctor ran the math twice. Then a third time... just in case. It doesn't work. And yet... here you are. Upside: harvest. During harvest, farmers often work from sunrise until way past dark. You never stop for a sandwich. You bring the corn in three days early. The whole co-op stares. How? Nobody knows. Downside: your brain. It uses about a fifth of all your body's energy, even though it's only around two percent of your weight. So by Saturday, things get foggy. You put the milk... in the mailbox. Then somebody films you skipping lunch for six days straight. The video title says 'Farmer Eats Once A Week.' Ten million views. Your phone won't stop buzzing. One email stands out. Rita. Marketing boss for a diet company called Slim Sunday. She flies out to the farm in bright white sneakers. She steps right into... yeah. That. Then she smiles anyway. Rio, imagine millions of people eating like you. We'll pay you two million dollars to be our face. Two million? The farm is behind on its loan... by a lot. Grandpa doesn't say a word. He just looks... at the barn. The problem? Nobody else can do what you do. For a normal body, going a week without food can be dangerous. Muscles break down. Heart rhythm can go wrong. Rita's lawyers have a cozy word for that... fine print. Is that honest? Not really. Then the world comes calling. Scientists want your blood. If they could copy your metabolism... food could stretch seven times further. The United Nations estimates hundreds of millions of people don't get enough to eat. You'd be the answer to a global problem. Amazing. And terrifying. Because every test comes back... totally normal. Nobody can explain you. And there's a cost. Remember the battery? The lower it gets, the more your body starts pulling energy from wherever it can. In a normal body, a long fast eventually means breaking down muscle protein for fuel. Yours seems to do the same thing... just faster at the end. How much faster? Nobody can say. By Sunday afternoon, your arms feel like wet rope. Last month, a flat tire made you late. Sundown hit while you were still on the highway. The world went gray at the edges. Your hands went numb. You pulled into a gas station with twelve minutes to spare. You ate four hot dogs off the roller... standing up, shaking. The cashier asked if you were okay. Were you? You weren't sure. That was close. Too close. And there's another cost nobody sees. Every night, Grandpa sets two plates. Every night, you say the same thing. I'm not hungry. Every night, he quietly puts one plate away. Seven nights a week... Grandpa eats alone. Grandpa is eighty-three. The average American farmer is somewhere in their late fifties. Grandpa passed that number a long time ago. He has a bad knee and a worse hat. Every morning, he still limps down to the low barn by the creek to check the calves. On the porch hangs an old iron triangle. A dinner bell. Grandma hung it there in 1962. Every evening at six, Grandpa rings it. Clang, clang, clang. Supper, Rio! And every evening, you yell back from the field. Save me a seat! It's your thing. You've said it since you were... six. One night you finally ask. Why do you still ring it? I'm never hungry. Grandpa taps the bell with one finger. Your grandma bought this because I always forgot to come in. She said a farm isn't the land, Rio. It's the table. Then he goes inside... and sets two plates. Still? Still. Sunday. The big one. Rita's car idles in the driveway at six. A TV crew waits in a hotel ballroom in Des Moines, forty minutes away. Tonight, at sundown, you'll eat your weekly meal live on national TV. Then you sign. Two million dollars. Then... the sky turns a sick shade of green. Rain comes sideways. In twenty minutes, the creek jumps its banks. Where's Grandpa? You already know. The low barn. The calves. You run. Your legs feel like sandbags. Day seven. The tank is almost empty. The barn is half underwater. Grandpa is clinging to the gate. Brown water swirls around his chest. The National Weather Service has a saying. Turn around, don't drown. Just six inches of fast-moving water can knock an adult off their feet. About a foot can carry away most cars. This? This is way more than a foot. And it's cold. Maybe fifty degrees. Water pulls heat from your body about twenty-five times faster than air... at the same temperature. Grandpa doesn't have long. Neither... do you. Your watch says seven ten. Sundown is seven forty-eight. Rita runs up behind you, holding her phone over her head. Rio! The driver is leaving! If you go in there, you'll miss your meal... and the deal. Two choices. Thirty-eight minutes. Ride to Des Moines and eat on live TV... or wade into that creek on an empty tank. Grandpa sees you. He shakes his head. Go, Rio. You'll miss your supper. You step into the water. Then save me a seat. The current slams your knees. Every step costs something you don't have. Ten feet. Twenty. You reach the gate and grab his overalls. He weighs about one hundred seventy pounds. Soaking wet? A lot more. You pull. Inch... by inch. You get him to the fence line. Then the world goes gray. Rain everywhere. No lights. You can't see the house. Which way? You can't even feel your hands. Then... clang, clang, clang. The dinner bell. Somebody is ringing Grandma's bell. You follow the sound. Step. Step. Step. Grandpa leaning on your shoulder. You stumble onto the porch at seven forty. Eight minutes. And holding the bell rope, soaked to the bone, white sneakers ruined... is Rita. She never got in the car. The pot roast? Still warm in Grandpa's gas oven. You eat wrapped in a horse blanket, shaking. Grandpa eats too. And Rita? She takes a plate. By morning, the neighbors show up with sandbags and casseroles. They round up every single calf. Rita calls her boss from the kitchen. Her voice is calm. One meal a week isn't a diet. It's a miracle. You can't sell a miracle. The campaign gets canceled. She stays for breakfast anyway. And that night, Grandpa rings the bell at six. Supper, Rio! You walk in. You sit down. Your plate is empty. You're not hungry. You sit anyway. Seven nights a week... Grandpa doesn't eat alone anymore. But here's what nobody explains. Your blood tests are normal. So where does the energy come from? Last week, your doctor ran one more scan. She stared at it for a long time. Then she asked a strange question. Rio, has anyone in your family ever done this before? Grandpa slowly put down his fork. So what would you do with one meal a week? Tell us your perfect Sunday supper in the comments. And if someone in your life always saves you a seat... go sit in it tonight. Hit like, and subscribe to Rio Animation for more fascinating videos!

long.title: What If You Could Run For 24 Hours Nonstop?
long.rel: dad recovering from surgery
long.rule: Rio never tires while moving, but the moment he stops, all the skipped fatigue hits at once and he collapses into hours of deep sleep.
long.plant: A cheap silver drugstore emergency blanket Dad tucks into Rio's race vest.
long.choice: Run on for the record and the money... or run six miles back for the medic.
long.script: Mile eighty. The sand is so hot it shimmers. Your shadow is the only shade for miles. And your legs? They feel brand new. Up ahead, a runner in a pink cap is lying on the trail. Resting? No. Not... moving. You don't even know her name. Six hours ago, she was trying to beat you. Now her skin is bright red... and dry. No sweat at all. That's bad. Really... bad. Your race radio crackles. It's Malik, your sponsor. Rio, you're eleven minutes ahead of the record. Keep going. Do not stop. Do you hear me? Do not stop. You look at the pink cap. You look at the finish line... twenty miles away. And you know exactly what happens if you stop. But let's go back. Your name is Rio. You're thirty-four. You fix air conditioners in Henderson, Nevada, which in July is basically... job security. Here's how normal running works. Your muscles burn sugar stored as glycogen. Most people carry enough for roughly twenty miles of hard running. That's why marathon runners talk about hitting the wall. Legs turn to cement. Brain turns... to soup. A typical first-time marathoner finishes in about four and a half hours. Then? A nap... and a cheeseburger. You? You can run for twenty-four hours straight. No wall. No cramps. No soup. Your legs never get tired... as long as you keep moving. That's the rule. The second you stop, all the tiredness you skipped arrives at once. Stop after one mile? You yawn. Stop after a hundred? You drop like a sack of flour... and you sleep for hours. No one can wake you. So what if you could run for twenty-four hours nonstop? Upside: your commute. Your boss sends you to a job across town. Traffic on the highway is a parking lot. You leave the van. You arrive... first. Downside: you arrive drenched. The customer asks if it's raining. Raining? In Las Vegas? Upside: errands. The grocery store is two miles away. You jog there, jog back, and the ice cream... is still frozen. Downside: you can't stop at the checkout. You jog in place in line. People stare. A kid jogs with you. His mom? She does... not. And there's a cost. Your legs never tire... but your body still burns fuel. Running costs roughly one hundred calories per mile for an average adult. Run all day? You need... a mountain of food. You eat five breakfasts. Your fridge looks like a bear... lives there. Then you try a real race. The Desert Fire One Hundred. One hundred miles across the Mojave. The finish line is near Death Valley, where the official record high temperature is one hundred thirty-four degrees. That was set in 1913. You don't win. You run past the winner... twice. The race organizers check your chip. Twice. Cheating? Nope. Then everybody notices. A video of you lapping the field goes everywhere. Upside: you're famous. Downside: you're famous. Strangers chase you at the gas station. They can't catch you... but still. Then Malik shows up. He runs marketing for a shoe company called Nonstop. Big smile. Bigger... watch. Rio, you could break the world record. One race. Win it, and we'll pay you a million dollars. A million? Your van needs a new transmission. Your rent just went up. And your dad... Your dad just had heart surgery. Here's the hidden cost. Fatigue isn't just a feeling. It's... a warning light. It tells you to slow down before your body hits its limits. Your warning light is broken. So you have to think about everything. Running in desert heat, a person can lose more than a liter of sweat an hour. Lose enough and your blood gets thicker. Your heart has to work harder. Drink too much plain water, though, and the salt in your blood can drop dangerously low. Doctors call that hyponatremia. You can't feel any of it coming. Your legs feel fine... right up until they don't. Last month, you ran three hours, then stopped for a red light. You woke up on a bus bench... at sunset. Your phone had nineteen missed calls. From who? All from Dad. Dad is sixty-two. He was a mail carrier for thirty years. Walked the same route every day, rain or shine. Then three blocked arteries. A triple bypass. Now the doctors say he has to walk again... slowly. A little farther every day. That's normal for heart surgery recovery. So every evening, Dad stands at the end of the driveway with a cane. He picks a mailbox. One mailbox. He walks to it. He rests... a while. Then he looks back at you and grins. One more mailbox. That's his line. He used to say it on his route when his feet hurt. You walk with him. And it's hard. Not for your legs. For your... patience. Walking is torture when your body wants to fly. You keep checking your phone. Dad notices. He always notices. The night before the race, he hands you something. A folded silver emergency blanket. The cheap kind from the drugstore. You'll be in the desert, Rio. Humor your old man. You stuff it in your race vest. You roll your eyes. He sees that too. Then he pats your cheek. One more mailbox, kid. Race day. Mile eighty. Back to the pink cap. You kneel. You finally stop. And the tiredness hits like a truck. Your knees buckle. Your vision tunnels. You have maybe... a minute before you black out. Think. Red skin. No sweat. Confusion. Those are classic signs of heat stroke. When your core temperature climbs above about one hundred four degrees, your brain and organs start to get hurt. Every minute counts. The air is one hundred eighteen. There's no shade. No cell signal. The last aid station was six miles back. A truck with ice and a medic sits there. The finish line is twenty miles ahead. Malik is still yelling in your ear. Rio, if you stop now, you'll be out for hours. The record is gone. The money is gone. Get up and run. Your hand touches the vest. Something crinkles. The silver blanket. You yank it open. You sit her up and tie it over her like a tent, shiny side up, blocking the sun. It's a tiny patch of shade. It will buy her minutes. Not hours. Then the choice. Run on for the record and the money... or run six miles back for the medic. Your eyelids are getting heavy. Your brain feels like warm syrup. What would Dad do? You know exactly. You stand. And here's the thing about the rule. Once you start moving again... the tiredness waits. So you don't walk. You run. Backward on the trail. Away from the finish. Away from a million dollars. You switch off the radio. Six miles. You run them in about forty minutes. Your heart is pounding. The heat waves bend the hills. At the aid station, the medic is a big guy. Gray beard. He sees your face and grabs the truck keys. You ride back in the truck bed with bags of ice. The runner is still under the silver tent. Still breathing. The medic packs ice around her neck and armpits. Why there? Big blood vessels run close to the skin. Cooling fast is everything with heat stroke. Her eyes flutter open. Rio? Why'd you come back? And then you stop moving. And the whole hundred miles hits you at once. You wake up nine hours later in a hospital in Las Vegas. The runner in the pink cap is in the next bed. She's going to be fine. The doctors say the shade and the fast cooling made a huge difference. And sitting in the chair by your bed, with his cane across his knees... is Dad. He drove four hours. His doctor is not thrilled. Did you win? No, Dad. I quit at mile eighty. He nods slowly. Good. You ran the right direction. Malik shows up that afternoon. You expect him to tear up the contract. Instead, he puts a box on the table. Running shoes. And a note. 'No deal. Just shoes. You earned these.' The video of you running backward goes everywhere. People don't care about the record. They care about the guy who turned around. And that evening, back home, Dad stands at the end of the driveway. He picks a mailbox. You walk beside him. Slowly. You don't check your phone. Not once. One more mailbox? One more mailbox. So... is any of this real? Partly. In 2004, scientists Dennis Bramble and Daniel Lieberman published a famous paper arguing that humans evolved to be endurance runners. Some groups of hunters have tracked animals for hours in the heat until the animals overheat. Humans sweat through millions of sweat glands, which helps us dump heat while running. Few animals can do that so well. And some people push it wildly far. Ultrarunner Dean Karnazes once ran about three hundred fifty miles... without stopping to sleep. The best runners in twenty-four hour races cover close to two hundred miles. But zero fatigue? Impossible. Fatigue protects your heart, your muscles, and your brain. Every real runner who goes that far pays for it. So here's the question. Would you even want to lose the warning light? But wait. Remember those nine hours you slept? The nurses say your legs never stopped moving. Left. Right. Left. Right. Like you were still running. Dad watched the whole time. And just before you woke up... you said one word in your sleep. A place. A place you've never been. Where were you going? Could you handle it? Tell us in the comments, and tell us what we should crank up next. Hit like, and subscribe to Rio Animation for more fascinating videos!

long.title: What If Time Froze Every Time You Blinked?
long.rel: best friend
long.rule: Each blink freezes time for three seconds in which Rio can move himself but cannot move or change anything he touches.
long.plant: Avery's two hand squeezes from the childhood high dive, meaning 'trust me, jump.'
long.choice: Get back in the box... or step out where everyone can see, and save Avery.
long.script: Your coworker trips. Her coffee flies off the tray. You blink... and the coffee stops. In midair. A brown blob, hanging there like a frozen jellyfish. The whole office is silent. No printer. No air conditioning. Nobody breathing. Wait... what? You stand up. You walk around the coffee. You check it from the left. Then from the right. Then you step one foot to the left. Time starts again. Splash. Right where you used to... be. Your coworker gasps. How are you not soaked? You shrug. Lucky... I guess. At lunch, your buddy challenges you to rock paper scissors. You blink. His hand is frozen halfway into a fist. You lean in. You study it. Rock? Definitely... rock. You throw paper. Twenty-two wins in a row. He wants a rematch. Will he win? He'll lose that... too. Your name is Rio. You're twenty-nine. You work tech crew at the Grand Ellery, a hundred-year-old theater in downtown Pittsburgh. You run lights. You fix ropes. You sweep up glitter... so much glitter. And every time you blink, the world stops. Here's what a normal blink looks like. It lasts somewhere between a tenth and four tenths of a second. Most adults blink around fifteen to twenty times a minute. Put it all together, and your eyes are closed for a surprising chunk of your waking day. Why don't you notice? Your brain... covers for you. During a blink, it turns down your vision, so the world doesn't flicker like a broken light bulb. You? You don't miss anything. Every blink freezes time for exactly three seconds. Your three seconds. Everyone else? They get... zero. But here's the rule. In frozen time, you can move... but nothing you touch will budge. Doors? Cups? People? Nope. It's like the whole world is welded in place. You can look. You can walk. You can think. But change a thing? You can't. So what if time froze every time you blinked? Upside: you're never late. Well... you're still late. But you always have three seconds to think of an excuse. Upside: you never lose a game of catch. You see where the ball is going. You walk there. You wait... and catch it. Downside: crowds. Picture walking through a packed train station. Every blink, you're surrounded by statues. Mouths open. Sneezes hanging in the air. Have you ever seen a frozen sneeze? You don't want to. Upside: work. Up in the fly loft, you blink, and you can check every rope... before anything moves. Your boss thinks you're a genius. Are you? Not exactly. Downside: screens. When people stare at screens, they blink less. Some studies have found their blink rate drops a lot. That helps you. You want normal time? Watch a movie. Want frozen time? Blink on purpose. You learn to control it like breathing. Mostly? Mostly. Then comes the cost. Do the math. Fifteen blinks a minute. Three seconds each. That's about forty-five seconds of extra time... every single minute. Over a day, that adds up to hours. Hours that only you live through. Your coworkers live one day. You live closer to... a day and a half. Upside: more life. Downside: more aging. Your body doesn't freeze. Your heart keeps beating. Your cells keep wearing out. You're twenty-nine. But your body? It's quietly... racing ahead. You've started finding gray hairs. The barber asks if work is stressful. Kind of? There's another cost. Blinking isn't just a reset button. Every blink spreads a thin layer of tears across your eyes. It keeps them wet. It washes away dust. So when you try not to blink, to stay in normal time, your eyes start to burn. Red. Gritty. Like... sand. You carry eye drops everywhere. You have three bottles in your hoodie right now. And then there's the quiet. Three seconds of total silence, fifteen times a minute. No voices. No music. You start to feel very... alone. Then you meet Cole. Cole is a stage magician. Slick hair. Sharp suit. The kind of guy who shuffles cards... while he talks to you. His new show is opening at the Grand Ellery. One night, a stagehand drops a mirror. You blink. You step around. You walk to the far side of the stage. Cole sees it. To him, you just... teleported. Later, he corners you by the soda machine. Rio, I don't know what you are. But I know what you could be. Partner with me. Vanishing acts. Teleporting acts. We'd be the biggest show in Vegas. A seven-figure tour. Think about it. You think about it. You think about it a lot. But the person you really think about is Avery. Avery is the stage manager at the Grand Ellery. She's also your best friend since fourth grade. Same street. Same bus stop. Same terrible taste in movies. Who else would watch them? Nobody. She wears a headset like a crown. long.title: What If You Could Never Feel Fear?
long.rel: younger brother
long.rule: Rio feels no fear and also cannot recognize fear on other people's faces, so he must be told when someone is scared.
long.plant: Bean's habit of counting seconds between lightning and thunder (five seconds per mile).
long.choice: Tag the summit for a million dollars... or turn around in the lightning for your brother.
long.script: Thunder cracks so close the rocks hum. You're on a knife-edge ridge, fourteen thousand feet up in Colorado. On your left, a drop of a thousand feet. On your right... about the same. A camera drone buzzes over your shoulder. Two million people are watching you live. The summit is maybe three hundred feet away. Your earpiece crackles. It's the producer. Rio, keep climbing! This is the shot! Then your radio clicks. A different voice. Small. Shaky. It's your little brother. Rio? I'm stuck. I can't... I can't move. Below you, the clouds turn black. Your heart rate? Calm. Steady. Totally normal. Your palms? Bone dry. Your stomach? Fine. Anyone else on this ridge would be shaking. You? You feel... nothing. And that's the problem. But let's go back. Your name is Rio. You're twenty-seven. You drive a delivery truck in Boulder, Colorado. You have a little brother named Boone. Everybody calls him Bean. He's nineteen. And you have never, ever been afraid. Here's how fear normally works. Deep in your brain sit two small clumps of neurons called the amygdala. Each one is roughly the size and shape of an almond. When you see a snake, or a cliff edge, or a car swerving at you, the amygdala sounds the alarm. Fast. Often before you even know what you saw. Your adrenal glands, sitting on top of your kidneys, pump out adrenaline. Your heart pounds. Your breathing speeds up. Your muscles get ready to run or fight. Scientists call it fight or flight. You? Your alarm is gone. Turned down? No. Gone. And here's the rule. You can't feel fear. But you can't see it either. A terrified face looks... blank to you. Like a mask. When someone is scared, you have to be told. So what if you could never feel fear? Upside: public speaking. Lots of people say they're more nervous about giving a speech than almost anything. You? You give a wedding toast at your cousin's wedding. Forty minutes. No notes. Did anybody ask for forty minutes? Nobody... asked. Upside: spiders. A big hairy one lands on your desk. You pick it up. You put it outside. You name it... Gary. Downside: horror movies. Your date screams. You yawn. Your date does not call back. Upside: work. A dog charges your delivery truck. You just... wait. Calm. The dog stops. Sniffs your hand. Friends now? Friends. Downside: you also don't flinch when you should. You step off a curb. A bus misses you by two feet. Did you even notice? Barely. Then somebody posts a video of you walking a narrow ledge on a hiking trail like it's a sidewalk. It goes viral. Upside: you're famous. Downside: everyone wants you to do something dumber. And there's a cost. Fear isn't just a bad feeling. It's information. It's your brain asking... are you sure about this? Without it, every danger has to go through the slow part of your brain. Thinking. Math. You have to reason your way to being careful. And reasoning takes time. Here's another cost. You can't read fear on faces. So you miss stuff. A lot of stuff. At the grocery store, a kid gets lost. Everyone sees his face crumple. You? You see a kid... standing there. Your coworkers think you don't care. Your ex said you never got worried about her. You did. You just didn't feel it. Is there a difference? You're not sure. Then you meet Professor Lane. She teaches neuroscience at the university. She runs you through a brain scanner. She shows you photos of scared faces. Your amygdala barely flickers. She takes off her glasses. Rio, fear is how humans stay alive. You're missing the brakes. Be careful. You laugh. What's the worst that could happen? That's your line. You say it all the time. Professor Lane does not laugh. Now, Bean. Bean is the opposite of you. He's scared of everything. Heights. Thunder. Escalators? Honestly... yes. When you were kids and a storm rolled in, Bean would hide under the table and count. Flash... one, two, three, four, five... boom. He learned it from a park ranger. Sound travels about a mile every five seconds. So you count the seconds between the lightning and the thunder, then divide by five. That's how many miles away the storm is. Bean still does it. Every storm. Out loud. It drives you crazy. He says it makes him feel better. Like the storm is just a number. Then the call comes. An extreme sports channel. They want a live show called 'Zero Fear.' One episode. You climb a famous ridge to a fourteen-thousand-foot summit. Live. No ropes. If the ratings are big, there's a three-year contract. A million-dollar deal. The producer is thrilled. Bean? Not so much. He shows up at your apartment. Please don't. You don't even know when to be scared. You shrug. What's the worst that could happen? Bean doesn't answer. He just looks at the floor. And you can't read his face at all. On climb day, Bean comes anyway. He says somebody has to be scared for both of you. Back to the ridge. Back to the radio. Back to Bean. He's about half a mile below you, on a narrow ledge. He slipped on wet rock. His ankle might be twisted. He's frozen. Literally frozen. How cold is it? Up here, the temperature drops about three to five degrees for every thousand feet you climb. It's under forty degrees. The wind makes it feel colder. Colorado mountains are famous for afternoon thunderstorms in summer. That's why hikers try to be off the summit by noon. It's one in the afternoon. You look at the sky. A flash. Then you hear Bean on the radio. Small voice. One... two... three... four... five... six... boom. Six seconds. That's barely more than a mile. The National Weather Service says if you can hear thunder, you're close enough to be struck. Lightning can hit about ten miles from a storm. And you're the tallest thing on this ridge. Your brain doesn't scream. It just does the math. Calmly. The summit is three hundred feet away. Bean is half a mile down. The producer is yelling. Rio! Two million viewers! You're almost there! Tag the summit and you get the contract! Then Bean again. I'm okay. Just go. Finish it. Is he okay? You check the drone feed on your phone. There's his face. Pale. Wet. And to you... blank. You can't tell. You honestly can't tell. Here's where the rule bites. Anyone else would feel it. That twist in the gut. That voice saying go to him. You have nothing. No feeling to follow. Only facts. So the choice is simple. And brutal. Tag the summit for a million dollars... or turn around in the lightning for your brother. You close your eyes. And for the first time ever, you say your line... and you actually answer it. What's the worst that could happen? Bean gets hit. Bean gets hypothermia. Bean falls. You open your eyes. That's enough. You switch off the earpiece. Then you turn around. And here's the upside of no fear. You don't freeze. Your hands don't shake. You climb down wet rock like it's a staircase. Fast... but careful. Flash. You count. One... two... three... four... boom. Closer. Under a mile. You find Bean wedged against the rock. His teeth are chattering. You can't read his face. So you do the next best thing. You ask. Bean. On a scale of one to ten, how scared are you? Eleven. Okay. Then I'll be the calm one. You be the scared one. Deal? He nods. You get him low. Away from the ridge. Down into a gully. You walk him, step by step, toward the trees. Lightning safety is clear on this. A high, exposed ridge is the worst place to be. Going lower helps. Forty minutes later, you reach the forest. Then the trailhead. Then your truck. You blast the heater. Bean's lips go from blue to pink. Outside, the storm slams the mountain. And you start to shake. Not from fear. From cold. From adrenaline. From something you don't have a word for. The show gets canceled. The producer calls you a coward on social media. That lasts about a day. Because somebody saved the drone footage. Two million people watched a guy turn his back on the summit... and climb down for his little brother. The comments explode. 'Best ending ever.' Professor Lane emails you. Just one line. 'You found the brakes.' A week later, Bean comes over. He brings a scanned photo from the trailhead. You and him, soaking wet, laughing. Rio, I always thought you didn't care if I got scared. long.title: What If You Aged Backward Starting Today?
long.rel: grandma and Rio's own daughter
long.rule: Every year that passes, Rio's body gets two years younger while his memories and mind stay, with no pause, so he has about eighteen years.

long.script: You roll out of bed. Your back doesn't crack. Weird... right? You take the stairs two at a time. Your left knee doesn't click. Weirder... much weirder. At breakfast, you reach for your reading glasses to check the cereal box. You don't need them. You can read the tiny print just fine. Riboflavin? Who knew? At the diner, the waitress squints at you. Can I see your ID, hon? You laugh. Your ID? You're thirty-six. Then you look in the bathroom mirror. The gray patch over your ear is... darker. And that bald spot from three years ago? Your hairline just... filed a return. Your name is Rio. You run the only hardware store in Maple Hollow, a small town in Vermont. Population, a little over two thousand. Everybody knows everybody. Secrets? Not really... a thing. And starting today... you're aging backward. Here's how aging normally works. Your body is made of trillions of cells. Many of them keep dividing to replace old ones. A red blood cell lives about four months. Then your body makes a new one. Your chromosomes have little caps on the ends, called telomeres. Every time a cell divides, those caps tend to get a bit shorter. Over decades, your body slowly loses its edge. Muscles shrink. Eyes stiffen. Hair grays. Most people start needing reading glasses somewhere in their forties. The average American now lives to a little under eighty. Forward. Always... forward. You? You're running the tape in reverse. Here's the rule. Every year that passes... your body gets two years younger. Not one. Two. Your memories stay. Your mind stays. But there's no pause button. No rewind button. Do the math. Thirty-six divided by two. Eighteen years. That's it. Eighteen years... and then what? So what if you aged backward starting today? Upside: your back. That ache you got from lifting paint cans? Gone... by spring. Upside: energy. Year two, your body is thirty-two. You fix the church roof on a Saturday. Then the library roof on Sunday. Downside: nobody believes your age. At the bank, the teller thinks your driver's license is fake. At the doctor? The nurse just stares at your chart... then at you... then at your chart. Year four. Your body is twenty-eight. People think you're your daughter's big brother. Upside: you feel amazing. Downside: the jokes. Somebody puts a sign on your store window. 'Fountain of Youth Sold Here.' You sell three hundred plastic water bottles that week. As a joke. Mostly... a joke. Then the news finds you. A local station. Then a national one. Then scientists. Nature already has a real creature that sort of does this. A tiny jellyfish called Turritopsis dohrnii. When it's stressed or injured, it can turn back into an earlier life stage... and start over. People call it the immortal jellyfish. A doctor from a big research lab in Boston drives up in a rental car. She takes blood. She takes skin. She takes a lot... of notes. Rio, if we can figure out how your cells do this... it could change medicine forever. Amazing. And terrifying. Because the clock keeps ticking. And there's a cost. Year six. Your body is twenty-four. And something feels off. You make bad choices. Fast ones. You buy a motorcycle... on a Tuesday. On a whim. Here's why. The front part of your brain, the prefrontal cortex, handles planning and self-control. In most people, it keeps maturing into their mid-twenties. Yours is going the other way. Your memories are forty-something. Your brakes? Getting younger every year. And there's another cost. It's waiting down the road. Kids grow about two inches a year. Once your body drops below eighteen... you run that film backward. Twice as fast. Your boots? Too big. Your coat? It swallows you. And the hardest cost of all... you're slowly disappearing from the life you built. Now, the two people who matter most. Nana Rose is your grandmother. She's eighty-two when this starts. She raised you after your parents passed. Now she helps raise your daughter. Nana Rose has a pickup truck from 1979, stick shift, painted the color of tomato soup. When you were twelve, she taught you to drive it in the back field. Your legs were too short to reach the clutch. So she taped a block of wood to the pedal. She called it your booster shoe. That block is still under the driver's seat. Your daughter is Jade. She's seven. Gap teeth. Rainbow socks. Very strong opinions about pancakes. Every night, you tuck her in. And every night, she asks the same thing. Will you still be my dad when you're little? And every night, you say the same three words. Still your dad. Then you tap her nose. Once. Years fly. Year eight. Your body is twenty. Jade is fifteen. You pick her up from school, and her friends ask if you're her boyfriend. She wants to vanish. You? Kind of... same. Year ten. Your body is sixteen. Jade is seventeen. She's taller than you now. She drives you. Nana Rose is ninety-two. Her lungs are tired. She uses an oxygen machine at night. It plugs into the wall. Year twelve. Your body is twelve. Jade is nineteen. She's studying to be a nurse at the state college an hour away. And you? You can't run the store anymore. Customers ask to speak to your dad. You are the dad. How do you explain that? You can't. Then the lab calls. They've found something. An experimental program. It might slow you down. Maybe even stop the clock. But you'd have to live in Boston. Years of tests. No promises. A car will pick you up on Friday night. One car. One spot. Miss it... and it goes to someone else. Friday. Six at night. The sky turns gray. Then white. By seven, the freezing rain starts. Ice storms are brutal in New England. Ice coats every power line. Branches snap like gunshots. At seven thirty, the whole town goes dark. Your phone buzzes. Jade. She's home for the weekend. Dad, Nana's machine stopped. The power's out at her house. Her backup tank is low. Nana Rose's farmhouse? Four miles out... on Ridge Road. The fire station on Main Street has a generator. It's the town warming center tonight. You have to get her there. Normal oxygen in the air is about twenty-one percent. Nana Rose's lungs can't pull enough from that anymore. Her backup tank? Maybe an hour left. Maybe less. It's dark. It's icy. And it's getting cold inside that house. And you? You're twelve. Four foot ten. About eighty-five pounds. Your young body is quick. Your lungs are strong. You could run four miles. But carry a grown woman? Drive a truck? Not with legs this short. Then the headlights. A black car pulls up outside your house. Seven forty. Early... because of the storm. The driver rolls down the window. Mr. Rio? We need to go. The roads are getting bad. Your bag is by the door. Your whole future... is in that car. More years. Maybe a lot more. Here's the choice. Chase more time in that car... or spend the time you have in the storm. You hear Nana Rose's voice in your head. She's said it your whole life. Nobody gets more time, Rio. You just get to choose what to do with it. You look at the car. You look at the dark road. You shut the door... and you run. The ice crunches under your sneakers. Every step slides. Your breath turns to smoke. Four miles. A grown-up might jog that in forty minutes on a dry road. You do it in thirty-five... on ice. When you burst through the farmhouse door, Jade is kneeling by Nana Rose. Nana is pale. Her lips are tinged blue. The backup tank gauge is near empty. Jade's eyes are wide. Dad, I can't carry her and drive. The truck is a stick shift. I don't know how. You do. You've known since you were twelve. You're twelve again. You yank open the driver's door of the old red pickup. You reach under the seat. There it is. The block of wood. Still wrapped in old silver tape. Your booster shoe. You tape it to the clutch with shaking hands. Jade lifts Nana Rose into the cab. You turn the key. The engine coughs... then roars. You drive like Nana taught you. Slow. Low gear. No hard brakes on ice. Twenty miles an hour. Fifteen on the curves. Jade holds Nana's hand. She keeps the last of the oxygen flowing. You glance over. Nana's eyes are half open. shorts.title: What If You Never Blinked Again?

shorts.title: What If You Never Felt Hungry Again?
shorts.topic: Ghrelin and leptin control hunger
shorts.script: Most people believe hunger is just an empty stomach complaining. Today, you get to test that. Your name is Rio, and this morning your hunger simply... switched off for good. shorts.title: What If You Could See Ultraviolet Light?

shorts.title: What If You Woke Up With A New Accent?
shorts.topic: Foreign accent syndrome and stroke warning signs
shorts.script: You're in a hospital bed, and your mom is crying, because you just said hello in a perfect Scottish accent. You're Rio. You've never been to Scotland. Let's rewind. Yesterday, during basketball, your words suddenly came out slurred, and your teammate Mia called nine one one right away. Doctors found... a small stroke. You recovered fast, but your voice came back... different. Is that real? Yes. It's called foreign accent syndrome, first described by a doctor back in 1907, and it's extremely rare. Damage to the parts of the brain that control speech changes the rhythm, the vowels and the melody of how you talk, so listeners hear an accent. You didn't learn anything new. And Mia did exactly the right thing. Sudden slurred speech can be a warning sign of stroke, so call emergency services immediately. Could you spot those signs in a friend? shorts.title: What If You Grew Two Inches Overnight?
shorts.topic: Why you're taller in the morning
shorts.script: Rio, why are you ducking under the doorway? You're Rio, and your sister Kayla is staring at you. Wait. Stand against the wall. Hold still. That pencil mark is from last night, and you're two inches above it. Mom is going to freak out. Your jeans are floating above your ankles, dude. Hmm. I read about this. Here's the thing. Everyone is a little taller in the morning. While you sleep lying down, the soft discs between the bones of your spine soak up fluid and spread out. During the day, gravity squeezes them back down. That's usually only about a centimeter, though. Two inches? That's astronaut level. In space, with no gravity pressing down, astronauts can grow about two inches... and shrink back when they come home. So either you went to space last night... or I'm calling Mom. How tall are you first thing in the morning? Subscribe to Rio Animation for more fascinating videos!

shorts.title: What If You Blushed Every Time You Lied?
shorts.topic: Why we blush and why it doesn't prove lying
shorts.script: Your teacher asks who finished the homework, and you raise your hand even though you didn't. Your face instantly turns tomato red. You're Rio, and since this morning, every lie makes you blush. I love your haircut, Grant... red. I'm almost there... red. Within a day, nobody believes a word you say. Why does this hurt so much? Because real blushing doesn't only happen when people lie. When you feel embarrassed or put on the spot, your body releases adrenaline, the blood vessels in your face widen, and warm blood rushes into your cheeks. Charles Darwin called blushing the most peculiar and the most human of all expressions. So here's a lesson you can use today. A red face, a shaky voice or looking away does not prove someone is lying. Nervous, honest people do all three. Judge the facts, not the face. Send this to someone who blushes at everything. shorts.title: What If You Could Taste With Your Fingers?
shorts.topic: How taste works across animals
shorts.script: You touch a doorknob, and your mouth fills with the taste of old pennies. Your name is Rio, and your fingertips can taste. There's one rule. The moment you lick your fingers, the power is gone forever. At first, it's incredible... you taste a strawberry just by picking it. You know the soup is too salty before you grab a spoon. Is this so strange? Not in nature. Flies taste with their feet, which is why they walk all over your food. And catfish have taste buds covering their bodies, from whiskers to tail. You have somewhere between two thousand and ten thousand, mostly on your tongue, and the taste cells inside them replace themselves every couple of weeks. Then Sunday comes. Grandma sets down a plate of her famous fried chicken. You grab a drumstick. Your fingers drip with flavor... and without thinking, you lick them. Would you have licked them too?
